1	<!-- What is established about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as it stands now, grouped by area: each entry the fact, its source and its test. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `FACTS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. -->
2	
3	# Facts on record
4	
5	## Execution model
6	
7	- F-7 **Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases, and only the compiled path runs the static type checker.** Walk switches the checker off, and no switch turns it on. So walk checks no static types of expressions: an ill-typed expression shows only when it runs, as a failed dispatch or as another run-time error, such as F-239's refusal of an `if` on a value that is not a `Boolean`. At load, walk refuses some ill-formed declarations: the `fortress-repo` skill's `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists them, with their evidence in F-29 (`comprises` clauses), F-142 (the Meet Rule for Functional Methods) and F-145 (uncovered abstract methods and `override`). The phases and where the two paths part: the skill's "How a program runs". Detail: `explorations/repo-internals.md`, "The two worlds".
8	- F-9 **`fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's library, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, so it is no oracle for walk programs.** `Shell.java` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` for the command (row 69). P-12 has walk run the checker on its own programs after the switch-over, and walk cannot do so as it stands: it runs with type checking and the Scala checker off, the Java checker is gone (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:228-229`), and it has no case for the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, by reading (row 833).
9	- F-11 **The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main representational cost of microGPT-shaped array code.** So a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (the `fortress-repo` skill, "The compiled runtime"). In Java models of microGPT's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`. No such kernel compiles yet: the compiler prelude has no array type (row 305), and the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (P-37). In a hot compiled loop, escape analysis removes the temporary boxes, and one box per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration stays (F-301), as long as C2's inline depth reaches each box's constructor chain (F-302). Detail: `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4; `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` section 4.
10	- F-12 **On the compiled path, the scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` ran in 0.74 s in one session's measurement; the loop still pays for its generator, for boxing and for a transaction check at each use of its accumulator.** `bench1t` is `for i <- seq(1#20000000) do acc := acc 0.9999999 + 0.0000001 end` on a `var acc: RR64`, with both literals written in the loop. The time is the median of three loop-only runs at one thread (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Times taken in different sessions differ on this machine, so compare only times from one session. What the loop does, read in its bytecode (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 5): the `seq` loop becomes the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, which runs the iterations in order by a recursive split over boxed indices, with a closure call per element; each value is boxed (F-11); and the accumulator is a volatile cell whose read and write each first call `BaseTask.inATransaction`, as for every mutable local (F-40, what a size costs at run time, whose sized loop pays the same check). Within the boxing and the cell, the report counts four allocations per iteration, an interface call to the native wrapper and the casts, the part that unboxed doubles and `double[]` would attack. No share of the 0.74 s is measured.
11	- F-17 **The bytecode cache can come up empty after a library order that reports exit 0.** Running the same commands again, one at a time, made the jars. The cause is not known. Check the five jars before a compiled run (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`, "The library order"). Detail: `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 1.
12	- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled runtime" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becomes `LFRR64;` in `Box⟦FRR64⟧`, and `[D` is no class name, so stamping alone keeps every number boxed (F-11). The team left two separate traces for unboxing. The plan in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java` lists what to unbox: a primitive, a singleton object, unboxed fields, and a `comprises` clause whose types are unboxable; it says nothing of the loader or of instantiations. The loader has an empty "expando" stub (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`). A loader that stamps an `RR64` instance with a `double[]` field, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), does not exist and is unmeasured. Walk instantiates generics in its own evaluator, not by classes. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 1; `coordinator/array-design.md` section 2 (probe 1); `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 3, way A4.
13	- F-19 **By the specification, the iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments of a call or an operator may run in parallel, and a program must assume that they do.** A `for` loop is sequential only if every generator is, as `seq(g)` or `sequential(g)` makes it. An implementation may also run them one after another (`evaluation/parallelism.tex:88-90`), so a program cannot count on parallel runs either. For the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator, each path starts a task only where it judges it worth it: walk by `TupleTask.worthSpawning`, which also governs a call's arguments, and the code generator by `ParallelismAnalyzer`. Compiled, the arguments of a function call and of a dotted method call fork where the analyzer marked the argument tuple (`CodeGen.evalArg`; joins: F-350); it counts no call in the prelude's files (row 982) or of a function declared later in the file (row 987). A `for` loop over a range without `seq` runs by splitting the range into `do … also do … end` blocks. Under walk, every such block is a task, and walk's library splits a `ZZ32` range into chunks of at most 16 elements (F-350), and a range with a stride down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1498-1585`). Compiled, the first block runs in place, and each other block forks only where `BaseTask.forkIfProfitable` judges it worth it, as tuple elements do; the compiler prelude's `parloop` splits down to `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK` elements, 1 by default. `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the pool of worker threads (the `fortress-repo` skill, "Parallelism and mutable state"). By grep, no program under `explorations/`, the model programs and the probes, writes `spawn`, which starts an explicit thread, or an `also do` block, so their parallelism comes only from loops, tuples and arguments. The revival's tests under `ProjectFortress/` write both. Source: `Specification/basic/expressions/for.tex:28-32`, `tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:58-59`, `evaluation/parallelism.tex:50-80`.
14	- F-20 **Sizes, the `nat` and `int` static parameters, are values at run time; they check shapes, and no optimization uses them (F-40, what a size costs at run time).** The compiled checker checks them (F-67), and a sized program loads and runs compiled (F-129). Under walk, `Vector` and `Matrix` take their sizes from an array built at run time: `f[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\])` takes `s` from `array[\RR64\](3)`, and overloads on `Vector` and `Matrix` dispatch by rank (row 214). The array-type syntax `T[n]` with a `nat` parameter does not unify with such an array, "Cannot unify … with ArrayType", where `T[3]` with a literal size does (row 23). Walk matches sizes at dispatch. A mismatch, such as a `DOT`, the library's inner product, of a 2×3 matrix by a 2×3 matrix, whose inner sizes differ, is a `ProgramError`, "Failed to find any matching overload", that no `catch` takes (row 254). Source: `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:96`.
15	- F-21 **The February 2011 Working Draft's bare `Nothing`, one object for every `T`, is accepted on neither path: the grammar refuses its `excludes` clause, and without that clause `T` is undefined.** The declaration is `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:40`). Both paths stop at a syntax error at `excludes`, since an object has no `excludes` clause (measured: `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, E4). Without that clause, both report `T is undefined` at the `T` of the `extends` clause: a `where` clause on an object binds no type variable of its `extends` clause, as row 17 holds for a trait. Today's specification refuses the form in any case, by instantiation exclusion, and marks it "Not allowed" beside the parametric `Nothing[\T\]` that the interpreter's library writes (F-167). P-90 still calls the bare `Nothing` future work that waits for such `where` clauses, not tried before then. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-maybe/REPORT.md` section 5.
16	- F-22 **When a component's name differs from the api that it exports, neither path finds the component, for an exported function or variable alike.** The specification resolves an imported api to any component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex`). The tree looks only under the api's name, unless a user maps the api to its component by hand with `LinkShell`'s `alink` or `clink`. The linker's component repository looks this way (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`), so `fortress link` and walk print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" before any code is generated. The code generator names a reference to an exported declaration after the api, and the declaring class after the component. The link step rewrites such a reference to the component only when the repository names it, so files compiled one by one, without `fortress link`, die with `NoClassDefFoundError`. The missing step is the repository's: finding the component that exports the api. The report names two repairs, neither built: the repository could search the source path for that component, or the code generator could emit api-named forwarders, for which three comments in `CodeGen.java` leave a place. Walk and `fortress link` need the first. Workaround: name the api after its component. Gated by the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test` (row 320). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-export-var/REPORT.md`, "The measurement that separates them".
17	- F-23 **A comment placed after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span and of the unambiguous name the parser derives from it.** The parser's `createSpan` trims back over spaces only, and a declaration that ends in `end` is unaffected (row 359). So a comment-only library edit can change the syntax tree, and a before-and-after comparison of parse trees or diagnostics maps positions back first. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/REPORT.md` section 6, D1.
18	- F-24 **Under `walk`, a native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees.** It throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object, as `Int.overflow()` does for `IntegerOverflow` (F-132; row 347, fixed). A native bound to a helper of `nativeHelpers/` raises the library's own exception where the helper raises a class of the compiled prelude, such as `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero`, so `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` (F-299, F-306, F-308, F-312). Any other Java exception of a native becomes a `ProgramError`, which no `catch` takes. Gated by the `overflows(...)` assertions of `tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`, and for a helper by `tests/NativeHelperRaiseWalk.fss` and, for each of the five types, `tests/<type>DivisionByZeroWalk.fss` and `tests/<type>RemainderByZeroWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md` section 4.1.
19	- F-25 **On the compiled path, the class loader loads each class under the JDK's class-loading lock, so the first load of an instantiation's class is safe on four threads at once.** `InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` holds `getClassLoadingLock(name)` for the whole load, as the JDK's own `ClassLoader.loadClass` does. Without the lock, two threads that first loaded such classes at the same time could race, and the run died with a `NullPointerException` (row 417, fixed). The test `compiler_tests/FirstLoadThreadsRungG` calls the generic overload `f[\T\](v: Vt[\T\])` at eight instantiations, `Vt[\A1\]` to `Vt[\A8\]`, from a parallel `for` loop of 800 iterations. Observed: at four threads it failed 5 runs of 5 before the lock, and passed 5 of 5 after. It is one of the gate's atomic runs, which run each program at four threads (`gate.md`). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1 (the runs) and 12 (why this lock).
20	- F-26 **Under walk, when one of two applicable declarations has static parameters of its own, the call chooses on their declared domains where exactly one lies inside the other, not by the order in which they are written.** It builds P-45, the choice among overloads by declared parameter types, under walk. A declaration has static parameters of its own if it is a generic function or constructor, or a functional method with static parameters in a trait or object without any. Its declared domain, walk's symbolic instance, is its parameter types with each type parameter standing for itself under its bounds. Where neither declared domain lies inside the other, where each lies inside the other, or where neither declaration has static parameters of its own, walk compares the domains of the instances that the call makes. So a functional method of a generic trait or object is compared on its instance, and a generic dotted method is chosen by F-253 (a generic method at a dotted call, also chosen on declared domains). If the chosen declaration is generic and its instance takes an argument only by a conversion, walk converts the argument and dispatches the converted arguments again, so the most specific declaration for the converted values runs. In two cases walk keeps the chosen instance, with no second dispatch: an overloaded dotted method, and a position whose conversion `Coercions.coercionFor` does not find, such as a tuple converted element by element. Two generic overloads whose static parameters agree in name, kind and bounds share one symbolic instance, even if their `where` clauses differ; no test or library declaration has such a pair (row 478). Gated by `tests/DispatchDeclaredDomain.fss` and `DispatchConvertedAgain.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.1, 5.2 (the second dispatch) and 5.5 (the symbolic instance).
21	- F-27 **Walk's load check reads again two kinds of overload pair that its parameter-by-parameter check refuses, and accepts those that pass: a generic declaration beside a plain one, read on their declared domains, and two plain top-level functions, not methods, whose overlap other declarations cover through `comprises` clauses.** To test a cover, the check cuts the overlap of the two domains, position by position, into parts by the `comprises` clauses. Each combination of parts must lie inside the domain of one declaration without static parameters that lies below both. So several such declarations may together cover the overlap. A search that does not settle refuses. A generic declaration beside a plain one passes where one declared domain lies strictly inside the other and the inner one's return type lies below the outer one's. Where neither lies inside the other, the pair needs the same cover, or declared domains that exclude each other read whole (F-258, exclusion over the whole parameter type). Equal declared domains are refused. It builds under walk P-46, by which a conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits, and P-60, by which several declarations below both may cover a meet. Two generic declarations are read on their declared domains too (F-252: the No Duplicates, Return Type and Meet Rules, each over its own instances). Walk still refuses the valid example of the POPL 2019 paper on symmetric multiple dispatch (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`, p. 11:13), a set of three generic declarations (row 539). Gated by `tests/ComprisesMeetWalk.fss` and `GenericBesidePlain*.fss`, among others. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.3 (generic beside plain) and 5.4 (the cover).
22	- F-28 **Walk instantiates a generic declaration declared to return `Any`.** `MakeInferenceSpecific` treats `Any` as it treats a trait type (row 157, fixed). The checker's Return Type Rule relies on it: with the rule relaxed alone, a program passes the checker and dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError` (`OverloadingOracle.scala:81-105`; the probe `ProbeMIEPick`). The team's JVM type mapping relies on it too: no closure of extends lists names one generic at two static arguments, so the class that template expansion makes for an instantiation carries the type relations over as Java ones (`Papers/Implementation/TypeMapping.tex:125`, read). F-48 gives the kinds of static argument that the rule compares. Walk applies no instantiation exclusion: it accepts a type that extends two instantiations, and its overloading check does not count them as excluding (row 416; the review's section 3). P-43 keeps the rule. Besides the flat number tower of P-43, the library meets it by three changes of `952892a00`: `TotalComparison` extends `Comparison` and `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, no longer `StandardTotalOrder[\TotalComparison\]`; `AnyMaybe` extends `AnyUniqueItem` alone, no longer `Equality[\AnyMaybe\]` beside it; and `andCondCombine` chooses `andRelCond` by a `typecase`, in place of a second `ANDCOND`. So under walk, a program's `p1 ANDCOND p2` of two relational predicates, conditions built from a relation over a generator, which `filter` fuses, is no longer itself a relational predicate (row 458). The distance holds no exclusion error (F-53). Detail: `reviews/multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md` sections 1 to 3; `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:123-125` (`TotalComparison`), `:1065` (`AnyMaybe`); `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:5088-5096` (`andCondCombine`).
49	- F-45 **Without the exclusion rule, every dispatcher would have to call its generic arms at the call site's static arguments, and no published work resolves a value that is in two instantiations of one generic under run-time dispatch.** The loader already gives a generic dispatcher the call site's static arguments; without the rule, its arms would have to use them instead of arguments read from the value (`reviews/mie-probes/scope-call-site-dispatch.md` section 3). The call at the dispatcher's static arguments is built for template dispatchers (F-136), and, by reading, not for one with an `opr` or `nat` static parameter (`compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` section 9). The team's 2012 patents allow a self-typed generic, one that comprises exactly its parameter, at several instantiations along a chain of subtypes: the forest rule (`reviews/mie-probes/patents-forest-rule.md` section 1). Alone, the forest rule leaves the specialisation hole open: a specialised declaration, more specific than the generic one, runs for a value at a narrower level of the chain, a subtype, and returns a type that a caller typed at that narrower level does not expect. Compiled under a shadow checker with the forest rule, a patched copy of the checker that never landed, such a run dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`; the tree's checker refuses such a program (the same note, section 3). Route C adds a return-type rule that closes the hole (F-46). Detail: `scope-call-site-dispatch.md` section 3; `reviews/mie-probes/literature.md`, "What the field settled and what it did not".
50	- F-46 **Route C, the patents' forest rule with a return-type rule over every level of a chain, closes the specialisation hole (F-45), but going back to a nested number tower under it needs work beyond the checker.** The library's tower was nested before route A flattened it (P-43). Built as a shadow checker on 2026-09-24 and run through the zero probe's stack on a library copy without the reduction markers, route C refuses 25 pairs at 21 of the nested tower's declarations: specialisations that a level below does not cover. Completing the tower needs seven more declarations and the identification of `Integral[\ZZ32\]` with `ZZ32`. The patents' `comprises T` on the self-typed traits licenses that identification, but it overflows the checker's stack (measured on the zero probe's copy of the checker, in the recursion of `Formula.scala` that the tree shares). A hierarchy check of its own could enforce the identification instead; none is built. Leaving route A for route C also needs: the tower nested again; the call-site fix in every dispatcher (F-136); in the code generator, a method for each middle level of a chain, whose absence, by the error text, makes such a chain die with `AbstractMethodError`; walk to accept the specialised pairs without overflowing on `comprises T`; and, for the identification, a way past the checker's overflow or the hierarchy check. Detail: `reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md` sections 2 to 5.
51	- F-47 **The exclusion rule refuses some of the specification's own examples; in their place, a parametric object with a factory, or a widening function, runs on both paths as a user program.** The refused examples are E1 to E10 of `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, "What was found": among them three `where`-clause examples, the Working Draft's `Nothing`, the nested number tower and `RationalQuantity`. The `where`-clause examples stop on both paths before the rule, in name resolution, at `T is undefined`. The alternatives were measured as user programs that declare their own types: a parametric object with a factory, such as `object Empty[\T\]` with `emptyList[\E\]()`, and a widening function, such as `widen[\T, S extends T\](c: C[\S\]): C[\T\]`. The library's `Nothing[\String\]` does not yet run on the compiled path's prelude (row 331, F-167). A marker object with a `coerce` in the generic trait, as `AltEmptyCoerce` has in `SList[\T\]`, also runs compiled, and walk applies such a coercion (row 389). The 2012 `covariant` keyword passes the compiled checker and dies at run time (row 404). The compiled checker refuses a coercion with its own static parameter between two instantiations, `coerce[\S extends T\](c: C[\S\])`, as a cyclic hierarchy. Inferred from the forest rule: route C (F-46) would rescue neither the `where`-clause examples, `Nothing` nor E8, the internal appendix's "Disjunctive Constraints"; only the tower (E5) and the root `Object`'s algebra (E7) would keep their original text under it. Detail: the same note.
52	- F-48 **The compiled checker's exclusion rule compares type arguments, and sizes only when both are literals.** Two boolean arguments count as no exclusion: `object F extends { Flag[\true\], Flag[\false\] }` passes the checker and dies in code generation (row 406, `compiler_tests/XXXBoolExtendsTwice`). Nor does a static parameter beside another argument: `object O[\nat n\] extends { Vec[\n\], Vec[\3\] }` passes the checker and dies at load with `ClassFormatError` (row 414, `XXXNatExtendsTwice`; the row also places its cause in `TypeHierarchyChecker`'s check of `extends` clauses). Two literal sizes do exclude: the checker refuses `object V extends { Vec[\3\], Vec[\4\] }`, "Types Vec[\3\] and Vec[\4\] exclude each other" (row 402, fixed). Gated by `compiler_tests/XXXNatExcludeChecker`, for the refusal of two literal sizes. The code is `TypeAnalyzer.scala:548-555`, "Todo: Handle bool args". Detail: `reviews/spec-refused-examples-judgement.md` section 6.
53	- F-49 **Under walk, a value form and a function form of one name are chosen by the argument's run-time type, so with the element type `Any` a function passed as the value goes to the function form.** Given a function, `fill` on an array of element type `Any` stored the function's results, `c[1] = 11`, not the function. The compiled checker refuses such a pair under the bound `Any`: a functional whose one parameter has a parametric type bounded by `Any` cannot be overloaded (the probe `FillBoxAny`). The one library has no such pair: `fill` takes a value and `tabulate` a function (F-158). Detail: `reviews/fill-overloads-ways.md` section 2.
54	- F-50 **The compiled checker lets overloads differ in static parameters, as the model of the OOPSLA 2011 paper does, which the specification now states (F-174); as ambiguous, it refuses only the pairs it cannot prove unambiguous.** It builds P-45. It cannot prove a pair over open traits, which no `excludes` or `comprises` clause closes, nor one whose domains exclude only through the exclusion rule and a bound, as the library's `CAP` on `ScalarRange[\I\]` beside `Range2D[\I,J\]` does. It also refuses some pairs that the paper accepts, by its Return Type Rule and by its positional rule, under which two generic declarations in the more-specific relation agree on their static parameters by position (F-75). Other gaps have their own owners: two generic arms on a bare type variable fail compiled (F-174, row 537); and walk runs an arm whose size the call leaves unfixed, with the size unbound, where the checker drops the arm or refuses the call (F-69, row 400). Detail: `reviews/overload-static-params-ways.md` sections 2 and 3.
55	- F-51 **A generic call converts a narrower argument for a parameter typed by a type variable that another argument fixes, on both paths.** For `scale[\T\](b: Box[\T\], x: T)` and `b: Box[\RR64\]`, `scale(b, 3)` takes `T = RR64` and converts the `3` (row 388, fixed). So under walk the library's array-scalar `+`, `-`, `MIN` and `MAX`, and the matrix-scalar juxtaposition and `DOT`, take a `ZZ32` scalar with `RR64` elements. F-73 and F-137 give each path's rule. Gated by `tests/InferCoercionRungK` and `compiler_tests/InferCoercionShapes`. Detail: `reviews/numeric-hierarchy-integration-review/row388-container-probe.md`.
56	- F-52 **Neither path can use `RationalQuantity` as the specification declares it: the advanced numbers chapter's rational type, refined by `bool` static parameters for its sign, infinities and NaN (`Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex`).** The team's `ProjectFortress/tests/conditionalExtension.fss` declares it as the chapter does: a trait that extends its own instantiations with weaker flags, under a `where` clause. The compiled checker refuses it, "Cyclic type hierarchy: Type RationalQuantity transitively extends itself". Walk runs that test only because nothing instantiates the trait; a probe that instantiates it fails under walk. Measured by the note's probes, which `84aef6a4f` removed (`reviews/flattening-questions-ways/Q3*.txt` in its parent). Detail: `reviews/flattening-questions-ways.md`, "Question 3", section 2.
57	- F-53 **At the last landed gate, climb batch 32's, the distance to the switch-over is 0 errors and the checker count is 0.** The distance counts the compiled checker's distinct errors over fourteen components of the interpreter's library and their apis: twelve, and `List`'s two imports, `CovariantCollection` and `OneShotFlag` (F-288). It runs every checker stage of each component whatever the earlier stages reported, and classes the errors by root cause (F-54). At that gate it checks `value object Char` to its end, with no crash (F-334). The checker count checks only the `FortressLibrary` component, with the apis it imports, and each unit stops at its first failing checker stage; the component's run ends clean, which the count stage reads as 0 (`tools/checker-count/run.sh`), and nothing crashes (F-233). A rise in either is reported and turns no gate red on its own; the count stage can still turn the gate red on the faults that F-66 names, such as a crash that no rung listed (P-39). A rung measured by either takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values: that batch's `compile-ladder/climb-batch-<N>/gate/distance.txt` and `checker-count.txt`, and the per-site list `compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`, which holds the last landed gate's sites, none now (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The checker count and the distance").
58	- F-54 **The gate classes the distance to the switch-over by root cause.** The `#class` rows of a gate's `distance.txt` hold the count of each class that occurs, such as X1 for an export error, BR for a big operator's body, and OT for the other body errors, one-off library slips and checker limits; `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/classify.py` assigns them, and at a distance of 0 there are none (`tools/distance/table.py:112`). F-53 gives the last gate's total. That gate's `distance.txt` reads '#crash none': the checker checks `value object Char` to its end (F-334), and the `FortressLibrary` component to its end too (F-233). Detail: `perf-probes/prelude/distance-triage.md` section 2; `reviews/batch-28-review.md`, section 1.
59	- F-55 **Static arguments are inferred with coercion on both paths: the compiled checker from the arguments' static types and the expected type, walk from their run-time types.** So a mixed-width call takes the narrowest type into which its arguments convert, as P-74 decides. F-73 gives the checker's rule and F-137 walk's; F-87 lists where the checker has an expected type. Under walk, a typed binding converts a call's result after the call and does not fix the call's static arguments: `a: BoxK[\ZZ64\] = wrapK(3)` infers `T` from `3` as `ZZ32` and is refused, since no coercion converts a `BoxK[\ZZ32\]` (row 510). A parameter with no written bound is bounded by `Any` on both paths, so a parameter that nothing fixes takes `Any` (F-78). Gated by `compiler_tests/InferCoercionShapes` and `tests/InferCoercionRungK`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-inference-checker/REPORT.md` section 3.2; `compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 9.
60	- F-56 **The compiled checker keeps the expected type, for inferring the call's static arguments, at a call written `f(x)`, which the parser builds as a tight juxtaposition: `f` and `(x)` with no space between.** It keeps it at a method call and an operator too; F-87 lists the other contexts. Only desugarings reach the `fnApp = true` path of `scala_src/typechecker/impls/Operators.scala:88-90`, so an edit of that path alone changes nothing for a call written `f(x)`. Gated by `compiler_tests/InferCoercionShapes`. Detail: `reviews/numerics-plan-coordinator/measure-D.md` section 1.

<!-- What is established about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as it stands now, grouped by area: each entry the fact, its source and its test. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `FACTS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. -->

# Facts on record

## Execution model

- F-7 **Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases, and only the compiled path runs the static type checker.** Walk switches the checker off, and no switch turns it on. So walk checks no static types of expressions: an ill-typed expression shows only when it runs, as a failed dispatch or as another run-time error, such as F-239's refusal of an `if` on a value that is not a `Boolean`. At load, walk refuses some ill-formed declarations: the `fortress-repo` skill's `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists them, with their evidence in F-29 (`comprises` clauses), F-142 (the Meet Rule for Functional Methods) and F-145 (uncovered abstract methods and `override`). The phases and where the two paths part: the skill's "How a program runs". Detail: `explorations/repo-internals.md`, "The two worlds".
- F-9 **`fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's library, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, so it is no oracle for walk programs.** `Shell.java` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` for the command (row 69). P-12 has walk run the checker on its own programs after the switch-over, and walk cannot do so as it stands: it runs with type checking and the Scala checker off, the Java checker is gone (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:228-229`), and it has no case for the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, by reading (row 833).
- F-11 **The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main representational cost of microGPT-shaped array code.** So a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (the `fortress-repo` skill, "The compiled runtime"). In Java models of microGPT's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`. No such kernel compiles yet: the compiler prelude has no array type (row 305), and the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (P-37). In a hot compiled loop, escape analysis removes the temporary boxes, and one box per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration stays (F-301), as long as C2's inline depth reaches each box's constructor chain (F-302). Detail: `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4; `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` section 4.
- F-12 **On the compiled path, the scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` ran in 0.74 s in one session's measurement; the loop still pays for its generator, for boxing and for a transaction check at each use of its accumulator.** `bench1t` is `for i <- seq(1#20000000) do acc := acc 0.9999999 + 0.0000001 end` on a `var acc: RR64`, with both literals written in the loop. The time is the median of three loop-only runs at one thread (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Times taken in different sessions differ on this machine, so compare only times from one session. What the loop does, read in its bytecode (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 5): the `seq` loop becomes the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, which runs the iterations in order by a recursive split over boxed indices, with a closure call per element; each value is boxed (F-11); and the accumulator is a volatile cell whose read and write each first call `BaseTask.inATransaction`, as for every mutable local (F-40, what a size costs at run time, whose sized loop pays the same check). Within the boxing and the cell, the report counts four allocations per iteration, an interface call to the native wrapper and the casts, the part that unboxed doubles and `double[]` would attack. No share of the 0.74 s is measured.
- F-17 **The bytecode cache can come up empty after a library order that reports exit 0.** Running the same commands again, one at a time, made the jars. The cause is not known. Check the five jars before a compiled run (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`, "The library order"). Detail: `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled runtime" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becomes `LFRR64;` in `Box⟦FRR64⟧`, and `[D` is no class name, so stamping alone keeps every number boxed (F-11). The team left two separate traces for unboxing. The plan in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java` lists what to unbox: a primitive, a singleton object, unboxed fields, and a `comprises` clause whose types are unboxable; it says nothing of the loader or of instantiations. The loader has an empty "expando" stub (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`). A loader that stamps an `RR64` instance with a `double[]` field, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), does not exist and is unmeasured. Walk instantiates generics in its own evaluator, not by classes. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 1; `coordinator/array-design.md` section 2 (probe 1); `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 3, way A4.
- F-19 **By the specification, the iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments of a call or an operator may run in parallel, and a program must assume that they do.** A `for` loop is sequential only if every generator is, as `seq(g)` or `sequential(g)` makes it. An implementation may also run them one after another (`evaluation/parallelism.tex:88-90`), so a program cannot count on parallel runs either. For the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator, each path starts a task only where it judges it worth it: walk by `TupleTask.worthSpawning`, which also governs a call's arguments, and the code generator by `ParallelismAnalyzer`. Compiled, the arguments of a function call and of a dotted method call fork where the analyzer marked the argument tuple (`CodeGen.evalArg`; joins: F-350); it counts no call in the prelude's files (row 982) or of a function declared later in the file (row 987). A `for` loop over a range without `seq` runs by splitting the range into `do … also do … end` blocks. Under walk, every such block is a task, and walk's library splits a `ZZ32` range into chunks of at most 16 elements (F-350), and a range with a stride down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1498-1585`). Compiled, the first block runs in place, and each other block forks only where `BaseTask.forkIfProfitable` judges it worth it, as tuple elements do; the compiler prelude's `parloop` splits down to `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK` elements, 1 by default. `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the pool of worker threads (the `fortress-repo` skill, "Parallelism and mutable state"). By grep, no program under `explorations/`, the model programs and the probes, writes `spawn`, which starts an explicit thread, or an `also do` block, so their parallelism comes only from loops, tuples and arguments. The revival's tests under `ProjectFortress/` write both. Source: `Specification/basic/expressions/for.tex:28-32`, `tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:58-59`, `evaluation/parallelism.tex:50-80`.
- F-20 **Sizes, the `nat` and `int` static parameters, are values at run time; they check shapes, and no optimization uses them (F-40, what a size costs at run time).** The compiled checker checks them (F-67), and a sized program loads and runs compiled (F-129). Under walk, `Vector` and `Matrix` take their sizes from an array built at run time: `f[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\])` takes `s` from `array[\RR64\](3)`, and overloads on `Vector` and `Matrix` dispatch by rank (row 214). The array-type syntax `T[n]` with a `nat` parameter does not unify with such an array, "Cannot unify … with ArrayType", where `T[3]` with a literal size does (row 23). Walk matches sizes at dispatch. A mismatch, such as a `DOT`, the library's inner product, of a 2×3 matrix by a 2×3 matrix, whose inner sizes differ, is a `ProgramError`, "Failed to find any matching overload", that no `catch` takes (row 254). Source: `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:96`.
- F-21 **The February 2011 Working Draft's bare `Nothing`, one object for every `T`, is accepted on neither path: the grammar refuses its `excludes` clause, and without that clause `T` is undefined.** The declaration is `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:40`). Both paths stop at a syntax error at `excludes`, since an object has no `excludes` clause (measured: `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, E4). Without that clause, both report `T is undefined` at the `T` of the `extends` clause: a `where` clause on an object binds no type variable of its `extends` clause, as row 17 holds for a trait. Today's specification refuses the form in any case, by instantiation exclusion, and marks it "Not allowed" beside the parametric `Nothing[\T\]` that the interpreter's library writes (F-167). P-90 still calls the bare `Nothing` future work that waits for such `where` clauses, not tried before then. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-maybe/REPORT.md` section 5.
- F-22 **When a component's name differs from the api that it exports, neither path finds the component, for an exported function or variable alike.** The specification resolves an imported api to any component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex`). The tree looks only under the api's name, unless a user maps the api to its component by hand with `LinkShell`'s `alink` or `clink`. The linker's component repository looks this way (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`), so `fortress link` and walk print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" before any code is generated. The code generator names a reference to an exported declaration after the api, and the declaring class after the component. The link step rewrites such a reference to the component only when the repository names it, so files compiled one by one, without `fortress link`, die with `NoClassDefFoundError`. The missing step is the repository's: finding the component that exports the api. The report names two repairs, neither built: the repository could search the source path for that component, or the code generator could emit api-named forwarders, for which three comments in `CodeGen.java` leave a place. Walk and `fortress link` need the first. Workaround: name the api after its component. Gated by the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test` (row 320). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-export-var/REPORT.md`, "The measurement that separates them".
- F-23 **A comment placed after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span and of the unambiguous name the parser derives from it.** The parser's `createSpan` trims back over spaces only, and a declaration that ends in `end` is unaffected (row 359). So a comment-only library edit can change the syntax tree, and a before-and-after comparison of parse trees or diagnostics maps positions back first. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/REPORT.md` section 6, D1.
- F-24 **Under `walk`, a native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees.** It throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object, as `Int.overflow()` does for `IntegerOverflow` (F-132; row 347, fixed). A native bound to a helper of `nativeHelpers/` raises the library's own exception where the helper raises a class of the compiled prelude, such as `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero`, so `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` (F-299, F-306, F-308, F-312). Any other Java exception of a native becomes a `ProgramError`, which no `catch` takes. Gated by the `overflows(...)` assertions of `tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`, and for a helper by `tests/NativeHelperRaiseWalk.fss` and, for each of the five types, `tests/<type>DivisionByZeroWalk.fss` and `tests/<type>RemainderByZeroWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md` section 4.1.
- F-25 **On the compiled path, the class loader loads each class under the JDK's class-loading lock, so the first load of an instantiation's class is safe on four threads at once.** `InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` holds `getClassLoadingLock(name)` for the whole load, as the JDK's own `ClassLoader.loadClass` does. Without the lock, two threads that first loaded such classes at the same time could race, and the run died with a `NullPointerException` (row 417, fixed). The test `compiler_tests/FirstLoadThreadsRungG` calls the generic overload `f[\T\](v: Vt[\T\])` at eight instantiations, `Vt[\A1\]` to `Vt[\A8\]`, from a parallel `for` loop of 800 iterations. Observed: at four threads it failed 5 runs of 5 before the lock, and passed 5 of 5 after. It is one of the gate's atomic runs, which run each program at four threads (`gate.md`). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1 (the runs) and 12 (why this lock).
- F-26 **Under walk, when one of two applicable declarations has static parameters of its own, the call chooses on their declared domains where exactly one lies inside the other, not by the order in which they are written.** It builds P-45, the choice among overloads by declared parameter types, under walk. A declaration has static parameters of its own if it is a generic function or constructor, or a functional method with static parameters in a trait or object without any. Its declared domain, walk's symbolic instance, is its parameter types with each type parameter standing for itself under its bounds. Where neither declared domain lies inside the other, where each lies inside the other, or where neither declaration has static parameters of its own, walk compares the domains of the instances that the call makes. So a functional method of a generic trait or object is compared on its instance, and a generic dotted method is chosen by F-253 (a generic method at a dotted call, also chosen on declared domains). If the chosen declaration is generic and its instance takes an argument only by a conversion, walk converts the argument and dispatches the converted arguments again, so the most specific declaration for the converted values runs. In two cases walk keeps the chosen instance, with no second dispatch: an overloaded dotted method, and a position whose conversion `Coercions.coercionFor` does not find, such as a tuple converted element by element. The commit of February 2011 changed only the copyright header. The team did not touch the list again, up to its last commit in 2012.

- multifix operators (the compiled checker's case, unchanged since the draft)
- identifiers with connecting punctuation
- ASCII conversion of names
- test functions under "fortress test"
- abstract methods in traits
- contracts under walk (since 2008)
- ZZ and QQ in walk's library (already there in 2009)
- components linking (the team's Linker.java, of January 2012, after the draft)

- widening coercion: the compiled path's is the team's, of 2009; walk's and its library's coerce declarations are the revival's
- type coverage check: both checks are the team's; coverage through a comprises clause and walk's refusal at load are the revival's
- generic overloading check: the checker's is the team's; the Return Type Rule over every instance and walk's load check are the revival's
- varargs: walk's is the team's, of 2007; the checker's typing is the revival's
- modifiers: atomic blocks, and walk's value and override, are the team's; SEQV on value objects when compiled is the revival's
- non-type static parameters: walk's nat and opr are the team's; the checker's nat and int are the revival's
- static expressions: sizes with arithmetic under walk are the team's; the fold of numerals and string literals is the revival's

## The question

The curator reads a page that shows Fortress's dispatch on every argument: two overloads `hit(a: Circle, b: Shape)` and `hit(a: Shape, b: Circle)`, and a functional method `touches`, each chosen at run time from the run-time types of both arguments (`explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/answers-2026-11-15.md`, "Note 10"). He asks, in a page comment of 2026-11-16:

> Okay, but like, how do you implement this multiple dynamic dispatch efficiently at runtime? This seems like performance nightmare to optimize correctly. Am I missing something?

He is a software engineer who knows Swift and Scala as a user, and no formal type theory. Answer him with what this tree does and what was measured, and say plainly where the cost is real.

## What to find

1. The compiled path. How a call of an overloaded name is compiled: read `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java` and the call sites in `compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java`. Say: what the dispatch method is (one per overloaded name? per arity?), in what order it tests the arguments' run-time types and by what test (`instanceof`, a descriptor for a generic arm), when the checker's static result narrows the set of declarations that the dispatcher tests, and when a call skips the dispatcher altogether because the checker resolved it to one declaration. Cite file and line for each.
2. What was measured. The record first: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'F-40'`, `'F-301'`, `'F-302'`, `'F-38'`, `'F-136'`, `'F-12'`, `'F-358'`, and their detail reports (`perf-probes/nat/size-cost.md`, `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md`). F-40 gives a dispatched call about 4 to 20 ns more than the same call resolved at compile time, on a call of about 23 ns; F-301 says C2 inlines the dispatcher on a hot path. Check each number at its report before you repeat it, and say what each was measured on and what it does not show.
3. Walk. How the interpreter chooses among overloads at a call, and whether it caches the choice (`interpreter/evaluator/`, the overloaded-function classes). One short paragraph.
4. What the team wrote about the cost and its implementation: `Papers/Implementation/` (the type mapping and the dispatch texts), the OOPSLA 2011 paper on modular multiple dispatch under `Papers/Types/` or `research/extracts/`, and the POPL 2019 extract. Quote at most two sentences, with file and line.
5. Peers, as context only and marked as from general knowledge, not from this repository: how Julia makes multiple dispatch fast (specialising a compiled method on its arguments' types, so that most calls are resolved when the method is compiled; a cache for the calls that stay dynamic), and how CLOS and Dylan do (caches at the generic function; sealing). And the contrast that he knows: Swift and Scala choose an overload at compile time from static types, and dispatch at run time on one receiver only.

## What to write

A reply for his comment thread as plain text of at most 3,000 characters, with no Markdown and no table, in `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/scratchpad/batch32/dispatch-cost-reply.txt`. Plain short sentences, each term defined where it is used, no shorthand of the project (no fact or row numbers in the reply). Its order: the answer in two or three sentences (is it a nightmare, yes or no, and why); what the compiled program does at such a call, on the `hit` example; when no run-time test is left; what was measured, with what it does not show; what the peers do; what is not yet known for this tree (for example, nothing of microGPT's kernels has run compiled against the interpreter's library).

Your final message, at most 14 lines: the answer; each claim of the reply with its file and line or its report and section; each number that you could not confirm at its source; the reply file's path.

## Which tier runs what

- Give each worker its tier's alias: `model: 'opus'`, `'sonnet'` or `'fable'`. Write no identifier that an alias resolves to.
- Use Sonnet only for archaeology and to fetch exact words, never for a judgement or a summary. Have an Opus worker turn the evidence into a report, and condense a long report into a summary or the exact quotes that you need.
- To recheck a point at its source, have a fresh Sonnet scout fetch the exact words from the transcript or the commits. Have an Opus worker set them against the curator's memory and against the report, entry or summary that it differs from. Until then, state neither side as right, and take no step that rests on the point until the recheck ends.
- Run an Opus worker that writes or condenses a long report at extra high effort, `xhigh`: the Agent tool's `effort` option, `agent()`'s `opts.effort`, or `--effort xhigh` on a headless session's command line.
- Run every writer on Opus: of skill text, of record entries, and of each longer report or page for the curator, also when this session runs on Fable. Fable writes no text that goes as written into the record, since its compressed register degrades the reasoning. A Fable worker may give corrections to a text that Opus writes, and Opus words them into the text. A Fable review may edit a batch record in place.
- The rules on Fable's text hold while Fable is at version 5.1. When this session runs on Fable, `explorations/coordinator/tools/model-now.sh` prints its version.
- Take a cross-area question in two steps. First, Opus workers gather cited evidence or a list of ways. Then, if neither the record nor the three principles (`SKILL.md`) settle it, run a Fable judgement, sparingly. If the fork stays consequential, put it to the curator as an ask.
- Four kinds of Fable work have a go in advance: the Fable judgement on a cross-area question, a judge's second ruling in a batch, the Fable review of each batch record, and the comparison of a rewritten skill part with the version that the curator approved. Ask first for any other Fable worker, such as one on your own conduct, one whose answer would reverse the curator's decision, or a Fable and an Opus worker run apart on one question.
- If you start a headless session on a tier other than Opus or Fable, set `FORTRESS_HEADLESS=1` in its environment. Otherwise the model check's alarm stops its work (`SKILL.md`, "The boot"). Today only the baseline interview does so.
- Start every headless session with `--session-id` and a new UUID. Without it, the session writes into your own transcript, where its prompts read as the curator's messages.
- A Fable token also uses the all-models limits, at three to four times an Opus token's share of the session limit.

content.content:
191	- F-112 **The test corpora cite the specification by file and section, never by line.** A test names the heading of the section that it cites. In the library chapters, it names the trait or method entry too. A rung that renames or removes a cited section updates the citation in the same commit. No test comment names a `.tex` file with a line number: `grep -rnE '\.tex:[0-9]+'` over `ProjectFortress/tests`, `compiler_tests`, `library_tests`, `other_compiler_tests` and `parser_tests` prints nothing; one bare `:400-401` stays after the section that `compiler_tests/IntLiteralWrapRepairR2.fss:12-14` cites, left as it was. Source: the one-time strip of `.tex` line numbers, commit `dc0eee2fe`. The `fortress-repo` skill gives the rule to workers (`tests-writing.md`, "Names, comments, citations").
192	- F-113 **A harness run against another build's classes must point `FORTRESS_CACHES` at that build's caches as well as passing `-Dfortress.caches`.** A `.test` file's `run` step is a separate `bin/fortress run`, whose class path comes from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. Without it, the run fails "Could not load ... Resource not found". The run step runs no checker code, so the tree's own classes serve it. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-return-type-rule/REPORT.md` section 4; the `fortress-repo` skill's `worktrees.md`.
193	- F-114 **`ant testSpecData` runs 130 of the specification's 133 extracted examples under walk, as a gate step, and all 130 pass.** `SpecDataJUTest` runs `SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries` and `advanced`, not `library/`'s three, and `testFast` excludes it. It builds P-124. Five examples write no static argument on a generic big operator whose bound mentions its static parameter, and they pass only because walk leaves that parameter open (F-143; row 424, fixed). The count and the time: the last landed gate's `summary.txt`.
194	- F-203 **`explorations/experiment/env.sh` sets up a shell for the gate's runners, and sets `FORTRESS_HOME` from its own place in the tree.** It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` two folders above itself, replacing any value that the shell had (`env.sh:4`), so sourcing another tree's `env.sh` runs that tree's code. It also sets the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` and `JAVA_FLAGS`, and unsets `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`. It deletes a `/tmp/fortress*rats` parser folder only if nothing in it was written for an hour and every running `java` process started after its last write, so sourcing it does not break a live run. The compile ladder's drivers source it: `compile-ladder/run-ladder.sh` and its copy in `baseline-2026-09-19/`, and the two that the gate's ladder regression runs, `repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh` and `baseline-2026-09-19/microgpt-phase.sh`. Each of these sets its own `JAVA_FLAGS` after it. `experiment/setup.sh` sources it too. `microgpt-phase.sh` names the main tree's `env.sh` by its absolute path; the gate rewrites that path in its copy (the `fortress-repo` skill's `gate.md`, "The ladder regression"). The count stage's and the distance stage's `run.sh` do not source it: their headers tell the caller to source it first. A worker does not source it. It starts each Bash call with the `fortress-repo` skill's setup lines, which give the same settings (`build-and-caches.md`, "Setting up each call"). Evidence: read in the scripts; the deletion rule also in `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/build-efficiency.md` section 4.
195	- F-234 **A Fortress command that a worker types itself (`bin/fortress`, `harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh`, or `java` of a Fortress main class) starts a fresh JVM, and that start costs too little to pay for a resident compiler.** A resident compiler is a background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did. The suites start one JVM for each test class, and one for each of `testSystem`'s four shards, not one for each test: the harness runs each test file inside its JVM. Only a compiled test's run step and a `.sh` test, such as `tests/concurrentPrinting.sh`, start another process. In one measurement over 267 worker transcripts, the one-off commands took 17.5 % of the wall time of the workers' shell commands, and the suites, builds and stages 47.8 %. Over the workers' whole running time, the one-off commands took 6.4 % (11.6 % if every wait that the measurement could not tie to a run was theirs). Removing their JVM start-up would save at most 1.8 % (P-150: no resident compiler is built). What runs inside the suites and the stages was not measured. Detail: `coordinator/process-engineering/fresh-jvm-commands.md`, "Summary", "What a resident compiler could save, at most" and "Decisions not taken".
196	- F-283 **The 52 programs of the team's `DemoTests` reach their end under walk.** Run one at a time from `ProjectFortress/demos`, each exits 0 and prints no "fail", within a 600 s limit and on an empty input, with `wordcount2` run from the tree's root and `tennisRanking` given the three files of `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/tests/unit_tests/FileTests.java:809-818`. The demos run in no suite, so a batch that changes walk or its library runs them again (P-79). `Generator2Demo` draws its arrays by `random`, so a product of them can overflow in `PROD`, and one such `IntegerOverflow` stop in a run is not a regression (row 986). The compiled checker still refuses `trips.fss` (row 817). No gated test: the command is the driver in `compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md` section 13, and its output on the code that `4445d848b` committed is 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. Detail: the same report, section 3; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-27/REPAIR-review.md`, section 2.
197	- F-295 **The distance stage counts each api's own errors and crashes, so an error in an api that only a later target checks cannot hide.** `table.py` turns `#total` into `none:` for an api whose `@@TC API` line gives `errors=` above 0 and that printed no `@@SC` line of its own, naming it with its count, and turns an `@@TC API-CRASH` line into a `#crash` row of kind `api` (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/table.py:54`, `:61-67`, `:94-104`). It does not read the `@@TC COMPONENT-CRASH` lines that `tools/distance/shadow-patch.py:111-113` prints. Test: `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/test_classify.py`, `Readings`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-list-imports/REPORT.md`, sections 1 and 2.
198	- F-354 **Two compiles of one source by different builds of the compiler need not give the same bytes, so a comparison of jars cannot show that a change left the compiled code as it was.** The code generator writes a class's methods and a dispatch method's tests in an order that follows the JVM's identity hashes (row 996). Two cold compiles of the prelude by one build give equal classes, 590 of 590, because the default identity hash is the same sequence in each run. Under another hash mode 18 of `CompilerBuiltin`'s 312 classes differ: the same methods in another order. So the tests, not the bytes, show that a change of the compiler left the prelude undisturbed, and a result that depends on the order can come and go between builds, as the choice between two copies of one method does (row 990). Measured once, on `832f7d0d91`'s code. Detail: `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/probe-y.md`, "6. A finding beside the question: the prelude's jars change with any change of the compiler".
199	## Landed semantics
200	
201	- F-117 **A compiled mutable variable's cell holds the language's top type, so a mutable variable of arrow type compiles and runs.** The cell holds `fortress.AnyType.Any`, not `FValue`, because a compiled closure is not an `FValue`. In row 682's program, with `trait NatParamT comprises { Nt[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, the checker refuses `f(x: NatParamT)` beside `f[\nat n\](x: Nt[\n\])` as two declarations of one parameter type, where walk runs the pair (row 682, contested). 247	- F-274 **Under walk, two declarations whose declared domains are equal are refused by the No Duplicates Rule, where one has static parameters of its own and the other has its own or none, whether or not the parameter-by-parameter check orders them.** The parameter check reads a type parameter as strictly below its bound. Walk compares the declared domains, each declaration's over all its own instances, and refuses the pair: "fails because their parameter lists have the same types" (F-257). 248	- F-275 **Under walk, where the parameter-by-parameter check refuses two declarations with static parameters of their own and one lies inside the other, the load check reads the Return Type Rule at one instance of the outer one, and refuses the pair unless that instance stands for every instance that applies.** The instance is the one that walk's inference finds for the outer one at the inner one's parameter types. A check at that instance alone would load pairs that the rule refuses, since an argument of the inner one can select a smaller instance of the outer one. The instance stands for every applicable instance in two cases. In the first, each static parameter that the outer one's return type names is fixed by a static argument of one of its parameter types. In the second, the outer one returns one of its own type parameters, and the inner one meets one of two conditions. Either it returns a type parameter of its own that is the whole type of at least one of its parameters and appears in no other parameter type than those at positions where the outer one's parameter type is that returned type parameter; or, at such a position, it has an object type below which its return type lies. Otherwise walk refuses the pair, "fails the Return Type Rule" (F-257). With `trait Shape`, `trait Round extends Shape` and `object Circle extends Round`, it refuses `f[\T extends Shape\](x: T, y: T): T` beside `f[\U extends Round\](x: U, y: Round): Round`, and `f[\T extends Shape\](x: T): Box[\T\]` beside `f[\U extends Round\](x: U): Box[\U\]`; the compiled checker refuses both too. 249	- F-280 **The library's `=/=` over `Any` and its three-argument `assert` see a value's own `=` only through a `FortressLibrary` trait, so `List` extends `Equality[\List[\E\]\]`.** Under walk they call `=` in `FortressLibrary`'s scope (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:98`, `:308`). A type that extends `Equality` reaches `Equality`'s own `=/=` before the one over `Any`: the negation of its `=` (`:102`; F-366). `List` extends `Equality[\List[\E\]\]` outside its conditional order (`Library/List.fsi:67`), so a list's `=` stays element by element there whatever the condition. Tests: `XXXNotEqualOwnEquality`, `ListEqualityElementwise`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-slices-list-equality/REPORT.md`, sections 1 and 2.
250	- F-304 **On both paths a numeral with a radix point becomes its `RR64` or `RR32` by one rounding of its exact value.** The compiled `CodeGen.forFloatLiteralExpr` rounds the exact quotient once (`roundToDouble`, `roundToFloat`; F-340); walk rounds once through `simpleDoubleArith.numeralToDouble` and `numeralToFloat` (F-79). The specification asks "at most one floating-point rounding error" (`basic/expressions/literals.tex`, "Literals"). Test: `compiler_tests/FloatNumeralOneRounding.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-natives-float/REPORT.md`, "Defects, each with its home".
251	- F-305 **`CHOOSE` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` names its helper on both paths, and the helper is exact, raises `IntegerOverflow` where the binomial coefficient does not fit, and shares no state between calls.** It builds P-73. Trait `ZZ32`'s and trait `ZZ64`'s `CHOOSE` name `simpleIntArith.intOverflowingChoose` and `simpleLongArith.longOverflowingChoose` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:845`, `:954`), which the compiler's prelude binds too, `NN32`'s compiled `CHOOSE` through the `ZZ64` helper; `NN32`'s binding in the one library names `simpleUnsignedIntArith.unsignedIntOverflowingChoose` through the `NN32` transfer (F-313). Past their safe-bound tables every coefficient overflows, from `34 CHOOSE 17` on `ZZ32` and `68 CHOOSE 34` on `ZZ64`, and the helpers raise `IntegerOverflow` there (`nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.java:222-225`, `simpleLongArith.java:200-203`); each slow-path call has its own scratch array (`simpleIntArith.java:174-175`, `simpleLongArith.java:153-154`), so calls in parallel no longer corrupt each other. Swept against the exact value, 64,649,240 `ZZ64` pairs and 6,023,925 `ZZ32` pairs give walk's glue arithmetic. Test: `tests/ChooseHelperWalk.fss`, `tests/ChooseHelperZZ64Walk.fss`, `compiler_tests/ChooseHelperCompiled`, `compiler_tests/ChooseHelperZZ64Compiled`, `compiler_tests/ChooseTableCompiledRungE`; the guards `tests/ChooseZZ32Walk.fss` and `tests/ChooseZZ64Walk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-natives-choose/REPORT.md`, sections 1, 2 and 5.
252	- F-316 **Under walk, `GCD` and `LCM` are nonnegative, `0 LCM 0` is 0, and on the four fixed widths `n CHOOSE k` answers 0 for `k < 0` or `k > n`.** `GCD` and `LCM` hold this on the four fixed widths and on `ZZ`. On `ZZ`, `CHOOSE` answers 1 for `k < 0` or `k > n`, where the specification gives 0 (row 887, `tests/XXXChooseZZOutOfRangeWalk.fss`). A `GCD`, `LCM` or `CHOOSE` result that its type cannot hold, such as a fixed width's `MIN GCD 0`, raises `IntegerOverflow` (F-132). `LCM` carries no sign, so code that takes a direction from it must compute the sign itself. The team's `tests/RangePrototype.fss` does so with `(a DIV (a GCD b)) DOT b`, `DOT` being multiplication. The library's ranges do not depend on that sign. Gated by `tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss` for `GCD` and `LCM` (rows 334 and 385, fixed), and by `tests/PowChooseLcmRungE.fss` for `CHOOSE` (row 337, fixed). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md` sections 4.2 and 7.
253	- F-318 **Under walk, the load check reads an own generic beside a functional method of a generic trait on their declared domains, `self` of a self-typed trait read as `C[\X\] & X` in the exclusion test.** It builds P-157 and P-152. Where the parameter-by-parameter check refuses an own generic function beside a functional method of a generic trait that declares no static parameters of its own, walk reads the pair as two own generics (`genericPairValid`), the trait's static parameters standing for the method's own; in `domainsExcludeTogether`'s meet, the self parameter of a trait self-typed directly (its parameter `X` bounded by the trait at `X`, no `comprises` clause or one that lists only `...`) excludes a type where the trait's instance or `X` does (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java`, `validOnDeclaredDomains`, `traitMethodPairValid`, `selfTypeParameter`). So a program's generic operators between an array of a number type and a number, beside a self-typed additive group's own, load and run as on the compiled path, and with `Number`'s `comprises` clause removed, in a scratch copy before F-324 removed it from the library, walk loads and runs `BooleanOps`, `ArrayScalarExtension`, `ArrayOperatorsBesideLibrary` and `extendNumber`. A trait self-typed through another self-typed trait, and a method with static parameters of its own, are not read so and keep the refusal. Walk applies no extender rule of P-146, so an object that extends a self-typed trait at a type it is not a subtype of now loads and runs one of two fitting declarations (row 893); the checker refuses a generic function more specific than such a method that walk loads (row 894). Gated by `tests/ExclusionVectorScalarWalk`, `ExclusionArrayScalarLibraryShapeWalk`, `GenericBesideTraitMethodInsideWalk` and `GenericInsideTraitMethodWalk` (load and dispatch), and the refusals `ExclusionVectorScalarOverlapWalk` and `GenericInsideTraitMethodReturnRuleWalk`. 254	- F-324 **The one library's `Number` declares nothing; each number type declares its own `asFloat` and an `=` at each number type it coerces from or into.** It builds P-160's second step and P-165. `Number`'s `comprises` clause, `asFloat`, `=` and `exactValue` are struck (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:381-382`, `.fsi:289-290`); the nine types declare `asFloat` in their apis; 42 declarations give a pair of `=` for each of the 21 coercions, so two numbers of different types compare by value where a coercion joins them, and otherwise by the fallback `a SEQV b` or a written `asFloat(x) = y`; the vector norm is declared at each of the eight types; the reflective generator chooses among the five former listed types. 255	- F-326 **Both paths answer `SEQV` by the specification's rule: values of different types never equivalent, value objects of one type field by field, floats by their bits, reference objects and strings only with themselves.** Walk in its value classes and `FTypeObject`'s field list; the compiled path in `equality.sEquiv`, which reads a `value` object by the mark `runtimeValues.ValueObjectMark` that the code generator adds to its class, and compares tuples element by element. Until the switch-over a compiled `===` reaches the prelude's family first, which answers `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR32` and `RR64` values, strings and booleans by `=` (P-38, row 908). Under walk a float numeral bound to `RR64` converts there, so it is `SEQV` a computed `RR64` of the same bits (F-341), and two string literals of one text are one object on both paths (F-343); a tuple of four or more compares by `SEQV` (row 923). Tests: `tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleWalk.fss`, `tests/ValueObjectCC64Walk.fss`, `compiler_tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleCompiled.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-seqv-meaning/REPORT.md`.
