<!-- The curator's decisions about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as they stand now. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- P-48 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `POSITIONS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. How the curator and the coordinator work is that skill's, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** The revival judges what the designers intended by the team's own sources: its Working Draft of February 2011, its texts on types and its code. `Specification/` holds the Working Draft as a living document: the revival revises it and states each change (P-95). The texts on types include the Types chapter of the specification's 2012 restart (P-25). In `Papers/`, they include the OOPSLA 2011 paper, Naden's 2012 write-up and the POPL 2019 paper with its technical report. P-26 says when code counts, and which source wins where two conflict. The revival does not redesign the language. A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.
- P-8 **Where the designers' own sources, the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations, give no answer, the curator decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and he stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** On the way to a compiled microGPT, he accepts the language's unfinished corners as they are, so that the work does not stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and he takes the designers to have known more than he does.
- P-9 **The revival searches for the most readable expression of the microGPT algorithm.** C4 is the flat microGPT program (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), whose data layout follows Aaron Hsu's flat style of APL (P-29: C4 is not edited for speed before microGPT runs compiled). In C4, the polishing happens in the vocabulary, the array operations that the model's lines call: `FlatArrays.fss` beside C4, and what of it has moved into the standard library (P-27: what a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library). P-87 holds the limit: the model's text is the notation, and a change to a model line is shown to the curator as a diff first. C4 is the target form of the APL microGPT program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`): the APL program is written so that each of its lines expands into the line that C4 writes by hand. C4 writes its hyperparameters as tuple bindings, such as `(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)`, the form to which the APL sub-language (P-10) expands a strand assignment, APL's binding of several names at once. The one-line form, declarations separated by semicolons such as `nEmbd = 16; blockSize = 16; ...`, is not used: the APL sub-language has no use for it.
- P-10 **The APL side quest is closed: its sub-language covers only what the APL microGPT program needs, and the parts of APL that it left unbuilt, tacit functions, characters and nested arrays, are not pursued.** The side quest built an APL sub-language in `explorations/apl/`: a DSL grammar that expands APL text into Fortress code over Fortress's native arrays, not an interpreter of APL. Its microGPT program, `explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`, stays in the microGPT check under walk (P-30: the check's limit of one minute; what the check runs: the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/interpreter.md`, "The model program").
- P-11 **The 2D notation is a gimmick: no work on it unless the curator asks.** The 2D notation is Fortify's rendering. Fortify (`Fortify/`, run by `bin/fortify` and `bin/fortick`) typesets Fortress source as mathematics in LaTeX, for the specification and the papers. Taken as programming syntax, such a rendering fixes one view of a computation, though the same mathematics can be written in many ways. APL, with one symbol for each transformation of the data, expresses a computation better. The rendering is presentation only, off the revival's path, and no argument in favour of Fortress. The verdict is on that typesetting only: the Unicode operators, such as `∑` and `×`, are the language's own syntax.
- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types; F-9 and F-290 say what walk and the library lack for that step. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).

## History he knows (do not re-explain)

- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.
- P-19 **The tree is not described as the third-party port's migration grafted onto the team's history.** The port is a third-party port of the tree to Java 9, which commit `8fe1daa8f` copied onto the team's last commit (the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/records.md`, "The repository's history"). By history, `main` descends from that commit. By content, most of the port's files are removed or redone, and only one piece of the port's code still runs: the `FTypeArrayList` fix for the JDK 8 `TreeSet` crash (F-165). Why: the tree is not built on the port, and the record must not lead anyone to think that it is. The files that still describe the tree so wait for the lineage cleanup; `coordinator/lineage.md`, "Files that still repeat it", lists them.

## Decisions on record

### The standard and the sources

- P-25 **`Specification/` stays the standard, and the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart is cited beside it.** The restart is a new specification that the team began in 2012 and left unfinished (F-166). Where its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, a worker cites it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, such as the exclusion rule, the chapter is the designers' latest intent, which the goal is to finish, and `Specification/` is revised to follow it. Three of the chapter's passages bear on the specification; P-97 holds how the revision uses the first two. It names the exclusion rule "instantiation exclusion" and gives it in two parts: which instantiations of a generic exclude each other (`types.tick:355-360`), and, in its note, a rule on trait declarations (`:361-376`). The revised `Specification/` takes that form: the first part in its chapter on types, the second in its chapter on traits. It adds a `covariant` modifier for a trait's static parameters, which neither path implements and which is future work, off the path to microGPT (P-62). Third, it says that `Bottom` cannot be written in a program, as `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` already says of `BottomType`.
- P-26 **The team's later decision wins over its earlier one, in a text or in code, where the team made it the language's rule.** P-7 names the texts, from the Working Draft to the POPL 2019 paper. Code counts as a decision where the team built it alike for all its types, or stated its rule in a commit message, a comment or the checker. Code that its author called a stub, and code that works around a limit of the JVM or of the checker, serve only the implementation. The decision that they depart from stands. "Later" is the date of the team's work on the point at issue. The revival revises `Specification/` to follow a later decision. The one library follows it too, in place of the team's earlier code, such as the interpreter's library. Where two later decisions conflict, the goal decides (P-8). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. Why: the Working Draft's early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run. So they learned what is feasible. They sought performance, and specialization was a must. Their later decisions include the exclusion rule, specialization and the number types of the compiler's prelude, siblings from 2009 to 2012 (P-43). The revival knows less than they did, so it does not second-guess them.
- P-27 **What a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library, in the library's own way.** A program written on this library has a part that states its algorithm, and it can have a part that builds domain-independent machinery that the library lacks, as both microGPT programs do. A form of that second part goes into the standard library when, on reasonable judgment, it is not an extension of the program's own domain; a form that the library has for one number type, rank or sibling trait and lacks for another is the plainest case. Whoever writes it there first studies how the library does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern, such as its `excludes` clauses. This rule governs how the library is extended; it does not choose between two of the team's designs of the language (P-26).
- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Its next layer is algebra: traits such as `Ring` and `Field`, which the library does not declare yet, and what machine learning's matrices and tensors need, so that the library's algebraic traits, such as `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, reach them too. Why: the curator wants those matrices and tensors to have the mathematical rigour that the library's way of building its types promises. The work edits the standard library itself, in `Library/`, not a separate tree of the revival's own outside it (P-27, how the library is extended). It is parked off the path to microGPT compiled. Two matrix ideas of his wait beside it: square matrices of one size as a multiplicative ring, and diagonal matrices of one size as a ring whose product commutes.
- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is far slower than Python's interpreter (`explorations/microgpt-port.md`, "Step-0 results", a measurement of 2026-08-23). Fortress's performance is judged on the compiled path, once the compiler runs programs. So no performance decision rests on walk's timings. In particular, until microGPT runs compiled, C4, the flat microGPT program, is not edited for speed. The gate never runs microGPT's two programs, C4 and the APL-style program, because they run too long to be tests. Why: walk is the unoptimised path, as a debug build is in Swift, where performance is not judged either.
- P-30 **The check of microGPT under walk after a batch must take less than a minute.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. The minute is the curator's goal, for a check that runs only about two forward-and-backward passes of the model, not a full training, and compares the results with reference values. That is enough to show that the model's mathematics still works, and that the library's changes, such as those to the arrays, did not break it. A slower check is to him a waste of time. The commit stage of each batch, the step that lands its changes, runs the check as `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh`, the quick versions of microGPT's two programs at once, outside the gate.
- P-32 **The record's maps are kept current and used, so that nothing that the record holds is worked out again from scratch.** The maps are `FACTS.md`, `INDEX.md` and the territory map, `explorations/coordinator/map/`. The territory map surveys the repository down to where the team wrote the intent of each design. Part of that intent is written only in the papers under `Papers/`, not in the specification. So the map covers the papers too, and shows where to look up a design's intent. `INDEX.md` is read whole at the coordinator's boot, at the start of each session and after each compaction, and each worker's brief carries a mission briefing from the territory map, not the whole map. The territory map's surveys date from 2026-09-16 (its README), so a status or a line number in them can be stale.
- P-33 **The work toward microGPT compiled follows the phases, in the order that the curator approved.** These phases are steps of the work, not the compiler's phases, and they are numbered 3 to 6, after two earlier ones. Phase 3 ends when the compiled checker reports no error on the apis and components of the interpreter's library that the distance to the switch-over counts (F-53 defines the distance, says what it counts and holds its value). The library's other components are not part of phase 3: each is cleared before the first program that needs it, and at the latest before walk runs the checker (P-12), so `System` by the switch-over, since the compiler's tests need it (F-293); F-290 counts their errors. Phase 4, the switch-over: first the natives, the library's `builtinPrimitive` bindings made to run on the compiled path, then the compiled path reads the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude is deleted; phase 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's open gaps; phase 6, microGPT runs fast. Code-generator work goes on beside that order, under either library (P-37). Row 320, an api implemented by a component of another name does not link, is part of the switch-over's design.
- P-175 **On the compiled path a call's arguments run in parallel where `ParallelismAnalyzer` judges them worth a task, as a tuple's elements do, so a reduction's two halves run in parallel; the one library's parallel range stops its split at a grain size, not at single elements.** The one library's range joins a reduction's halves as the arguments of one call, `red.join(loop'(lo, mid-1), loop'(mid, hi))`, and split down to single elements when the curator decided (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1312-1350`); the code generator evaluated a call's arguments in order, under the team's comment "Why isn't this parallel???", so every `SUM`, `DOT` and `BIG MAX` of microGPT would have run its bodies one at a time once compiled programs ran the one library. The split stops at a chunk that runs efficiently in sequence: in his words, "you need the right forking constants", as Steele's parallel trees end in sequential leaves and Clojure's persistent vectors take their branching factor from B-trees. It needs a group of forked arms to join every arm before it completes abruptly, which the compiled path did not do (`CodeGen.genParallelExprs` joined on the normal path only; `reviews/parallelism-foundations-2026-11-08.md`, section 7.1); F-350 gives what it does now. The library binding the halves as a tuple, and reductions left in sequence, are declined. Why: the specification evaluates each argument of a call in an implicit thread of its own (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex:60-64`), walk forks a call's arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:342`), and the model's parallelism is its reductions (the review, section 6). Detail: the review, sections 1.8, 6, 7.1 and 8.

### The one library and the compiled checker

- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). There are two exceptions, each so that both paths do the same before the switch-over, and each copy goes with the prelude: the numerals, where the prelude carries the design of P-174 and P-176; and the built-in number types, where it takes the form of P-178. The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.
- P-38 **The compiler prelude's own text is not repaired: its defects go with it at the switch-over.** A helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is fixed for the one library, and the prelude's value moves with it (F-313). Its `Maybe` block and its `REM` guard `if other = -1 then 0` stay as landed until the prelude is deleted, and their tests stay. Then the compiled tests respell its reversed wrapping and saturating operators (row 348), `ZZ64`'s compiled shift closes (row 381), and the specification's `shift` reaches the compiled path (row 383). `XXXShiftDeclRungI` is then promoted, and the switch-over batch finds the compiler tests that bind `shift`, a reserved name from then on.
- P-39 **Every batch's gate measures the checker count, and its total never turns the gate red.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. Its gate runs the gate's steps on their merged tree, and then the checker count, as step 8 (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`); the gate of `fortress-repo`'s gate part has no such step. The checker count and the distance to the switch-over both count the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library. The count stops where the checker crashes or meets an error that it cannot get past; the distance counts every error, over all apis and components (F-53 defines both and holds their values). A rise of the count's total is reported and never fails a batch on its own. The count's stage can still turn the gate red on the faults that F-66 names. One is a checker crash that no rung of the batch listed in advance as expected, in the field `expectedCheckerCrash` of the batch's manifest, the part of the batch's script that declares each rung's task. Until the switch-over lands, every batch's gate also measures the distance, in a stage that only reports. Why: the count checks only the `FortressLibrary` component (F-53), so a native binding moved onto a helper in another component is checked by the distance alone, and P-58 has each moved binding checked from the step that moves it.
- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size that inference leaves unknown is an error only where it is used.** A size is a `nat` or `int` static parameter, such as the length of an array in its type. The compiled checker checks sizes, and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140, the bound on both paths). The bound is this implementation's, for the sizes of arrays, vectors and matrices, to match the JVM's `int` indices; a numeral type's four static parameters have none, and read as values are `ZZ` (P-174). Wherever the array design, the compiled path's design for arrays (P-85), creates a JVM array, it checks the length there, at run time, and refuses one over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. So a declaration may declare a size that none of its types uses, and pass. A call that cannot fix a size of the declaration that it would choose is refused, also inside an overload set, instead of passing over that declaration. In the rule that no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait, two instantiations differ when any static argument but an operator differs, so `Vec[\3\]` and `Vec[\4\]` are two; boolean arguments count too once the checker has boolean parameters. A size used as a number, as in the range `0#n`, converts to `ZZ32` where one is needed, as a numeral does. The 17 vector and matrix operators of the `FortressLibrary` api declare only the sizes that their types use, the change of `explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch`. It finishes the team's own fix of 2008, which removed those sizes from the component only. The JVM length check waits for the array design; under walk such an array stops at its store's factory with walk's own error, which no catch sees (row 527). The checker still passes over a declaration whose unfixed size occurs in its own parameter type (row 400). The checker compares no boolean arguments (row 406).
- P-41 **On the compiled path, a size static argument travels at run time as a descriptor object, as a type argument does.** A generic type's descriptor has a field for each of its static parameters that is not an operator. The team's code generator already emitted that field for a size, with nothing to put in it, and the size's descriptor fills it. Each size value, such as the 3 of `Vec[\3\]`, has one descriptor, which `RTTIsize.of` takes from a table; no Java class is written for it. This is the team's pattern for instantiating types, applied to numbers. An operator static argument, by contrast, stays a name known only at compile time (F-39, how both paths carry it). The curator sees no need for an operator argument to be carried at run time the way types and sizes are. F-129 holds what runs and its open rows.
- P-42 **A type parameter declared without a bound has the implicit bound `Any`, not `Object`.** `Any` holds tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not. The library instantiates its generic containers at tuple types: its arrays indexed by pairs, such as `(ZZ32,ZZ32)`, are among them. The specification states the bound `Any`, with a callout that records that the Working Draft of February 2011 said `Object`.
- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.
- P-44 **`AnyIntegral` stays closed by its `comprises` clause, and the compiled checker reads the clause as the team's 2012 texts do.** The library's `AnyIntegral`, whose `comprises` clause lists the five integer types `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64`, stays closed. Beside the clause stays a comment in the team's `NOT YET` form, by which the team's library records a clause that it cannot write yet: here `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]`. The `where` form is built (P-151), but neither path takes this clause yet: the front end of both paths refuses it on a trait that declares a coercion (row 831), and walk refuses the library at load with it (row 804). `Integral[\I\]` extends `AnyIntegral` and is not in the list. The checker accepts such a generic trait below a closed trait when every type that the checker knows below it is listed. The clause's text in the library, and walk, stay as they are. Why: the team's 2012 texts, Luchangco's Types chapter and Welterweight, are its later word (P-25), and by them the clause is right as written. The rule leaves a hole that every way of closing `AnyIntegral` shares, except the team's 2008 way, a `comprises` clause on `Integral[\I\]` itself: a program's own subtype of `Integral`, declared in another component, is accepted although no listed type is above it. Row 487 records the hole, and this decision does not close it.
- P-45 **Overloaded declarations may differ in their static parameters.** The specification drops its sentence that forbids this, and keeps it as superseded text. It states instead the overloading model of the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which the compiled checker already used. The checker keeps the paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type. It checks the Return Type Rule over every instance of a generic declaration that the argument types allow, not over one guessed instance. One rule of the old sentence survives: if one generic declaration is more specific than another, their static parameters must line up position by position, as Java's rule for overriding a generic method requires. The compiled checker tests it only where the two declarations have as many static parameters of their own (F-75). Walk chooses among overloads by the parameter types that each declaration declares, not by the order in which they are written. At load, walk judges each pair of two generic declarations by the checker's rules on their declared parameter types. It does not refuse a pair only because none of their parameter types exclude, as when one declaration is more specific than the other. Walk and the checker must accept the same pairs. The library repairs, by declarations of its own, the overload sets that the checker refused, and no line of microGPT's two programs changes. Where walk or the checker still judges a pair against these rules: walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on the instance that a call makes (F-26); both paths refuse the paper's own valid example (row 539); walk refuses two generic functional methods of a trait without static parameters whose declared domains lie one inside the other, and fails at a call on such a pair in a generic trait (rows 779 and 780); and walk and the checker disagree on three kinds of pair (rows 786 to 788).
- P-46 **A conversion only makes a call possible: it never changes which declaration runs when one already fits, except a numeral's own conversion.** The declaration that runs is chosen on the parameter types that each overload declares: first those that apply, then the most specific of them (P-45). A generic declaration applies if some type within its bounds takes the arguments. Only then is the chosen declaration instantiated by promotion: at the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce (P-74). So beside `op(a: Any, b: Any)`, `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` applies to a call with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`, at `T = Number`. It is the more specific, so it runs, at `ZZ64`. - P-48 **A type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`.** The arguments leave a parameter unfixed when it occurs only in the result type; when two arguments meet at it with no narrowest type into which both convert (a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` have one, `ZZ64`, by P-74); or when dispatch, at run time, picks a generic declaration and must choose the instance to run. Its instance is then the intersection of its upper bounds (`Any` if it has none). At checking, that is narrowed by what the call's expected type (P-49 defines it) requires of the declared return type; at run time, by the static type that the checker gave the call. It is never `Bottom`, never the union of the arguments' types, and never the value's type alone. The rule sets the instance, not which declaration runs (P-46). Why: the rule is the team's later word, from the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch, and the curator trusts the team's later work above his own understanding. The rule changes nothing in microGPT, whose types are concrete. The library keeps the team's declarations of `fail`, `builtinPrimitive` and `List`'s empty comprehension, whose type parameters have no written bound, without the `extends Object` that a batch had added. Under walk, which has no static types, dispatch takes the value's type. Row 538: a compiled dispatcher that carries the static type that the checker gave the call, so that a generic declaration reached only at run time gets this instance. Rows 587, 591 and 612: three cases in which walk still gives `Bottom`.
- P-49 **The compiled checker tries a call first by subtyping, without the expected type, and coerces its arguments only when that attempt is not kept.** The expected type is the type that the call's context requires. The checker's first attempt checks the call by subtyping alone, without the expected type. It keeps that attempt when its result converts to the expected type, by coercion if need be. If it does not keep that attempt, it tries coercion of the arguments, with the expected type. So a declaration that fits the arguments as they are is not passed over for one that coercion reaches. A call with a numeral argument is the exception: where the numeral's own coercion reaches a more specific declaration than the first attempt chose, that declaration runs, so `u = 0` for `u: NN32` is checked at `NN32`'s own `=`, with the numeral an `NN32` (P-46 gives the numeral's rule and its ground). Why: in the curator's words, coercion should be tried when there are no matches.
- P-50 **The body of a `label` expression, and each value that an `exit` gives it, take the expected type of the whole `label`.** A `label` is a named block that code inside it can leave early with `exit`, giving a value with `with`. The specification types a `label` as the union of its body's last expression and the values that its `exit` expressions give. So when a `label` has an expected type, the compiled checker passes it into the body and into each of those values, as it does into each clause of a `typecase`. The specification's inference chapter lists the body and those values as contexts that carry an expected type. P-51 decides the same question for a call written as another call's argument. F-87 lists the checker's contexts that carry an expected type.
- P-51 **The checker retries a call written as another call's argument against each declaration's parameter type.** Take an outer call `f(g(x))`, whose argument is an inner call `g(x)`. The retry covers every inner call with inferred static arguments, not only one whose type parameter occurs in its result type alone. Why: the curator wants the type inference rules unified across contexts, which covers cases that the team did not build. As built, a generic declaration of `f` is first instantiated from the other arguments. The declaration whose retry succeeds is kept, or the most specific of several; otherwise the call goes on as it would without the retry. The measurement behind the decision is in `explorations/reviews/argument-context-probe.md`.

It does not use the tuples' lexicographic order, which serves sorting. So `((0,0):(9,9)).narrowToRange((2,-1):(5,5))` raises `IndexOutOfBounds`, since -1 lies below 0 on the second axis.

### Numbers

- P-66 **The integer principle: Java's and the JVM's defaults stay where they make sense, and are corrected where they fail high performance or mathematical precision.** The team did so with rounding. A hardware behaviour that bytecode can express gets its own explicit spelling, as the specification's wrapping and saturating operators do. Where the JVM prevents a correct implementation, the project gives way for now. The peers to compare are Julia, X10, Swift and Rust.

129	- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every edit of source code in the original tree starts from a failing test. The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The test and the fix may land in one commit. Why: the rule replaces one-off validation scripts, which no later build runs. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.
130	- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test's result is pass or fail, as the team designed the suites. A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. Why: when the suite's designers let a test pass without a further check, what it prints need not be checked.
131	- P-124 **The specification's examples are a step of the gate, and every one must pass.** `ant testSpecData` runs the examples extracted from `Specification/` under walk (F-114 says which 130 it runs), and the gate fails if any of them fails. 132	- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** `build.xml` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS` to 4 for the two suites, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`, so that every run of them uses four threads, whatever the calling shell sets. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.

- P-76 **An integer numeral has the Working Draft's type `NaturalNumeral` (P-174), which each of the eight number types converts from: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32`.** Where nothing fixes a type it is a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit (P-173). `NaturalNumeral` takes the place of `IntLiteral`, the name that the compiler's prelude and the interpreter's library gave the type, and `IntLiteral`'s own arithmetic goes, since an expression of numerals alone folds before the checker (P-173). Walk, before it runs the checker (P-12), converts an integer numeral from its exact value at each place that fixes a type, and elsewhere evaluates it at its default, which walk already gives it by its value (F-74). Walk gaps: coercion through tuple and varargs parameters (rows 395 and 511).
- P-77 **Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only, as the compiler's prelude declares them (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`).** Why: a JVM array has at most as many elements as the largest `ZZ32`. A range over another integer type is a static error. A loop whose counter needs a wider type runs over a `ZZ32` range and widens each element, as in `j: ZZ64 = i`. A range of rank 2 or 3 is a tuple of `ZZ32` scalar ranges. The public range traits, such as `Range[\I\]`, stay generic in their index type: the ranges of rank 2 and 3 extend them at pairs and triples of `ZZ32`.
- P-78 **`SUM` and `PROD` are one generic reduction each over the library's algebra, in place of the team's catch-all over `Number`, and take their identity from the static argument.** `SUM` is generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `PROD` over `MultiplicativeRing`. A reduction written with generators writes its static argument where nothing at the call fixes the element type. The compiled checker fixes it from the reduction's expected type, else from the type of its body, where a `SUM` or `PROD` leaves it out (F-364). It is written as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. A sum without generators is written as before, with no static argument: `SUM e` over a collection `e`, and the dot product `x DOT y`. `BIG MAXN`, `BIG MINN` and `BIG MINMAXN`, the team's `Number`-typed big operators for the maximum, the minimum and both, each with an identity, are gone; no program called them. `MAX` and `MIN` get no identity on the integers or the floats, so an empty `BIG MAX` or `BIG MIN` raises `EmptyReduction` (F-60: a maximum's identity is its type's least value, which a coercion into a wider type does not carry). Under walk, an empty `SUM` or `PROD` over another algebra, such as a user `AdditiveGroup`, still fails (row 436) until the specification's `HasIdentity` is built.
- P-79 **Every team demo is kept running as the tree changes.** The team demos are the programs in `ProjectFortress/demos/`; no suite or step of the gate runs them. If a change breaks a demo and the way to repair the demo is known, the batch that makes the change also rewrites the demo. A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. For example, the change that made `10^(-4)` an error (P-153, the integer power) also wrote `10.0^(-4)` in `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, and `10.0^(-6)` for `10^(-6)` in `npbft.fss`. A demo that fails for want of a feature is made to run again once the feature is built. So the demos known to fail today are to be respelled where the way is known. Under walk, the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reach their end (F-283). The compiled checker refuses `trips.fss` (row 817).
- P-80 **The specification's sign-refined number types are a superseded design: a program tests such a subset of a type at run time.** These types are the specification's subtypes by sign, such as positive ℚ, non-negative ℚ and non-zero ℚ, and the same refinements of the integers. The machine types `NN32` and `NN64` are separate types, not among them. The specification's number chapters now test a value's sign by comparison, and a float with two getters of `RR64`: `check` returns `Just(x)` for a finite `x`, `check_star` returns `Just(x)` for an `x` that is not a NaN, and each returns `Nothing` otherwise. The chapter that held the design, `Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex`, stays word for word, marked superseded by a callout in the form of every specification change (P-96), so that the original design stays on record. Their possible return belongs to P-62: once the `covariant` keyword is built, a worker tries to bring them back as covariant static parameters.
- P-153 **The integer power splits on the base: an integer base gives an integer or raises an error, and a float or rational base gives the fraction.** Each integer type's `^` returns its own type at every exponent. At a negative exponent, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code gives an integer power the type of its integer base at a signed exponent. Overloads choose by type, and no type tells a negative exponent from a non-negative one, since a signed integer or a numeral can be either. So the split is on the base, and the sign of the exponent is tested at run time, as the library tests a value's sign everywhere (P-80, run-time sign tests in place of sign-refined types). Row 441: the same rule on the compiled path, whose own powers give 0 at a negative exponent and a raw Java exception at a base of 0, and overflow silently or with a raw Java exception (row 523).
- P-159 **A float compared with a NaN answers: `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` give `false`, and `CMP` gives `Unordered`, on both paths.** On `RR64` and `RR32` the four ordering operators answer `false` when either side is a NaN, and `CMP` answers `Unordered`, as the team built them. `FloatingComparisonError` stays declared in both libraries, and nothing raises it. The specification's overview of operators said that this comparison threw that error, and the sentence before it that a rational comparison at 1/0 or 0/0 threw `RationalComparisonError` (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:283-288`). Both sentences are revised, in the form of Appendix I, to the rationals chapter's reading: 0/0 compares `false` "for compatibility with floating-point arithmetic", and the infinities are ordered (F-319). Row 672 closed with that edit. Why: a NaN test in software would slow the comparison against the hardware's own; measured, it is noise on today's boxed compiled path and costs 15 to 20 percent a comparison on unboxed doubles in Java, and whether it stops vectorisation is open (`perf-probes/nan-check-cost/REPORT.md`). The team built `false` and `Unordered` everywhere and never raised the error, and Java, Swift, Python's floats, Julia and Haskell all answer `false`.
- P-161 **The integer conversions: checked `as…` getters that raise `IntegerOverflow` on every integer type, `bitsAs…` getters for the bit pattern, today's names as the low-bits forms, and `ZZ`'s `narrow` and `widen` deleted.** On each of `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64` and `ZZ`, the getters `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` and `asZZ` raise `IntegerOverflow` where the value does not fit: of the 25, 5 are identities, 7 equal the coercions and 13 can raise. The four fixed widths have the compiler prelude's `bitsAs…` getters. `narrow`, `widen`, `unsigned`, `signed` and `big` keep the low bits, each declared on every type where it applies, so that no call reaches one through a coercion. `ZZ`'s conversions out are its five getters; the callers of its `narrow` and `widen` (`Library/Format.fss`, `Library/QuickCheck.fss`, the demo `sudoku.fss`, the test `XXXZZNarrowRungP`) move onto `.asZZ32` or `.asZZ64` with their values unchanged. The specification states the getters and names beside `narrow`'s sentence in `basic-integers.tex`, drops `ZZ` from it, and gives an Appendix I entry. P-72 (`narrow` keeps the low 32 bits on the fixed widths), P-73 (fixed-width arithmetic raises) and P-74 (an exact conversion is implicit) stand. So `z.asZZ64` raises for a `ZZ` too large, and `unsigned` of a negative value keeps the low bits, with `x.asNN32` or `x.asNN64` as its check. Why: the team's later work, Steele's prelude, made `asZZ32` raise in 2011 and named the bits `bitsAs…` in 2012; the specification's general sentence says that an integer result that overflows throws `IntegerOverflow`; a plain name that checks beside a name that tells its loss is Swift's and Julia's pattern; and `ZZ`'s two are wrong code: its `widen` can narrow, and turns 2^63 negative.
- P-165 **`asFloat` and the `=` built on it leave `trait Number`; each built-in number type keeps its own `asFloat`.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` each declare `asFloat`, so the written conversion `asFloat(x)` into `RR64` is unchanged at every concrete type; the numeral types declare none, since no numeral value exists when a program runs (P-174). Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other (P-74); otherwise the program writes the conversion, `asFloat(x) = y`. The vector norm takes a bound that promises a float; its form is the default of a fork on his review list: the norm at each of the eight number types, each by its own `asFloat` (F-324). `Float`'s `^` at a `Number` exponent, `random`, `atan2` and `printThreadInfo` are declared at `RR64`, and coercion carries `ZZ32`, `RR32` and numerals to them. The specification's sentence follows (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex:58-75`). P-74's rule, an exact conversion implicit and a lossy one written, stands. Why: the team's compiler prelude declares `Number` with nothing in it (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:509`), and the specification does not ground the method: its sentence that names it on `Number` is the revival's revision. The curator's rule for such a case: an early idea of the interpreter's library goes where the specification does not ground it and the later prelude eliminated it. With `Number` open (P-160), an abstract `asFloat` would force a program's own number, such as a complex number, to invent a float, and `Number`'s `=` would compare two different complex numbers by it.
- P-166 **`ZZ`'s and `QQ`'s values are value objects, and the specification's list of reference objects stops naming arbitrary-precision numbers.** The library declares `value object BigNum extends ZZ` (`LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:544`, `.fsi:196`), so every `ZZ` value is a value object, and `QQ`'s object `Ratio` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:649`) is a `value object` too. By the specification's rule two value objects of one type are strictly equivalent when their fields are, so two `ZZ` values built apart are `SEQV` when their integers are equal, `SEQV` converting each into its bits and comparing those, and two equal rationals built apart are `SEQV` in the same way. The specification's list in `Specification/basic/objects.tex` ("Reference objects include arbitrary-precision numbers") is revised to name them among the value objects, in the revision form (P-96) with one Appendix I entry. Why: the library's `value` declaration is the deliberate word, and where it is, the curator's rule brings the specification's example in line with the code. Detail: `reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, section 2.4, point 11, which found the split.

1	# Delegating: briefing, launching, watching and resuming workers
2	
3	**Workflow run**
4	: Run of a script by the Workflow tool, which launches one agent for each `agent()` call.
5	
6	**journal**
7	: Workflow run's log, `journal.jsonl` in `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/`: one `launched` line, then a `started` line for each agent call and a `result` line with its structured result.
8	
9	**headless session**
10	: `claude -p` session started from your shell.
11	
12	**archaeology**
13	: Search of git and the transcripts for how something came about. It returns cited evidence, not a judgement.
14	
15	**writer stream**
16	: Headless Opus session that writes a long writing pass in chunks, one slice of its entries or sections at a time, started and resumed by `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/writer-stream.sh`.
17	
18	## Which tier runs what
19	
20	- Name each worker's tier by its alias only: `model: 'opus'`, `'sonnet'` or `'fable'`.
21	- `explorations/coordinator/tools/tier-mode.sh fable` puts every agent of the workflow scripts and the headless writers on Fable. `regular` puts them back on this section's tiers, and `status` prints the setting. Switch only at the curator's word, and only while no workflow runs. Under the `fable` setting every worker runs on Fable, and this section's rules on which tier runs what do not apply.
22	- Use Sonnet only for archaeology and to fetch exact words. Have an Opus worker turn the evidence into a report, and condense a long report into a summary or the exact quotes that you need.
23	- To recheck a point at its source, have a fresh Sonnet scout fetch the exact words from the transcript or the commits. Have an Opus worker set them against the curator's memory and against the report, entry or summary that it differs from. Until the recheck ends, state neither side as right, and take no step that rests on the point.
24	- Run an Opus worker that writes or condenses a long report at `xhigh` effort: the Agent tool's `effort` option, `agent()`'s `opts.effort`, or `--effort xhigh` for a headless session.
25	- Run every writer on Opus: of skill text, of record entries, and of each longer report or page for the curator, also when this session runs on Fable. Fable writes no text that goes as written into the record, since its compressed register degrades the reasoning. A Fable worker may give corrections to a text that Opus writes, and Opus words them into the text. A Fable review may edit a batch record in place.
26	- The rules on Fable's text hold while Fable is at version 5.1. `explorations/coordinator/tools/model-now.sh` prints this session's model.
27	- For a cross-area question, Opus workers first gather cited evidence or a list of ways. Then, if neither the record nor the three principles (`SKILL.md`) settle it, run a Fable judgement, sparingly. If the fork stays consequential, put it to the curator as an ask.
28	- Four kinds of Fable work have a go in advance: the Fable judgement on a cross-area question, a judge's second ruling in a batch, the Fable review of each batch record, and the comparison of a rewritten skill part with the version that the curator approved. Ask first for any other Fable worker, such as one on your own conduct, one whose answer would reverse the curator's decision, or a Fable and an Opus worker run apart on one question.
29	- If you start a headless session on a tier other than Opus or Fable, set `FORTRESS_HEADLESS=1` in its environment. Otherwise the model check's alarm stops its work (`SKILL.md`, "The boot").
30	- Start every headless session with `--session-id` and a new UUID. Without it, its prompts read as the curator's messages in your own transcript.
31	- A Fable token also uses the all-models limits, at three to four times an Opus token's share of the session limit.
32	
33	## What a brief holds
34	
35	A brief holds what only you know: the problem, the question, what the answer is for, and where the sources are. Give the readings that the task needs and no more, and an order or steps only where they matter. A worker on the repository has `fortress-repo` loaded, and that skill loads the parts that the work needs. So leave the choice of those parts to the worker. Each extra reading costs your context, and the worker chooses well without it.
36	
37	- The problem, never the expected answer. On a design choice, ask the worker to list every way that the language and the library offer, and give it none of our notes or options.
38	- If a rule blocks an option, ask how the library gets around it.
39	- For a review, an ask to sort its findings by what each needs. The reviewer names each finding that would change a decision of the curator's, and gives options for those findings only.
40	- A pointer to the research on file, not a restatement of it.
41	- The record's measurements, as findings to cite, not claims to check again, even for a worker kept clean of our options. Name the one new thing to measure. Ask for a new measurement only if the tree has changed under a finding, and say what changed.
42	- The entries that it needs, by number. If the task needs an entry's linked entries or its history, name `facts-extract.sh`, which prints them. Quote whole, with its limit and its example, only a rule of the curator's that no entry holds yet.
43	- The people of the project by name and role, as the record and the authorship map `research/authorship.md` name them, never in your own words, since a worker copies your description into its text; where the task needs who wrote what, a pointer to the map.
44	- Before you quote the curator's words from a message, clean them. Fix the obvious typos of the phone's swipe keyboard and of dictation, and keep the meaning. Put `[?]` after each word whose reading is a guess.
45	- For an update of a document: a length cap against the version before. The update adds what landed.
46	- No second reader named in the brief, since that reframes the document.
47	- No request to measure or cap its own token spend. The spend is yours to watch.
48	- For an Agent-tool worker: every wait under 240 s. A long run is polled in steps, or handed to a script while the agent ends its turn.
49	
50	`fortress-repo` tells a worker on the repository which choices are its own. A worker loads no part of this skill by itself. If it does part of your work, such as an analysis, name the parts of this skill that the work needs.
51	
52	## Watching a run
53	
54	- If you launch a long or large run outside a batch, such as a probe that builds and runs suites for an hour, write its estimate of tokens written in the boot note. A probe can write ten times its estimate.
55	- Watch its spend: `spend.py <since-epoch> <path>`, where the path is the session's `subagents/` folder for agents, or the project's folder for headless sessions. If it passes the estimate, give the worker an instruction or end it. Watch no other run this way.
56	- When an overnight or long run starts, arm its check-ins: `send_later` reminders 45 minutes apart, in one turn (`cloud-container`, its stops part). An hourly check-in would let the cache expire.
57	- Keep each wait of yours under an hour. The `Monitor` tool can watch a run.
58	- Send a follow-up question to the worker that already holds its material, with `SendMessage`, also when it has finished: it goes on from its transcript and does not search again. If a worker waits on the curator between tasks, run it as a headless session and resume it within the hour (`--resume <id>`).
59	
60	## Interrupts and process stops
61	
62	An interrupt or a process stop kills every running Workflow agent and Agent-tool worker (`fortress-repo`, its session part). A compaction between turns leaves a Workflow run alive.
63	
64	- After an accidental interrupt, tell the curator, and resume the run.
65	- Resume a Workflow run, never relaunch it: `resumeFromRunId`, with the same script and arguments as at launch, byte for byte. A finished agent keeps its result. An unfinished one runs from its start, on its worktree's leftovers.
66	- The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of `agent()` calls, in call order. A hash given short where the launch gave it in full misses from the first call.
67	- If the script has changed since launch, resume from a copy as launched: `git show <launch commit>:<path>`. # Delegating: briefing, launching, watching and resuming workers

**Workflow run**
: Run of a script by the Workflow tool, which launches one agent for each `agent()` call.

**journal**
: Workflow run's log, `journal.jsonl` in `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/`: one `launched` line, then a `started` line for each agent call and a `result` line with its structured result.

**headless session**
: `claude -p` session started from your shell.

**archaeology**
: Search of git and the transcripts for how something came about. It returns cited evidence, not a judgement.

**writer stream**
: Headless Opus session that writes a long writing pass in chunks, one slice of its entries or sections at a time, started and resumed by `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/writer-stream.sh`.

## Which tier runs what

- Name each worker's tier by its alias only: `model: 'opus'`, `'sonnet'` or `'fable'`.
- `explorations/coordinator/tools/tier-mode.sh fable` puts every agent of the workflow scripts and the headless writers on Fable. `regular` puts them back on this section's tiers, and `status` prints the setting. Switch only at the curator's word, and only while no workflow runs. Under the `fable` setting every worker runs on Fable, and this section's rules on which tier runs what do not apply.
- Use Sonnet only for archaeology and to fetch exact words. Have an Opus worker turn the evidence into a report, and condense a long report into a summary or the exact quotes that you need.
- To recheck a point at its source, have a fresh Sonnet scout fetch the exact words from the transcript or the commits. Have an Opus worker set them against the curator's memory and against the report, entry or summary that it differs from. Until the recheck ends, state neither side as right, and take no step that rests on the point.
- Run an Opus worker that writes or condenses a long report at `xhigh` effort: the Agent tool's `effort` option, `agent()`'s `opts.effort`, or `--effort xhigh` for a headless session.
- Run every writer on Opus: of skill text, of record entries, and of each longer report or page for the curator, also when this session runs on Fable. Fable writes no text that goes as written into the record, since its compressed register degrades the reasoning. A Fable worker may give corrections to a text that Opus writes, and Opus words them into the text. A Fable review may edit a batch record in place.
- The rules on Fable's text hold while Fable is at version 5.1. `explorations/coordinator/tools/model-now.sh` prints this session's model.
- For a cross-area question, Opus workers first gather cited evidence or a list of ways. Then, if neither the record nor the three principles (`SKILL.md`) settle it, run a Fable judgement, sparingly. If the fork stays consequential, put it to the curator as an ask.
- Four kinds of Fable work have a go in advance: the Fable judgement on a cross-area question, a judge's second ruling in a batch, the Fable review of each batch record, and the comparison of a rewritten skill part with the version that the curator approved. Ask first for any other Fable worker, such as one on your own conduct, one whose answer would reverse the curator's decision, or a Fable and an Opus worker run apart on one question.
- If you start a headless session on a tier other than Opus or Fable, set `FORTRESS_HEADLESS=1` in its environment. Otherwise the model check's alarm stops its work (`SKILL.md`, "The boot").
- Start every headless session with `--session-id` and a new UUID. Without it, its prompts read as the curator's messages in your own transcript.
- A Fable token also uses the all-models limits, at three to four times an Opus token's share of the session limit.

## What a brief holds

A brief holds what only you know: the problem, the question, what the answer is for, and where the sources are. Give the readings that the task needs and no more, and an order or steps only where they matter. A worker on the repository has `fortress-repo` loaded, and that skill loads the parts that the work needs. So leave the choice of those parts to the worker. Each extra reading costs your context, and the worker chooses well without it.

- The problem, never the expected answer. On a design choice, ask the worker to list every way that the language and the library offer, and give it none of our notes or options.
- If a rule blocks an option, ask how the library gets around it.
- For a review, an ask to sort its findings by what each needs. The reviewer names each finding that would change a decision of the curator's, and gives options for those findings only.
- A pointer to the research on file, not a restatement of it.
- The record's measurements, as findings to cite, not claims to check again, even for a worker kept clean of our options. Name the one new thing to measure. Ask for a new measurement only if the tree has changed under a finding, and say what changed.
- The entries that it needs, by number. If the task needs an entry's linked entries or its history, name `facts-extract.sh`, which prints them. Quote whole, with its limit and its example, only a rule of the curator's that no entry holds yet.
- The people of the project by name and role, as the record and the authorship map `research/authorship.md` name them, never in your own words, since a worker copies your description into its text; where the task needs who wrote what, a pointer to the map.
- Before you quote the curator's words from a message, clean them. Fix the obvious typos of the phone's swipe keyboard and of dictation, and keep the meaning. Put `[?]` after each word whose reading is a guess.
- For an update of a document: a length cap against the version before. The update adds what landed.
- No second reader named in the brief, since that reframes the document.
- No request to measure or cap its own token spend. The spend is yours to watch.
- For an Agent-tool worker: every wait under 240 s. A long run is polled in steps, or handed to a script while the agent ends its turn.

`fortress-repo` tells a worker on the repository which choices are its own. A worker loads no part of this skill by itself. If it does part of your work, such as an analysis, name the parts of this skill that the work needs.

## Watching a run

- If you launch a long or large run outside a batch, such as a probe that builds and runs suites for an hour, write its estimate of tokens written in the boot note. A probe can write ten times its estimate.
- Watch its spend: `spend.py <since-epoch> <path>`, where the path is the session's `subagents/` folder for agents, or the project's folder for headless sessions. If it passes the estimate, give the worker an instruction or end it. Watch no other run this way.
- When an overnight or long run starts, arm its check-ins: `send_later` reminders 45 minutes apart, in one turn (`cloud-container`, its stops part). An hourly check-in would let the cache expire.
- Keep each wait of yours under an hour. The `Monitor` tool can watch a run.
- Send a follow-up question to the worker that already holds its material, with `SendMessage`, also when it has finished: it goes on from its transcript and does not search again. If a worker waits on the curator between tasks, run it as a headless session and resume it within the hour (`--resume <id>`).

## Interrupts and process stops

An interrupt or a process stop kills every running Workflow agent and Agent-tool worker (`fortress-repo`, its session part). A compaction between turns leaves a Workflow run alive.

- After an accidental interrupt, tell the curator, and resume the run.
- Resume a Workflow run, never relaunch it: `resumeFromRunId`, with the same script and arguments as at launch, byte for byte. A finished agent keeps its result. An unfinished one runs from its start, on its worktree's leftovers.
- The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of `agent()` calls, in call order. A hash given short where the launch gave it in full misses from the first call.
- If the script has changed since launch, resume from a copy as launched: `git show <launch commit>:<path>`. If the call order would differ, wrap `agent()` in the copy, so that the finished calls come in the journal's order of `started` lines. `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/design-batch10-opus.md` has such a wrapper (`resumeOrder`).
- If a batch's commit stage was killed before it committed, its edits are in `/home/user/fortress`. Resume with a commit prompt that names them.
- If a batch's gather was killed mid-work, resume the run, and leave the main tree as the gather left it. On the resume, the batch script's `recoverGather()` gives the gather a prompt that takes the uncommitted changes as its earlier attempt's work, so you write no prompt. Only the gather's first start checks that the main tree is clean.
- A new session cannot resume another session's run.
- An Agent-tool worker that a process stop killed goes on from its transcript on a `SendMessage`. One that an interrupt killed cannot. Relaunch it only at the curator's explicit ask, and tell the new worker its predecessor's leftovers.
- Give a Fable successor the leftovers in the tree, never the transcript: the safety filter can end a Fable worker that prints one.

## The Workflow tool

- The tool runs at most two agents at once in each Workflow run. The run's other agents wait. Several runs go side by side, each with its own two.
- Across agents, the cache serves the first message only when the whole prompt is identical. A project agent type's system prompt is cached for every agent of the type, so put text that every agent needs there.
- A project agent type written during the session is found only after a process stop. A project skill appears at once.
- `agent()` can return null for an agent that the harness marks failed after it delivered its result. Read its branch before you run it again.
- Check a script by parsing it as an async function body, not with `node --check`: `explorations/coordinator/tools/workflow-scenarios.js`.

## A long writing pass

A long writing pass, such as a run of the record or ledger clarity workflow, rewrites many entries or rows in chunks. To make it fast, run several Workflow runs side by side. In October 2026, four or five runs at once, eight or nine agents, ran to the end on this machine. More has not been tried. The orientation workflow takes no chunks, so it runs as one run.

- Split the items into chunks of about ten, or of the size that the workflow's README gives.
- Share the chunks evenly among the runs. Pass each run its share in its `chunks` argument.
- Give the chunks names that differ across all the runs. Each chunk writes only into its own folder, the run's `out` plus the chunk's name.
- If the workflow writes with writer streams, give each run its own `stream` name. Runs that share a stream take turns.
- Before the launch, write each run's exact arguments into a `runs.json` file in the pass's folder, and name that file in the boot note. After the launch, add each run's ID to it.
- The script resumes a stream while its context is small and its prompt cache is warm. Its header gives the limits. Otherwise it starts a fresh session.
- So the round that fixes a chunk after its checks resumes the session that wrote it, with its evidence still in the cache. A fresh writer would read everything again.
- End each round with one judge. For each item that a chunk's checks raise, it rules apply or hold, and writes the held items for the review queue. No chunk goes through a second fix round.
- Only you write the record files, so the runs do not conflict.
- As each run ends, apply its judged chunks to the record, check the record, commit and push, by "After a chunk" in the workflow's README. Then take the next run that has ended.
- If a chunk splits or merges an entry that another chunk also changes, apply that chunk first.
- If an interrupt or a process stop kills the runs, resume each one from its ID in `runs.json`, as "Interrupts and process stops" says.

## A second session

A second coordinating session contributes reviews and their commits, on a branch of its own from `main`. It runs no batch and does not change PLAN's order.
