<!-- What is established about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as it stands now, grouped by area: each entry the fact, its source and its test. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `FACTS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. -->

# Facts on record

## Execution model

- F-7 **Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases, and only the compiled path runs the static type checker.** Walk switches the checker off, and no switch turns it on. So walk checks no static types of expressions: an ill-typed expression shows only when it runs, as a failed dispatch or as another run-time error, such as F-239's refusal of an `if` on a value that is not a `Boolean`. At load, walk refuses some ill-formed declarations: the `fortress-repo` skill's `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists them, with their evidence in F-29 (`comprises` clauses), F-142 (the Meet Rule for Functional Methods) and F-145 (uncovered abstract methods and `override`). The phases and where the two paths part: the skill's "How a program runs". Detail: `explorations/repo-internals.md`, "The two worlds".
- F-9 **`fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's library, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, so it is no oracle for walk programs.** `Shell.java` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` for the command (row 69). P-12 has walk run the checker on its own programs after the switch-over, and walk cannot do so as it stands: it runs with type checking and the Scala checker off, the Java checker is gone (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:228-229`), and it has no case for the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, by reading (row 833).
- F-11 **The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main representational cost of microGPT-shaped array code.** So a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (the `fortress-repo` skill, "The compiled runtime"). In Java models of microGPT's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`. No such kernel compiles yet: the compiler prelude has no array type (row 305), and the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (P-37). In a hot compiled loop, escape analysis removes the temporary boxes, and one box per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration stays (F-301), as long as C2's inline depth reaches each box's constructor chain (F-302). Detail: `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4; `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` section 4.
- F-12 **On the compiled path, the scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` ran in 0.74 s in one session's measurement; the loop still pays for its generator, for boxing and for a transaction check at each use of its accumulator.** `bench1t` is `for i <- seq(1#20000000) do acc := acc 0.9999999 + 0.0000001 end` on a `var acc: RR64`, with both literals written in the loop. The time is the median of three loop-only runs at one thread (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Times taken in different sessions differ on this machine, so compare only times from one session. What the loop does, read in its bytecode (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 5): the `seq` loop becomes the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, which runs the iterations in order by a recursive split over boxed indices, with a closure call per element; each value is boxed (F-11); and the accumulator is a volatile cell whose read and write each first call `BaseTask.inATransaction`, as for every mutable local (F-40, what a size costs at run time, whose sized loop pays the same check). Within the boxing and the cell, the report counts four allocations per iteration, an interface call to the native wrapper and the casts, the part that unboxed doubles and `double[]` would attack. No share of the 0.74 s is measured.
- F-17 **The bytecode cache can come up empty after a library order that reports exit 0.** Running the same commands again, one at a time, made the jars. The cause is not known. Check the five jars before a compiled run (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`, "The library order"). Detail: `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled runtime" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becomes `LFRR64;` in `Box⟦FRR64⟧`, and `[D` is no class name, so stamping alone keeps every number boxed (F-11). The team left two separate traces for unboxing. The plan in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java` lists what to unbox: a primitive, a singleton object, unboxed fields, and a `comprises` clause whose types are unboxable; it says nothing of the loader or of instantiations. The loader has an empty "expando" stub (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`). A loader that stamps an `RR64` instance with a `double[]` field, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), does not exist and is unmeasured. Walk instantiates generics in its own evaluator, not by classes. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 1; `coordinator/array-design.md` section 2 (probe 1); `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 3, way A4.
- F-19 **By the specification, the iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments of a call or an operator may run in parallel, and a program must assume that they do.** A `for` loop is sequential only if every generator is, as `seq(g)` or `sequential(g)` makes it. An implementation may also run them one after another (`evaluation/parallelism.tex:88-90`), so a program cannot count on parallel runs either. For the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator, each path starts a task only where it judges it worth it: walk by `TupleTask.worthSpawning`, which also governs a call's arguments, and the code generator by `ParallelismAnalyzer`. Compiled, the arguments of a function call and of a dotted method call fork where the analyzer marked the argument tuple (`CodeGen.evalArg`; joins: F-350); it counts no call in the prelude's files (row 982) or of a function declared later in the file (row 987). A `for` loop over a range without `seq` runs by splitting the range into `do … also do … end` blocks. Under walk, every such block is a task, and walk's library splits a `ZZ32` range into chunks of at most 16 elements (F-350), and a range with a stride down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1498-1585`). Compiled, the first block runs in place, and each other block forks only where `BaseTask.forkIfProfitable` judges it worth it, as tuple elements do; the compiler prelude's `parloop` splits down to `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK` elements, 1 by default. `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the pool of worker threads (the `fortress-repo` skill, "Parallelism and mutable state"). By grep, no program under `explorations/`, the model programs and the probes, writes `spawn`, which starts an explicit thread, or an `also do` block, so their parallelism comes only from loops, tuples and arguments. The revival's tests under `ProjectFortress/` write both. Source: `Specification/basic/expressions/for.tex:28-32`, `tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:58-59`, `evaluation/parallelism.tex:50-80`.
- F-20 **Sizes, the `nat` and `int` static parameters, are values at run time; they check shapes, and no optimization uses them (F-40, what a size costs at run time).** The compiled checker checks them (F-67), and a sized program loads and runs compiled (F-129). Under walk, `Vector` and `Matrix` take their sizes from an array built at run time: `f[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\])` takes `s` from `array[\RR64\](3)`, and overloads on `Vector` and `Matrix` dispatch by rank (row 214). The array-type syntax `T[n]` with a `nat` parameter does not unify with such an array, "Cannot unify … with ArrayType", where `T[3]` with a literal size does (row 23). Walk matches sizes at dispatch. A mismatch, such as a `DOT`, the library's inner product, of a 2×3 matrix by a 2×3 matrix, whose inner sizes differ, is a `ProgramError`, "Failed to find any matching overload", that no `catch` takes (row 254). Source: `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:96`.
- F-21 **The February 2011 Working Draft's bare `Nothing`, one object for every `T`, is accepted on neither path: the grammar refuses its `excludes` clause, and without that clause `T` is undefined.** The declaration is `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:40`). Both paths stop at a syntax error at `excludes`, since an object has no `excludes` clause (measured: `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, E4). Without that clause, both report `T is undefined` at the `T` of the `extends` clause: a `where` clause on an object binds no type variable of its `extends` clause, as row 17 holds for a trait. Today's specification refuses the form in any case, by instantiation exclusion, and marks it "Not allowed" beside the parametric `Nothing[\T\]` that the interpreter's library writes (F-167). P-90 still calls the bare `Nothing` future work that waits for such `where` clauses, not tried before then. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-maybe/REPORT.md` section 5.
- F-22 **When a component's name differs from the api that it exports, neither path finds the component, for an exported function or variable alike.** The specification resolves an imported api to any component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex`). The tree looks only under the api's name, unless a user maps the api to its component by hand with `LinkShell`'s `alink` or `clink`. - F-37 **On the compiled path, a `typecase` clause on a sized type, such as `Vec[\ZZ32,3\]`, tests the value's own class, also when the size is a static parameter of the enclosing function.** The test is one `INSTANCEOF` on the class of the instantiation, `Vec⟦FZZ32,3⟧`. In a generic function, the class loader puts in the size when it makes the function's instance. So a `typecase` tells `Vec[\ZZ32,3\]` from `Vec[\ZZ32,4\]`, and does not read the descriptor that a size has (P-41). Limit: a `typecase` that is a whole function body, with clauses that need a coercion, fails in code generation, with a size or without (row 340). Gated by `compiler_tests/NatRtCase` and `NatRtCaseGen`; the bytecode was read in `perf-probes/nat/size-probes.md` section 4.
- F-38 **The compiled dispatcher chooses an overload arm generic in a size by the value's size, and the arm reads its size.** Called with an argument typed `Any`, the dispatcher reads the size off the value's descriptor. The checker's return-type rule compares the arms' own sizes (row 410). The dispatcher skips a size parameter's bound (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:1501-1502`). Gated by `compiler_tests/NatRtDisp`, `NatRtDispSize` and `NatRtDispTrait`. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/size-probes.md` section 2.
- F-39 **An operator static argument is a name substituted when the declaration is instantiated, on both paths and by the specification; no code reads it at run time.** An operator static parameter is declared `opr`, as in `object Op[\opr ODOT\]() end`. The specification and walk substitute the operator's name into the declaring trait's or object's methods. The compiled path carries it in the name of the instantiation's class; the operator has no descriptor, where a type or a size has one (P-41). No live declaration of the one library has an `opr` static parameter: `FortressLibrary`'s two, in `embiggen` and `Monoid`, are inside comments. In `tests/`, `compiler_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`, nine test files declare one. Compiled, `Op[\+\]()` dies with `NoSuchMethodError` on `Op❮+❯$RTTIc.factory()`, the factory of the instance's descriptor class, where walk prints `Op[\+\]` (row 366, open; its expected failure is `compiler_tests/XXXOprParamRungS`). A three-line change to `MethodInstantiater`, measured but not landed, fixes row 366's program run as a probe, `compile-ladder/rung-default-rendering/probes/skeptic/SkOprParam.fss`; the gated `XXXOprParamRungS` was not run with it (`perf-probes/nat/size-probes.md` section 5). Detail: `perf-probes/nat/opr-kind-history.md` sections 2 (the specification and both paths) and 3 (no reader at run time).
- F-40 **Measured on 2026-09-24 for two size designs that were not built, a size cost a few kilobytes at load and nothing in a hot loop, and only the overload dispatcher read a size off a value.** The two designs were design A, descriptor classes stamped for each size of each generic, and design B, a class for each number, passed to the generic's descriptor factory; both ran on the size probes' private build (`perf-probes/nat/size-cost.md` section 1). The built design, one descriptor object per size value from `RTTIsize.of` (F-129), is neither, and nobody has measured its load size or its loops. Under either design, a size's classes came to a few kilobytes, against the 8.6 MB of classes that every run loads. A loop bounded by the size constant was not measurably faster than one bounded by the storage's length read at run time. The loop cost about 31 ns per element, which the bytecode shows going to a transaction check on each read and write of a local, to boxing, and to a method call for each element read. Once C2 compiles a hot loop, a native helper's call is inlined whole and costs nothing, and the boxes of its mutable variables stay (F-301). A call dispatched on a size cost about 4 to 20 ns more than the same call that the checker resolved at compile time. The built design's rung measured only the dispatcher's lookup of a literal size's descriptor: 0.9 ns on the landed build, its six runs from -2.2 to 7.0 ns, and 2.6 ns on an earlier build, on a dispatched call of about 23 ns. By reading the code of 2026-09-24, no optimization uses a size (F-20 holds it for today's tree), and a dispatched call tests a size once per overload arm tried, as the built dispatcher's literal leaf also does (`OverloadSet.java`, `SizeLiteralStructure`). Detail: `size-cost.md`, "The answers"; `compile-ladder/rung-size-runtime/REPORT.md` section 12.
- F-41 **The compiled dispatcher tests a size that two parameters share, in `DOT`'s shape, for equality in both directions before it chooses the arm that shares it.** `compiler_tests/NatRtDot` declares `dot[\nat n\](a: Vec[\RR64,n\], b: Vec[\RR64,n\])` over a user object `Vec`, beside a catch-all `dot(a: Any, b: Any)`. Sizes 3 and 4 reach the catch-all: typed statically, in the one order that the test makes, and dispatched at run time, in both orders. Walk printed the same in the probe. A static mismatch compiles with no error: the checker gives it the catch-all's signature. The dispatcher's equality test is the team's own check for a type variable in two invariant positions (`OverloadSet.java`). The library's `DOT` was not run compiled; by reading, the matrix product's shared inner size takes the same check. Gated by `compiler_tests/NatRtDot`, which checks the four outputs. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/size-rung-probes.md` section 3.
- F-42 **The compiled checker skips a compilation unit's (an api's or a component's) overloading and return-type checks when an earlier stage of that unit has reported an error.** `StaticChecker` returns before `OverloadingChecker` if the earlier stages found errors (`StaticChecker.java:268-279`). So clearing an early error can raise the checker count, which sees only the errors before each unit's early return (F-53). The distance runs every stage of every unit whatever the earlier stages reported, so these errors are not hidden from it (`tools/distance/run.sh`, header). Detail: `perf-probes/nat/zero.md`, its opening section.
- F-43 **The overloading checker's memo hides some errors, and which ones changes from one build of the checker to another, so the gate's checker count and distance run with the memo off.** The memo keeps a "valid" verdict per pair of declarations. A pair that several traits inherit is checked once per trait, at that trait's instantiation, in hash-set order, so a pair valid for one trait is taken as valid for the next (`perf-probes/nat/triage.md` section 1). The memo is on by default (`OverloadingChecker.scala:79`), so an ordinary `fortress compile` can miss these errors. The JVM property `-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false` turns it off; the gate's checker count and distance stages set it.
- F-44 **The compiled checker enforces the multiple instantiation exclusion rule and relies on it, and the one library meets the rule.** The rule: no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait. The checker's Return Type Rule relies on it: with the rule relaxed alone, a program passes the checker and dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError` (`OverloadingOracle.scala:81-105`; the probe `ProbeMIEPick`). The team's JVM type mapping relies on it too: no closure of extends lists names one generic at two static arguments, so the class that template expansion makes for an instantiation carries the type relations over as Java ones (`Papers/Implementation/TypeMapping.tex:125`, read). F-48 gives the kinds of static argument that the rule compares. Walk applies no instantiation exclusion: it accepts a type that extends two instantiations, and its overloading check does not count them as excluding (row 416; the review's section 3). P-43 keeps the rule. Besides the flat number tower of P-43, the library meets it by three changes of `952892a00`: `TotalComparison` extends `Comparison` and `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, no longer `StandardTotalOrder[\TotalComparison\]`; `AnyMaybe` extends `AnyUniqueItem` alone, no longer `Equality[\AnyMaybe\]` beside it; and `andCondCombine` chooses `andRelCond` by a `typecase`, in place of a second `ANDCOND`. So under walk, a program's `p1 ANDCOND p2` of two relational predicates, conditions built from a relation over a generator, which `filter` fuses, is no longer itself a relational predicate (row 458). The distance holds no exclusion error (F-53). Detail: `reviews/multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md` sections 1 to 3; `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:123-125` (`TotalComparison`), `:1065` (`AnyMaybe`); `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:5088-5096` (`andCondCombine`).
- F-45 **Without the exclusion rule, every dispatcher would have to call its generic arms at the call site's static arguments, and no published work resolves a value that is in two instantiations of one generic under run-time dispatch.** The loader already gives a generic dispatcher the call site's static arguments; without the rule, its arms would have to use them instead of arguments read from the value (`reviews/mie-probes/scope-call-site-dispatch.md` section 3). The call at the dispatcher's static arguments is built for template dispatchers (F-136), and, by reading, not for one with an `opr` or `nat` static parameter (`compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` section 9). The team's 2012 patents allow a self-typed generic, one that comprises exactly its parameter, at several instantiations along a chain of subtypes: the forest rule (`reviews/mie-probes/patents-forest-rule.md` section 1). Alone, the forest rule leaves the specialisation hole open: a specialised declaration, more specific than the generic one, runs for a value at a narrower level of the chain, a subtype, and returns a type that a caller typed at that narrower level does not expect. Compiled under a shadow checker with the forest rule, a patched copy of the checker that never landed, such a run dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`; the tree's checker refuses such a program (the same note, section 3). Route C adds a return-type rule that closes the hole (F-46). Detail: `scope-call-site-dispatch.md` section 3; `reviews/mie-probes/literature.md`, "What the field settled and what it did not".
- F-46 **Route C, the patents' forest rule with a return-type rule over every level of a chain, closes the specialisation hole (F-45), but going back to a nested number tower under it needs work beyond the checker.** The library's tower was nested before route A flattened it (P-43). Built as a shadow checker on 2026-09-24 and run through the zero probe's stack on a library copy without the reduction markers, route C refuses 25 pairs at 21 of the nested tower's declarations: specialisations that a level below does not cover. Completing the tower needs seven more declarations and the identification of `Integral[\ZZ32\]` with `ZZ32`. The patents' `comprises T` on the self-typed traits licenses that identification, but it overflows the checker's stack (measured on the zero probe's copy of the checker, in the recursion of `Formula.scala` that the tree shares). A hierarchy check of its own could enforce the identification instead; none is built. Leaving route A for route C also needs: the tower nested again; the call-site fix in every dispatcher (F-136); in the code generator, a method for each middle level of a chain, whose absence, by the error text, makes such a chain die with `AbstractMethodError`; walk to accept the specialised pairs without overflowing on `comprises T`; and, for the identification, a way past the checker's overflow or the hierarchy check. Detail: `reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md` sections 2 to 5.
- F-47 **The exclusion rule refuses some of the specification's own examples; in their place, a parametric object with a factory, or a widening function, runs on both paths as a user program.** The refused examples are E1 to E10 of `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, "What was found": among them three `where`-clause examples, the Working Draft's `Nothing`, the nested number tower and `RationalQuantity`. The `where`-clause examples stop on both paths before the rule, in name resolution, at `T is undefined`. The alternatives were measured as user programs that declare their own types: a parametric object with a factory, such as `object Empty[\T\]` with `emptyList[\E\]()`, and a widening function, such as `widen[\T, S extends T\](c: C[\S\]): C[\T\]`. The library's `Nothing[\String\]` does not yet run on the compiled path's prelude (row 331, F-167). A marker object with a `coerce` in the generic trait, as `AltEmptyCoerce` has in `SList[\T\]`, also runs compiled, and walk applies such a coercion (row 389). The 2012 `covariant` keyword passes the compiled checker and dies at run time (row 404). The compiled checker refuses a coercion with its own static parameter between two instantiations, `coerce[\S extends T\](c: C[\S\])`, as a cyclic hierarchy. Inferred from the forest rule: route C (F-46) would rescue neither the `where`-clause examples, `Nothing` nor E8, the internal appendix's "Disjunctive Constraints"; only the tower (E5) and the root `Object`'s algebra (E7) would keep their original text under it. Detail: the same note.
- F-48 **The compiled checker's exclusion rule compares type arguments, and sizes only when both are literals.** Two boolean arguments count as no exclusion: `object F extends { Flag[\true\], Flag[\false\] }` passes the checker and dies in code generation (row 406, `compiler_tests/XXXBoolExtendsTwice`). Nor does a static parameter beside another argument: `object O[\nat n\] extends { Vec[\n\], Vec[\3\] }` passes the checker and dies at load with `ClassFormatError` (row 414, `XXXNatExtendsTwice`; the row also places its cause in `TypeHierarchyChecker`'s check of `extends` clauses). Two literal sizes do exclude: the checker refuses `object V extends { Vec[\3\], Vec[\4\] }`, "Types Vec[\3\] and Vec[\4\] exclude each other" (row 402, fixed). Gated by `compiler_tests/XXXNatExcludeChecker`, for the refusal of two literal sizes. The code is `TypeAnalyzer.scala:548-555`, "Todo: Handle bool args". Detail: `reviews/spec-refused-examples-judgement.md` section 6.
- F-49 **Under walk, a value form and a function form of one name are chosen by the argument's run-time type, so with the element type `Any` a function passed as the value goes to the function form.** Given a function, `fill` on an array of element type `Any` stored the function's results, `c[1] = 11`, not the function. The compiled checker refuses such a pair under the bound `Any`: a functional whose one parameter has a parametric type bounded by `Any` cannot be overloaded (the probe `FillBoxAny`). The one library has no such pair: `fill` takes a value and `tabulate` a function (F-158). Detail: `reviews/fill-overloads-ways.md` section 2.
- F-50 **The compiled checker lets overloads differ in static parameters, as the model of the OOPSLA 2011 paper does, which the specification now states (F-174); as ambiguous, it refuses only the pairs it cannot prove unambiguous.** It builds P-45. It cannot prove a pair over open traits, which no `excludes` or `comprises` clause closes, nor one whose domains exclude only through the exclusion rule and a bound, as the library's `CAP` on `ScalarRange[\I\]` beside `Range2D[\I,J\]` does. It also refuses some pairs that the paper accepts, by its Return Type Rule and by its positional rule, under which two generic declarations in the more-specific relation agree on their static parameters by position (F-75). The second lets a call whose untyped function argument only the expected type fixes type-check, since the coercion attempt cannot check such an argument (row 507). - F-137 **Under `walk`, a generic call's static arguments are inferred with coercion, by P-74's promotion, also for the declaration that an overloaded call chooses (P-46).** A lone type parameter is one that is the whole declared type of some argument and that no other argument fixes through a type such as `List[\T\]`. So `ZZ32` with `ZZ64` gives `ZZ64`. `ZZ64` with `RR64` gives the declared bound, the only candidate that admits both, since a `ZZ64` goes into `RR64` only when written out (P-74). With no narrowest candidate, the parameter takes its bound where every argument is below the bound (F-141), and otherwise the arguments' join. Walk, which has no static types, promotes from the run-time types. So where a static type is wider than its value, the two paths instantiate differently (row 509). The rule does not reach these open defects: a static argument that only the call's result mentions, at a typed binding (row 510); and a varargs or tuple parameter over mixed widths (row 511). Nor does it reach, by inference and not measured, a numeral that fits `ZZ32` passed alone for a parameter whose bound a `ZZ32` neither extends nor coerces into, since walk reads such a numeral as a `ZZ32` (P-76). - F-138 **Each integer type declares its own `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX`, so under `walk` the family answers at the type that its arguments promote to.** It builds P-47. Walk reads and computes a size exactly, with no wrap: it reads a size used as a value as a `ZZ32` up to 2^31-1 and as a `ZZ64` above. The checker types such a value `ZZ32` (P-173, F-342). - F-141 **Under `walk`, a type parameter that nothing at a call fixes takes its declared bound, and a lone one with no narrowest candidate takes its bound where every argument is below it.** It builds P-48. A lone type parameter is one that is the whole declared type of some argument and that no other argument fixes (F-137); where some argument is not below its bound, it takes the arguments' join. A type parameter that the declared parameter types mention only in function domains, an odd number of arrows deep and never inside a static argument, as `T` in `g: T -> ZZ32`, is bounded by the arguments only from above. Where nothing bounds it from below, it takes the meet of its declared bound and the bounds that the arguments place on it. An F-bounded parameter stays open (F-143). A reduction or comprehension that writes no static argument fixes its big operator's parameter by the declared type of its value, else by its elements' join (F-228). ## The library's arrays and algebra

- F-151 **In the interpreter's library, `Vector`, `Matrix` and their factories and operators bound their element type by `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`.** `Number` declares no arithmetic, so the compiled checker accepts the bodies' arithmetic only through `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]`. `Number` stays in the bound, though it has no `comprises` clause now (F-324). The four juxtapositions of a vector or a matrix with a scalar `T`, in either order, stand beside the library's juxtapositions with a `String`, and the checker finds no error in them (F-53); no run measures what now keeps a scalar `T` apart from `String`. The vector norm is declared at each of the eight number types, by its own `asFloat` (F-324). The eight number types meet the bound. `Number` itself and the numeral types do not, since none is a ring at its own type. So `Vector[\Number,n\]` is not a well-formed type, and `array1` and `array2` have no branch for `Number`: called at `Number`, they give a plain array at run time, not a vector or a matrix (F-229). The checker accepts a call whose argument's type is built from the caller's own type parameter under the same bound, such as the norm's `squaredNorm(me)` (F-227). The scalar extension, the eight operators between an array and a scalar, has bounds of its own, also with `Number` (F-119). Gated under walk by `tests/ArrayElementAlgebra.fss`. The bound is the default that `reviews/array-fork2-judgement.md` recommended. Detail: that judgement, sections 2.5 (what `Number`'s `comprises` clause gives), 2.9, way 3 (the ring alone, measured) and 4 (the bound and its cost).

Walk accepts, unchecked, a carrier that extends both `Matrix` and `MultiplicativeRing`, and its `+` then fails (row 371). The specification's `T^n` denotes these traits (row 24), and neither path takes it. Detail: `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 2.

- F-162 **Citing `Specification/library/apis/*.tex` as an independent standard is circular.** The team says that the library part "is largely automatically generated from the API code" (`Specification/library/structure.tex:25-31`). The build renders these listings from the `.fsi` files of `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, and the listings are not in the tree. So a listing cannot justify an edit of an `.fsi` file: the edit changes the listing in the next built PDF. Cite the `.fsi` line. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` holds the rule.
- F-163 **Of the two copies of the specification, `Specification/` is the one to search and change; `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is byte for byte the Working Draft of 2011-02-02, and only its `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the 1.0 text.** `git diff --quiet 2f8b4331a:Specification c02fa44d0:Specification-1.0-frozen` succeeds; `2f8b4331a` is the team's last commit of the draft (2011-02-02). In the frozen copy, Appendix I, the changes appendix, is a stub that the team left; in `Specification/` it holds the revival's changes (P-96). `Specification/fortress.pdf` is a draft build, so the team's `\note` boxes print. A third text, the team's unfinished restart, is later on some topics (F-166). The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` says how to cite and change each copy. Detail: `reviews/spec-change-form.md` sections 5 and 7.
- F-165 **The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, and `main` descends from `8fe1daa8f`, which copied a third-party Java 9 port onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`.** The port shares no history with this tree, and most of its 1,506 files are removed or redone. Of the port's code, only the `FTypeArrayList` fix for the JDK 8 `TreeSet` crash still runs. `lineage.md` lists what can go with no change of behaviour: that fix, replaced by `clean-ladder`'s two-line repair, and the port's dead jars, dead files and cosmetic edits. The branch `clean-ladder` (`8332bd34f`) rebuilds on `a874948ac` without the port and never replaced `main`. Detail: `coordinator/lineage.md`, "The facts" (the fork, the graft and the port's files), and "Verification against Pavol's recollection (the same worker, re-briefed)", items "Working code" and "Verdict" (the running piece and what can go).
- F-166 **On the topics of its Types chapter, such as the exclusion rule and covariance, the team's latest word is the unfinished restart, not `Specification/`.** The restart, `Documentation/Specification/`, was never adopted. Its Types chapter restates the exclusion rule as "instantiation exclusion" and adds `covariant`. On the rest of static parameters, and on traits beyond a stub, exceptions, components and the numeric library, `Specification/` is the only statement. Which text governs is the curator's: `Specification/` stays the standard, the Types chapter is cited beside it, and `covariant` is future work (P-25). The type group's POPL 2019 paper is later than both (F-271). Detail: `coordinator/spec-lineage.md` section 6 and its "Coordinator's check (2026-09-26)".
- F-167 **The specification states instantiation exclusion and keeps each example that the rule refuses, marked "Not allowed"; the calculi of Appendix A carry a callout that they predate the rule.** It builds P-97. It also bars a `where`-clause variable from an `extends` clause's static arguments. The covariance example, the empty list, the empty optional value and the root type `Object`'s algebraic supertraits each stand beside the library's shape, which runs on both paths except `Nothing[\String\]` on the compiled prelude (row 331). A subtrait of every instantiation stays as the counterexample that introduces the rule, and the internal appendix's refused examples get a callout each. The checker does not yet refuse two cases: an object that extends two instantiations that differ only in a `bool` argument (row 406), and one that extends two instantiations of one trait where one instantiation's argument is the object's own static parameter, such as `O[\nat n\] extends { Vec[\n\], Vec[\3\] }` (row 414). Detail and examples: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md` sections 2 and 3; its section 4.2 (the calculi's callout).
- F-168 **The specification's number chapters describe the flat library, and its advanced chapter on rational quantities stays word for word under a callout that marks it superseded.** The eight number types are siblings under `Number` (F-131). They convert by the library's coercions (P-74), and every other conversion is explicit, such as `asFloat(x)`. The sign-refined types, such as positive ℚ, are gone; a program tests a value's sign at run time (P-80). ℚ holds +∞, −∞ and 0/0, and claims neither a field nor a total order. `QQ` extends the four algebraic traits that the library declares on it, `StandardPartialOrder`, `StandardMinMax`, `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, and their laws hold for the finite rationals. F-172 gives the integer chapter's rules. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-numbers/decision-record.md` section 3; `Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex:245-250` (ℚ's traits); `Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex:14` (the callout).
- F-169 **The Working Draft never wrote static-argument inference, never named the type that a library gives an integer numeral, and never named a range's integer type; the specification's text on these is the revival's.** The Working Draft's inference chapter is a heading and notes. It described numeral types, such as `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]`, and said that libraries define coercions from numerals to integers and rationals. But a note of its own leaves the numeral types' hierarchy undescribed, and it names no type that a library declares for a numeral. Its ranges section names no integer type. The later restart adds nothing on the three. So a citation of the specification on them cites the revival, not the team. The revised text states F-173's inference rule and F-170's ranges, and gives an integer numeral the Working Draft's `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]`, its four numbers as static arguments (P-174). Detail: `reviews/numerics-plan-coordinator/evidence-B.md` sections 1 and 2; `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:87-96` and `:132-148` (the note and the coercions); `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:146-161` (the callout on the numeral types).
- F-170 **The specification's ranges are over ℤ32, and its own ranges over wider integer types are respelled.** An integer numeral, and a `nat` or `int` parameter, used as an operand of an explicit range, such as `a` or `n` in `a#n`, converts to ℤ32 (row 485, fixed). An operand of any other integer type is a static error. A loop whose counter must have a wider integer type runs over a range of ℤ32 values and widens each element. The two examples that built `ZZ64` ranges run over ℤ32, and `ant testSpecData`, a gate step, runs both (F-114). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-ranges/decision-record.md` sections 2 and 3; `Specification/basic/expressions/ranges.tex:42-60` and `:90-111`.
- F-171 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause as the restart's Types chapter does: every value of the trait is a value of a listed type.** So a trait or object that extends the closed trait must be below a listed type, with two exceptions. A trait with a `comprises` clause of its own may stay unlisted if each of its own listed types is below a listed type of the closed trait. A trait with static parameters may stay unlisted if at least one type extends it and every type that extends it is below a listed type. A listed type may be an instantiation at the trait's static parameters or `where`-clause variables. The text does not say whether a bare type variable may be listed; walk overflows its stack on one (row 407). The compiled checker departs in three ways: it checks only the closed trait's immediate subtypes (row 487), it reads the clause in the subtrait's own type-variable names (row 489), and it finds extenders by the simple text of a name (row 490). Whether the team's commented `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]` is valid is open (F-121). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-comprises/decision-record.md` section 2; `Specification/basic/traits.tex:246-269`.
- F-172 **The specification's integer chapter states the library's integer rules.** The getters `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` and `asZZ` keep the value or throw `IntegerOverflow`. `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the bits and throw nothing: `narrow` converts a `ZZ64` to `ZZ32`, and an `NN64` to `NN32`, by keeping the low 32 bits, so a value that does not fit wraps. `ZZ` has neither `narrow` nor `widen`. `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` work on the five integer types. On `ZZ` they are `shift`, which is exact at any count. On a fixed-size type, `LSHIFT` loses the bits shifted out and throws nothing. `GCD` and `LCM` are nonnegative, and one that a fixed-size type cannot hold throws `IntegerOverflow`. At a negative power, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 throws `DivisionByZero`, and any other base throws `IntegerOverflow`. The library follows the same power rule under walk; the compiled path's own library does not (F-263). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-integer-rules/decision-record.md` section 2; `Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:39-98` (the conversions and the shifts) and `:562-574` (the power); `Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:262-268` (`GCD` and `LCM`).
- F-173 **The specification's type-inference chapter states the rule that the compiled checker builds: the declaration is chosen first, then its static arguments are inferred.** It states P-46, P-48 and P-49. A type parameter that a parameter's declared type mentions inside another type, as `List[\T\]` mentions `T`, is fixed by the argument at that position. One that is the whole declared type of one or more parameters, as `T` is of `x: T`, and that nothing else fixes, takes the narrowest type, within its bounds, that every one of those arguments has or converts into: `ZZ64` for a `ZZ32` and an `NN32`. Where there is none, and no numeral settles the tie, it takes its bound, narrowed by what the call's expected type requires of the return type (P-48). So does a type parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes. Inference never gives a type parameter `BottomType`. The compiled path departs from the chapter in these ways, among others. Its prelude lacks the coercion of `NN32` into `ZZ64`, so a `ZZ32` and an `NN32` instantiate a type parameter at `ZZ`, not `ZZ64`; no callout names this (row 442, `compiler_tests/XXXInferPromoteNN32`). The callouts at `Specification/basic/inference.tex:284-346` and `:447-511` also give walk's departures, such as the return type `BottomType` that walk gives a function expression that declares none (row 587). Plain tests gate the rule for a type parameter that is a parameter's whole type, at its bound where no argument type is narrowest, on both paths: `compiler_tests/InferLone*` and `tests/InferLone*Walk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-instance-bound/REPORT.md` (the bound rule); `Specification/basic/inference.tex:45-125` (the chapter's rule).
- F-174 **The specification states the type group's 2011 overloading model: declarations of one name may differ in their static parameters, and a declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration over all its instances within its bounds.** It states P-45 and P-42. The section "Declarations with Static Parameters" states the OOPSLA 2011 paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Return Type and Meet. It gives one more restriction as the compiled path's, not the language's. Where one generic declaration is more specific than another with as many static parameters, the two must declare them of the same kinds, position by position. Also, the more specific one's return type must be a subtype of the other's when their static parameters are matched by position, so the checker refuses an override whose return type reorders its static parameters (row 398, fixed). The section "Principles of Overloading" forbids overloading a functional whose single parameter's type is a type parameter with the bound `Any` written, as `T extends Any`. A type parameter with no `extends` clause, whose bound is also `Any`, is exempt. Both paths refuse such an overload: the checker in `OverloadingChecker.checkBoundAny`, and walk since row 534's fix. Neither path runs every set that the rules allow. Appendix I's entry "Overloading with static parameters" names the sets that each path fails. In row 542, the checker refuses a generic declaration beside a plain one over an object type, as `ident[\T\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: Circle): Circle`. In row 537, the code generator fails on two generic declarations whose bounds differ. In row 539, walk refuses at load the 2019 paper's valid set over an array list and a list. In rows 779 and 780, walk fails on two generic functional methods one of whose declared domains lies inside the other's: in a trait or object without static parameters it refuses them at load, and in a trait with static parameters it loads them, but a call to which both apply fails. Detail: `Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:134-150` and `:531-674`; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 3 and 4.
- F-175 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause at the level of values in every passage.** It builds P-60. Appendix I's entry "Traits with comprises clauses read at the level of values" records the change. A call whose argument's static type stands between two closed traits runs the declaration that covers its value. Where its declarations have no static parameters, its type is the intersection of its most specific declarations' return types. Appendix I names five places where the compiled path departs. The checker checks a `comprises` clause at the closed trait's immediate subtypes only (row 487). The code generator crashes on a method call on a result typed by that intersection (row 540). Where any declaration of the overload set has static parameters, the checker types such a call by one of its most specific declarations instead, a deliberate choice (row 543). The checker refuses the Meet Rule's example for closed traits when its declarations have static parameters (row 546). The checker's verdict on an overload set can depend on the components compiled before it in the same JVM (row 547). Detail: `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:3464-3660`, with the rows at `:1674-1677` and `:3730-3737`; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 8 and 9.
- F-176 **The specification allows arithmetic in a size, and two size arguments are identical when they are written alike once each operation whose operands are numerals is replaced by its value.** It states P-55. By the grammar, a size is a numeral, a name, a sum, a difference, a product, a power to a numeral or a name, or a bracketed size. So `2 3` and `6` are identical, but `s0 s1` and `s1 s0` are not. Two types are identical when they have the same name and identical static arguments, sizes compared this way. Two sizes are known to differ when they are two different numerals. A static parameter, or a size in which one occurs, is not known to differ from a numeral, since an instance may make them equal. F-146 gives the compiled checker, and F-222 walk's arithmetic. When walk infers a size parameter from a call's argument type, it matches a numeral and binds a name, and solves no size written as an operation: read in `IntNat.unifyStaticArg` (`interpreter/evaluator/types/IntNat.java:126-147`), and observed in row 767. Source: `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:49-62`; `Specification/appendices/grammars/concrete-syntax.tex:533-547` (`IntExpr`).
- F-223 **The specification's No Duplicates Rule is the papers' non-strict rule, and the compiled checker applies it, to functional methods wherever their `self` parameters stand, abstract ones included.** Two declarations of one name may not each be applicable to every call to which the other is, as in the type group's papers of 2011 and 2019 (P-26). The checker refuses such a pair, two functional methods at different `self` positions and an abstract functional method beside a concrete one among them: "There are multiple declarations of f with the same parameter type", naming the domain of the declaration written first. It checks symbolic operators too (F-281): `opr ||(self, y: S)` beside `opr ||(x: S, self)` in a trait `S` is refused, 'There are multiple declarations of || with the same parameter type: (S)'. Walk refuses at load such a pair of two generic declarations whose parameter types mention their static parameters, as `dup[\T\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `dup[\U\](x: Box[\U\])`; it refuses too a generic declaration beside one whose parameter types are its bounds, a plain one or a generic one whose parameter types mention none of its static parameters, 'fails because their parameter lists have the same types'. Gated by `compiler_tests/XXXNoDuplicatesRule`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositions`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsPlain`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstract` and `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstractSelfPositions`, the symbolic operator's case by `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsOperator`, walk's refusal by `tests/NoDuplicatesRuleWalk`, and those two refusals by `tests/GenericBesidePlainSameDomain` and `GenericBesideGenericSameDomain`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-popl-examples/REPORT.md` section 4, its `SKEPTIC.md` section 2, `compile-ladder/rung-duplicates-coverage/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 8, and `compile-ladder/rung-checker-abstract-callsite/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-271 **The type group's POPL 2019 paper gives P-48's instance rule, and its soundness proof does not cover the library's F-bounded functions, such as `SUM` and `BIG MAX`.** By P-48's rule, a type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes the intersection of its upper bounds. The paper is later than both the specification and the team's restart (F-166). Its calculus does not let a method type parameter occur in an upper bound, so F-bounded method parameters are outside it. It also leaves out top-level functions and functional methods, among other limits. `reviews/decisions-review/popl-recheck.md` checks the curator's decisions against the paper. Detail: `research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md` sections 6 and 8.
- F-272 **The coercion example of the specification's "Coercion Resolution", over its own traits `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and `ZZ128`, declares the exclusions that the chapter's definitions need: `ZZ32 excludes { ZZ64, ZZ128 }` and `ZZ64 excludes { ZZ128 }`.** A type `T` rejects `U` when every type that coerces to `T` excludes `U`. `T` is no less specific than `U` when it is a subtype of `U`, or excludes, coerces to and rejects it. So the choice of the more specific declaration depends on the exclusions. In the rung's probe, with the traits renamed `S32`, `S64` and `S128`, since the first two names are the library's, the revised example ran on both paths: `f(S32Of)`, on an `S32` value, chose `f` on `S64` and gave 1. No gated test runs the printed example. Row 394, fixed, names `tests/CoercionMostSpecificRungC.fss`, a walk test of the choice of the more specific coercion over three traits of the example's shape, each of which excludes both others. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-integer-rules/decision-record.md` section 4, decision 6; `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:558-574` (the definitions) and `:641` onward (the example).
- F-273 **The specification gives the run-time instance of a generic declaration that dispatch reaches, and that the static call did not select, by the POPL 2019 paper's rule.** It builds P-48. A declaration that the static call selected runs at the instance inferred for the call (F-173). content.content:
1	<!-- The record-landing workflow: after a climb batch's post-batch review, bring the record in line with the landing (FACTS, POSITIONS and their histories, the ledger rows the evidence names, PLAN, PLAN-history, the review queue, INDEX and line fixes in other notes) in a worktree of its own, land its two commits on `main` and run the orientation update after them; then have the skill writer bring the `fortress-repo` skill in line, a cold read, the writer's fixes, the page of the skill's changes and the pushes; then the revival page's update, its commit and push, and its republish; how to launch it, what it writes, and how the coordinator reviews the landed commits. -->
2	
3	# The record-landing workflow
4	
5	`record-landing.js` does the record's work after a landing, which the coordinator did by hand through a record writer and a routing worker until climb batch 24. It is the smallest first version of the design `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-landing-workflow.md` (`5384a4f35`), which the curator approved with its eight defaults on 2026-11-02. It runs in six stages for the record, in the pattern of the orientation workflow (`../orientation/orientation.js`), five more for the skill after the orientation update ("The skill update"), and one for the revival page ("The revival page"):
6	
7	1. **Sort** (Opus, `sort.md`): `prepare.sh` makes the worktree and its branch and writes the evidence into the run's folder (`evidence.py`'s header lists its six files; `plan.md` ends with the PLAN lines that look stale, from `plan-moves.py --stale-at`, cut at 40,000 characters, past which the whole list is in `plan-stale.txt`, which the cut line names); the sorter reads it, the review's routing part and the batch record's items, and writes `owed.md`, one line per change with its number, its home, its kind, its weight, its ground and its writer, and marks each kind and each "Needed by" that no source states as set by the workflow.
8	2. **Write**: a Sonnet driver runs `drive.sh 1` in the background and waits for it in steps of 240 s, under the five minutes that its prompt cache lives. `drive.sh` starts two headless Opus writer streams side by side through the worktree's copy of `../record-clarity/writer-stream.sh`: the entries writer (`entries.md`: FACTS, POSITIONS, an entry's history, ledger rows, as `record.apply` and `rows.rewrite`) and the routing writer (`routing.md`: PLAN, PLAN-history, the queue, INDEX, other notes, edited in the worktree). Then `checks.sh 1` writes `mech-1.md`.
9	3. **Check**: the checker (`check.md`: coverage, fidelity, form and routing) and the clarity cold reader (`../record-clarity/coldread.md`, unchanged, told to write its report in parts of five entries) on `clean.txt`, side by side.
10	4. **Fix**: `drive.sh 2` resumes both streams once with the three reports, then `checks.sh 2` writes `mech-2.md`.
11	5. **Judge** (Opus, `judge.md`): apply or hold each change once, `final.apply` and `final.rewrite`, `diff.md` (within 10,000 characters), and `final.sh`, which runs every check again and makes two commits on the branch. The judge writes nothing after the commits.
12	6. **Land** (Sonnet, in the script): only when the judge's checks pass (the branch holds its commits past AT, `mech-final.md` says every check passes, the worktree is clean), the lander puts the two commits on `main`, runs the checks on `main`, pushes, and removes the worktree and the branch; then the script runs the orientation workflow in update mode as a child workflow (`../orientation/orientation.js`, one level deep), on the entries in the orientation call of `diff.md`'s "Next". "Landing its result" gives each step.
13	7. **Skills** (a Sonnet driver; the skill writer, a headless Opus session): `skills.sh N 1` writes the writer's task from `skill-task.md` and the landed files, and starts a fresh writer on it through `../skill-writer.sh new`; the writer installs what the orientation judge accepts and brings the `fortress-repo` skill in line with the landing, and commits on `main`.
14	8. **Cold read** (Opus): the changed parts, by `../../skill-cold-read-brief.md`, as a worker new to the repository.
15	9. **Fixes**: `skills.sh N 2` resumes the same writer on the cold read's flags (`skill-fixes.md`).
16	10. **Page** (Opus, `page.md`): the page of `fortress-repo`'s landed changes, by the source and the URL that the boot note names, published by that URL.
17	11. **Push** (Sonnet, in the script): `folders.sh N` commits the run's folders, then the pushes as the Land stage's; the result's `line` is the one line for the coordinator's chat message.
18	12. **Revival page** (Sonnet, in the script; then a Sonnet publisher, `revival-publish.md`): `../revival-page/update.py --landing N --run-start base` in the main tree, the files that it names committed by named paths and pushed as the Push stage's; then the page published by its URL with the Artifact tool. The result's `line` gains the page's commit and version.
19	
20	The mechanical checks (`checks.sh`): the six record files reset to the worktree's base, the cut-only POSITIONS lines checked with `../record-clarity/words-subset.py --root`, the writers' files applied with `record.py apply`, `../ledger-clarity/apply.py` and `ledger.py add` (the new rows of `rows.add`, or at the final round the judge's `final.add` where it wrote one), each history block "by climb batch N landing workflow (Opus)"; then `record.py check --base`, `ledger.py check`, `ledger.py landing-check`, `check-index.sh`, `plan-moves.py`, `queue-check.py` and `lengths.py`.
21	
22	- `plan-moves.py` fails a line out of PLAN that is not word for word in PLAN-history. Its `LOOK` lines, which never fail, name each PLAN line that still looks stale: a line whose own review-queue item is in (a) and that carries no cleanup's mark ("closed at the cleanup of DATE"), a list of items that names a settled one or differs from the queue's list that it names, and a review finding that a commit outside the record names. The checker takes each as a coverage failure, unless `owed.md` or the routing report says why the line stays.
23	- `queue-check.py` fails a gap in the new numbers, a new open item without "Needed by", a count that its items do not make, and an item new in "Answered by a decision of his" that cites no word of his on that same item, or that names a default taken without him ("at its default", "by the coordinator"). Such an item stays open, landed and then reviewed. The rule leans to keeping an item open: a true answer of his worded with those phrases fails too, and is reworded.
24	- `lengths.py` informs: each changed entry's length, and each entry already over 600 that grew, which the judge holds unless the owed clause alone explains the growth.
25	
26	`drive.sh --dry-run` prints the commands of a round and starts nothing. The streams' headless sessions run `facts-extract.sh` and the `git` reads that `writer-stream.sh` allows, and not `record.py`, `ledger.py` or the checks, which need an approval that a headless session cannot get. So `checks.sh` is the first to apply and check the writers' files, after each round, and the fix round reads its output in `mech-1.md`.
27	
28	Every brief reads the record only through `facts-extract.sh`, `record.py` and `ledger.py` in the worktree, and entries are written only through `record.py`. The run takes three arguments and no text, so a run gives the workflow data, never rules of its own. The briefs change only at the curator's yes.
29	
30	## Running it
31	
32	After the post-batch review is committed:
33	
34	    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/record-landing.js',
35	               args: { batch: 'N', base: 'BASE', landing: 'LANDING' } })
36	
37	It makes `/home/user/fortress-landing-N` on the branch `record/landing-N` at `main`'s head. A replay adds `at`, the commit to make the worktree at, and its worktree and branch end in `-replay`; it stops after the judge, and lands nothing and runs neither the orientation update, the skill update nor the revival page. The replay of climb batch 24's landing, before the first live run at climb batch 25's:
38	
39	    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/record-landing.js',
40	               args: { batch: '24', base: 'b0f6cd6b7', landing: '25238e60c', at: '43cd61b62' } })
41	
42	That one runs in `/home/user/fortress-landing-24-replay` on `record/landing-24-replay`. A killed run resumes with the same script path, `resumeFromRunId` and the same args, byte for byte; each script skips a step whose output exists. During a run the coordinator writes none of the files that the workflow writes; a decision that the curator gives meanwhile is recorded after the landing. The design's estimate for a landing like climb batch 24's was 0.9M to 1.7M tokens written and 1 to 1.5 hours; the replay wrote 2.06M in 65 minutes (`process-engineering/record-landing-replay-24.md`, section 6). With the driver's waits under five minutes and the cold read in parts, a like landing writes about 1.8M, an estimate. The skill update adds about 0.4M to 0.7M, an estimate: at climb batch 25's landing the coordinator's two writer tasks wrote 107K to the cache, the rest is the cold read, the page and the drivers.
43	
44	## What it writes
45	
46	Until the landing, everything goes in the worktree, and the main tree is not touched. The run's folder, `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/record-landing/` in the worktree, holds `run.env`, the evidence, `owed.md`, the writers' files, briefs and reports (the entries writer's new ledger rows in `rows.add`: each row line, `| ? | ...`, under a line `## TITLE` that names its section, a title of `ledger.py sections`, as in `## 10. Strings, maps and printing`; `checks.sh` adds each with `ledger.py add` after the other applies, so the first commit carries it, and names in its summary a row line with no such line above it, which it does not add), `check.md`, `cold-read.md`, `mech-1.md`, `mech-2.md`, `mech-final.md`, `final.apply`, `final.rewrite`, the commit messages and `diff.md`, and the logs of the rounds, which git ignores. The markers of finished rounds are in the worktree's `tmp/record-landing/`, which git ignores too, so the worktree is clean after the commits. The branch holds two commits: FACTS, POSITIONS, their histories and the ledger; then PLAN, PLAN-history, the queue, INDEX, the other notes and the run's folder. Each message ends "By the climb batch N landing workflow (Opus).", then the committing part's footer. The landing puts the two commits on `main`, and the run's folder with them, at `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/record-landing/` in the main tree; the logs go with the worktree. The workflow's result names the worktree, the branch and `diff.md`, holds the judge's final message with the two hashes, and adds `land` (how the commits landed, their hashes on `main`, the refs pushed, what was removed, the entries given to the orientation update) and `orientation`, the child workflow's result; then `skills`, `coldRead`, `fixes`, `page` and `push`, the skill update's stages, and `line`, the one line for the coordinator's chat message; then `revival` and `revivalPublish`, the revival page's two agents; on a stop, `stopped` says where and why. The skill update writes in the main tree, in `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/skills/`: `base.txt`, `task-1.md`, `writer-1.md`, `cold-read.md`, `task-2.md`, `writer-2.md`, and the logs, which git ignores; its markers and its writer's session are under the main tree's `tmp/record-landing-N/`. The writer's commits are on `main`; `folders.sh` commits the `skills/` folder and the orientation update's `orientation/` folder in one more commit. The revival page's stage writes, through `update.py`, the files that the script's README names (the page's two files, `landings.csv` and its row for the batch, the chart and `measure.py`'s five data files, the GitHub Pages copy under `docs/`), and commits them in one more commit, "Revival page: where it stands at the landing of climb batch N, the record chart regenerated"; its log and marker are `revival.log` and `revival.done` under the main tree's `tmp/record-landing-N/`, and its commit message `tmp/revival-msg-N.txt`.
47	
48	## Landing its result
49	
50	The workflow lands its own result, by the curator's rule of 2026-11-03 (`../../HELD.md`, "Held in chat (2026-11-03)", 06:2x); the design's decision 6, the coordinator's cherry-pick, is reversed. After the judge, the lander, in the main tree:
51

# The record-landing workflow

`record-landing.js` does the record's work after a landing, which the coordinator did by hand through a record writer and a routing worker until climb batch 24. It is the smallest first version of the design `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-landing-workflow.md` (`5384a4f35`), which the curator approved with its eight defaults on 2026-11-02. It runs in six stages for the record, in the pattern of the orientation workflow (`../orientation/orientation.js`), five more for the skill after the orientation update ("The skill update"), and one for the revival page ("The revival page"):

1. **Sort** (Opus, `sort.md`): `prepare.sh` makes the worktree and its branch and writes the evidence into the run's folder (`evidence.py`'s header lists its six files; `plan.md` ends with the PLAN lines that look stale, from `plan-moves.py --stale-at`, cut at 40,000 characters, past which the whole list is in `plan-stale.txt`, which the cut line names); the sorter reads it, the review's routing part and the batch record's items, and writes `owed.md`, one line per change with its number, its home, its kind, its weight, its ground and its writer, and marks each kind and each "Needed by" that no source states as set by the workflow.
2. **Write**: a Sonnet driver runs `drive.sh 1` in the background and waits for it in steps of 240 s, under the five minutes that its prompt cache lives. `drive.sh` starts two headless Opus writer streams side by side through the worktree's copy of `../record-clarity/writer-stream.sh`: the entries writer (`entries.md`: FACTS, POSITIONS, an entry's history, ledger rows, as `record.apply` and `rows.rewrite`) and the routing writer (`routing.md`: PLAN, PLAN-history, the queue, INDEX, other notes, edited in the worktree). Then `checks.sh 1` writes `mech-1.md`.
3. **Check**: the checker (`check.md`: coverage, fidelity, form and routing) and the clarity cold reader (`../record-clarity/coldread.md`, unchanged, told to write its report in parts of five entries) on `clean.txt`, side by side.
4. **Fix**: `drive.sh 2` resumes both streams once with the three reports, then `checks.sh 2` writes `mech-2.md`.
5. **Judge** (Opus, `judge.md`): apply or hold each change once, `final.apply` and `final.rewrite`, `diff.md` (within 10,000 characters), and `final.sh`, which runs every check again and makes two commits on the branch. The judge writes nothing after the commits.
6. **Land** (Sonnet, in the script): only when the judge's checks pass (the branch holds its commits past AT, `mech-final.md` says every check passes, the worktree is clean), the lander puts the two commits on `main`, runs the checks on `main`, pushes, and removes the worktree and the branch; then the script runs the orientation workflow in update mode as a child workflow (`../orientation/orientation.js`, one level deep), on the entries in the orientation call of `diff.md`'s "Next". 7. **Skills** (a Sonnet driver; the skill writer, a headless Opus session): `skills.sh N 1` writes the writer's task from `skill-task.md` and the landed files, and starts a fresh writer on it through `../skill-writer.sh new`; the writer installs what the orientation judge accepts and brings the `fortress-repo` skill in line with the landing, and commits on `main`.
8. **Cold read** (Opus): the changed parts, by `../../skill-cold-read-brief.md`, as a worker new to the repository.
9. **Fixes**: `skills.sh N 2` resumes the same writer on the cold read's flags (`skill-fixes.md`).
10. **Page** (Opus, `page.md`): the page of `fortress-repo`'s landed changes, by the source and the URL that the boot note names, published by that URL.
11. **Push** (Sonnet, in the script): `folders.sh N` commits the run's folders, then the pushes as the Land stage's; the result's `line` is the one line for the coordinator's chat message.
12. **Revival page** (Sonnet, in the script; then a Sonnet publisher, `revival-publish.md`): `../revival-page/update.py --landing N --run-start base` in the main tree, the files that it names committed by named paths and pushed as the Push stage's; then the page published by its URL with the Artifact tool. # The platform's stops, and check-ins

This part says when the platform's stops come, how to tell them apart, and what they do here. What any process stop kills and keeps, and a worker's steps after one, are `fortress-repo`'s `references/session.md`. How to resume a run is the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`.

## What stops the process

- **The cap.** The platform stops the process after about 12 h 58 min of continuous running, and starts it again in resume mode, the same session, within seconds. No crash, memory limit or message causes it. The next stop comes 12 h 58 min after the last start.
- **Idleness.** The process also ends when the session goes idle, after a few minutes to a few hours. It runs continuously only while the curator or a check-in keeps it busy, so the cap's stops fall in busy stretches.
- **A VM restart.** The machine boots again. The disk usually survives (below).

Every start, after a VM restart too, resets the cap's clock.

The environment manager's log records every stop and start:

    grep -E 'Received signal|context cancellation|Set session mode' /tmp/env-manager.log | tail

A stop is three lines: a `SIGTERM` ("Received signal, shutting down gracefully"), then "Claude Code stopped due to context cancellation" with the run's length in `duration_ms`, then "Set session mode for environment" `resume`, the next start. To tell the kinds apart:

- The cap's stop has a `duration_ms` near 46,640,000.
- An idle stop has a shorter one, and the boot time that `uptime -s` prints stays earlier than the stop.
- After a VM restart, `uptime -s` prints a boot time between the stop and the next start.

## A VM restart that rolls the disk back

A VM restart can bring the disk back to an earlier state. Other restarts have kept it whole, and nothing tells in advance which kind comes. So only what is pushed is safe.

The signs of a rollback:

- The local `main` ends at an earlier commit, and the commits made since are on `origin` only. The reflog jumps from that commit to the first commit made after the restart.
- The newer files of the scratchpad and of the tree's `tmp/` are gone, and so are the later lines of the backup's log. The session's own transcript stays whole.

To recover:

1. Run `git fetch`.
2. On each branch that you work on, `main` included, run `git rebase origin/<branch>`. With no commit after the restart, this moves the branch forward to the pushed commit.
3. Push your own commits, as `fortress-repo`'s `references/committing.md` says.
4. In the coordinating session, after the next turn ends, read the backup's last log line (`hooks.md`).

If the source file of a published Artifact page was lost, the `coordinator` skill says how to rebuild it from the page.

## The weekly usage limit

When the account's weekly limit on all models is reached, each new agent launch is refused ("You've hit your weekly limit"), and a running Workflow run ends. Later, turns and launches can be served again while the usage panel still shows the limit as reached. A launch that succeeds is the sign. If the limit ended a run, resume it as after a process stop.

## What a stop kills and keeps here

Any process stop kills and keeps what `fortress-repo`'s `references/session.md` says. On this platform, also:

- `send_later` reminders survive. They live on the server.
- A command started with `nohup` survives the cap and an idle stop. A VM restart ends every process.
- Each start writes the platform's git-check script again, and the repository's `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh` turns it off again (`hooks.md`).

A new session is not a process stop. It starts on a fresh machine and cannot resume another session's run. Only its pushed work and the files of the repository carry over.

## Check-ins, for the coordinating session

Check-ins keep the session busy across a long run. Each wake falls inside the main session's one-hour prompt cache, so it reads the cache instead of writing the whole context again. Each turn's end also runs the transcript backup (`hooks.md`).

- Arm all the check-ins of a series in one turn, 45 minutes apart. Use no cron trigger, whose shortest interval is an hour. Do not chain reminders, each check-in arming the next one.
- The scheduler refuses more than about ten trigger creations a minute ("Trigger creation rate limit reached"). If it refuses one, arm the rest a minute later.
- A series ends with its last check-in. If the run outlasts it, have the last check-in arm a whole new series.
- Add one check-in a few minutes after the cap's next stop, 12 h 58 min after the last start. In its message, tell the session to resume what the stop killed.
- After a stop, or when you relaunch a run, delete or re-arm the reminders to fit the run.
- An interrupt of any turn, one that a check-in started included, kills the run's agents. If the curator means to stop the session while agents run, ask them to wait until the turn has ended and about 10 s more, for the backup's pass.

The record update for run 1 started at 06:04 UTC (07:04 your time). It needs nothing from you. Here is the first of the two questions for run 2.

**Question: after the merge, what type does `round` of an `RR64` give: `ZZ64`, as today, or `ZZ`?**

**Context**
- `round` takes a float to the nearest integer: `round(2.5)` is 2, and `round(3.5)` is 4.
- Today the one library declares `round` on `RR64` two times:
  - `trait RR64` declares `round(self): ZZ`.
  - Walk's object `Float`, below that trait, declares `round(self): ZZ64`. This is the declaration that runs, so walk gives a `ZZ64`.
- The compiler's prelude declares `round(self): ZZ64`. So today both paths give a `ZZ64`.
- The merge makes `RR64` one `value object`, so it can keep only one of the two declarations.
- Your decision on rounding already sets the type. `round`, `truncate` and the brackets ⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉ give `ZZ`, the unbounded integer. The record plans this change as one task after the switch-over, and that task first counts the tests whose output changes.
- No line of microGPT calls `round`. The switch-over does not need this answer. Run 2 needs it, because its merge task keeps one of the two declarations.

**Options**
- **a. `ZZ64` now.** The merge keeps the body that runs today. Nothing changes for a program, and both paths stay at `ZZ64`. Later, the task after the switch-over changes `round`, `truncate` and the brackets to `ZZ` together.
- **b. `ZZ` now.** The merge keeps the trait's declaration. Walk's `round` gives `ZZ`, and the compiled path still gives `ZZ64` until the switch-over. `truncate` and the brackets stay `ZZ64` until the later task. Nobody counts first which tests change their output.

**How they compare**
- Option a keeps the two paths equal. It also makes the change of your decision in one step, with its count. It delays `ZZ` for `round` until after the switch-over.
- Option b gives `round` your type sooner. But it separates `round` from `truncate` and the brackets. It also makes walk and the compiled path give different types until the switch-over. That goes against your words of 11-08: "bring the two implementations to do the same thing."

**Default and recommendation:** a.

The argument is in the review of run 1, section "For the curator": https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/reviews/batch-31-review.md

usage: facts-extract.sh [--check] [--part N] [--page-bytes N] [--root DIR] [--common] [QUERY ...]

Prints what the queries name, whole and in the order they are given; a rung's
briefing is one such command. Each piece comes under a line naming its file
and section. The output comes in parts of at most PAGE_BYTES (default 28000);
part 1 opens with the size of the whole output in bytes and estimated tokens,
then what was asked for, where it is and what was not found; each part says
whether there is a next one, and --part N prints part N.

QUERY is one of:
  F-87, P-48             the entry of that number in FACTS.md or POSITIONS.md
  F-87+                  the entry, then each entry it points to and each entry
                         that points to it, each once, one level
  history:F-87           the entry's blocks in FACTS-history.md or
                         POSITIONS-history.md, oldest first: the provenance line
                         of each change and the line it replaced
  TITLE                  the FACTS.md entry whose title holds TITLE: an entry's
                         title is its bold opening, or where it has none, its
                         opening words up to the first colon, semicolon or full
                         stop; when no current title holds it, the entry one of
                         whose former titles (in FACTS-history.md) does, with a
                         line saying it was retitled
  section:HEADING        every entry of the FACTS.md section whose heading holds HEADING
  index:WORDS            the INDEX.md lines that hold every one of WORDS (at most 10)
  ledger:ROW             row ROW of the gap ledger, whole, under its section and
                         the table's header
  ledger-find:WORDS      one line for each gap ledger row that holds every one of
                         WORDS: its number, its status and the first 150 characters
                         of its claim (at most 10, then how many more matched)
  positions:TITLE        the entry of POSITIONS.md whose bold title holds TITLE, as
                         a TITLE query does in FACTS.md, former titles included;
                         exactly one must, else the nearest titles are named
  positions:DATE WORDS   the entry of POSITIONS.md dated DATE (YYYY-MM-DD, the first
                         date in the entry) whose head, the entry's text up to its
                         first colon and space, holds every one of WORDS; when no
                         entry of POSITIONS.md matches, the entry of
                         POSITIONS-history.md, from the latest of its sections
                         that hold one, with the line saying what became of
                         it; the output says which file it came from
  map:FILE#HEADING       the section of explorations/coordinator/map/FILE whose

A skill is a minimal set: it holds only the change to what the model does by itself, and leans on what its training already does well. Each rule states a goal or a principle, with the benefit that it brings, and the reader applies it with judgement. A rule is not a program of steps and conditions. A principle with its reason reaches the cases that it does not name. Many instructions, each for its own case, conflict, and the reader must then settle which one holds.
4

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Print the FACTS.md entries that POSITIONS.md cites, each whole, in the order of their numbers, in the parts of facts-extract.sh: the coordinator's first read at a boot, before POSITIONS.md whole, so that the decisions are read with the facts that they rest on (the coordinator skill, "The boot").
#
#   positions-facts.sh            part 1, with the size of the whole output and the numbers not found
#   positions-facts.sh --part N   part N
#   positions-facts.sh --list     only the cited numbers, one a line
#
# The numbers are every F-<n> that POSITIONS.md holds today, so the set follows the record with no list to keep.
set -euo pipefail
root="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../.." && pwd)"
positions="$root/explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md"
mapfile -t nums < <(grep -o 'F-[0-9]\+' "$positions" | sort -u -t- -k2,2n)
if [[ "${1:-}" == "--list" ]]; then
  printf '%s\n' "${nums[@]}"
  exit 0
fi
cd "$root"
exec explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh "$@" "${nums[@]}"
