<!-- The curator's decisions about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as they stand now. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- P-48 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `POSITIONS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. How the curator and the coordinator work is that skill's, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** The revival judges what the designers intended by the team's own sources: its Working Draft of February 2011, its texts on types and its code. `Specification/` holds the Working Draft as a living document: the revival revises it and states each change (P-95). The texts on types include the Types chapter of the specification's 2012 restart (P-25). In `Papers/`, they include the OOPSLA 2011 paper, Naden's 2012 write-up and the POPL 2019 paper with its technical report. P-26 says when code counts, and which source wins where two conflict. The revival does not redesign the language. A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.
- P-8 **Where the designers' own sources, the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations, give no answer, the curator decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and he stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** On the way to a compiled microGPT, he accepts the language's unfinished corners as they are, so that the work does not stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and he takes the designers to have known more than he does.
- P-9 **The revival searches for the most readable expression of the microGPT algorithm.** C4 is the flat microGPT program (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), whose data layout follows Aaron Hsu's flat style of APL (P-29: C4 is not edited for speed before microGPT runs compiled). In C4, the polishing happens in the vocabulary, the array operations that the model's lines call: `FlatArrays.fss` beside C4, and what of it has moved into the standard library (P-27: what a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library). P-87 holds the limit: the model's text is the notation, and a change to a model line is shown to the curator as a diff first. C4 is the target form of the APL microGPT program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`): the APL program is written so that each of its lines expands into the line that C4 writes by hand. C4 writes its hyperparameters as tuple bindings, such as `(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)`, the form to which the APL sub-language (P-10) expands a strand assignment, APL's binding of several names at once. The one-line form, declarations separated by semicolons such as `nEmbd = 16; blockSize = 16; ...`, is not used: the APL sub-language has no use for it.
- P-10 **The APL side quest is closed: its sub-language covers only what the APL microGPT program needs, and the parts of APL that it left unbuilt, tacit functions, characters and nested arrays, are not pursued.** The side quest built an APL sub-language in `explorations/apl/`: a DSL grammar that expands APL text into Fortress code over Fortress's native arrays, not an interpreter of APL. Its microGPT program, `explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`, stays in the microGPT check under walk (P-30: the check's limit of one minute; what the check runs: the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/interpreter.md`, "The model program").
- P-11 **The 2D notation is a gimmick: no work on it unless the curator asks.** The 2D notation is Fortify's rendering. Fortify (`Fortify/`, run by `bin/fortify` and `bin/fortick`) typesets Fortress source as mathematics in LaTeX, for the specification and the papers. Taken as programming syntax, such a rendering fixes one view of a computation, though the same mathematics can be written in many ways. APL, with one symbol for each transformation of the data, expresses a computation better. The rendering is presentation only, off the revival's path, and no argument in favour of Fortress. The verdict is on that typesetting only: the Unicode operators, such as `∑` and `×`, are the language's own syntax.
- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types; F-9 and F-290 say what walk and the library lack for that step. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).

## History he knows (do not re-explain)

- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.
- P-19 **The tree is not described as the third-party port's migration grafted onto the team's history.** The port is a third-party port of the tree to Java 9, which commit `8fe1daa8f` copied onto the team's last commit (the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/records.md`, "The repository's history"). By history, `main` descends from that commit. By content, most of the port's files are removed or redone, and only one piece of the port's code still runs: the `FTypeArrayList` fix for the JDK 8 `TreeSet` crash (F-165). Why: the tree is not built on the port, and the record must not lead anyone to think that it is. The files that still describe the tree so wait for the lineage cleanup; `coordinator/lineage.md`, "Files that still repeat it", lists them.

## Decisions on record

### The standard and the sources

- P-25 **`Specification/` stays the standard, and the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart is cited beside it.** The restart is a new specification that the team began in 2012 and left unfinished (F-166). Where its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, a worker cites it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, such as the exclusion rule, the chapter is the designers' latest intent, which the goal is to finish, and `Specification/` is revised to follow it. Three of the chapter's passages bear on the specification; P-97 holds how the revision uses the first two. It names the exclusion rule "instantiation exclusion" and gives it in two parts: which instantiations of a generic exclude each other (`types.tick:355-360`), and, in its note, a rule on trait declarations (`:361-376`). The revised `Specification/` takes that form: the first part in its chapter on types, the second in its chapter on traits. It adds a `covariant` modifier for a trait's static parameters, which neither path implements and which is future work, off the path to microGPT (P-62). Third, it says that `Bottom` cannot be written in a program, as `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` already says of `BottomType`.
- P-26 **The team's later decision wins over its earlier one, in a text or in code, where the team made it the language's rule.** P-7 names the texts, from the Working Draft to the POPL 2019 paper. Code counts as a decision where the team built it alike for all its types, or stated its rule in a commit message, a comment or the checker. Code that its author called a stub, and code that works around a limit of the JVM or of the checker, serve only the implementation. The decision that they depart from stands. "Later" is the date of the team's work on the point at issue. The revival revises `Specification/` to follow a later decision. The one library follows it too, in place of the team's earlier code, such as the interpreter's library. Where two later decisions conflict, the goal decides (P-8). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. Why: the Working Draft's early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run. So they learned what is feasible. They sought performance, and specialization was a must. Their later decisions include the exclusion rule, specialization and the number types of the compiler's prelude, siblings from 2009 to 2012 (P-43). The revival knows less than they did, so it does not second-guess them.
- P-27 **What a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library, in the library's own way.** A program written on this library has a part that states its algorithm, and it can have a part that builds domain-independent machinery that the library lacks, as both microGPT programs do. A form of that second part goes into the standard library when, on reasonable judgment, it is not an extension of the program's own domain; a form that the library has for one number type, rank or sibling trait and lacks for another is the plainest case. Whoever writes it there first studies how the library does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern, such as its `excludes` clauses. This rule governs how the library is extended; it does not choose between two of the team's designs of the language (P-26).
- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Its next layer is algebra: traits such as `Ring` and `Field`, which the library does not declare yet, and what machine learning's matrices and tensors need, so that the library's algebraic traits, such as `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, reach them too. Why: the curator wants those matrices and tensors to have the mathematical rigour that the library's way of building its types promises. The work edits the standard library itself, in `Library/`, not a separate tree of the revival's own outside it (P-27, how the library is extended). It is parked off the path to microGPT compiled. Two matrix ideas of his wait beside it: square matrices of one size as a multiplicative ring, and diagonal matrices of one size as a ring whose product commutes.
- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is far slower than Python's interpreter (`explorations/microgpt-port.md`, "Step-0 results", a measurement of 2026-08-23). Fortress's performance is judged on the compiled path, once the compiler runs programs. So no performance decision rests on walk's timings. In particular, until microGPT runs compiled, C4, the flat microGPT program, is not edited for speed. The gate never runs microGPT's two programs, C4 and the APL-style program, because they run too long to be tests. Why: walk is the unoptimised path, as a debug build is in Swift, where performance is not judged either.
- P-30 **The check of microGPT under walk after a batch must take less than a minute.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. The minute is the curator's goal, for a check that runs only about two forward-and-backward passes of the model, not a full training, and compares the results with reference values. That is enough to show that the model's mathematics still works, and that the library's changes, such as those to the arrays, did not break it. A slower check is to him a waste of time. The commit stage of each batch, the step that lands its changes, runs the check as `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh`, the quick versions of microGPT's two programs at once, outside the gate.
- P-32 **The record's maps are kept current and used, so that nothing that the record holds is worked out again from scratch.** The maps are `FACTS.md`, `INDEX.md` and the territory map, `explorations/coordinator/map/`. The territory map surveys the repository down to where the team wrote the intent of each design. Part of that intent is written only in the papers under `Papers/`, not in the specification. So the map covers the papers too, and shows where to look up a design's intent. `INDEX.md` is read whole at the coordinator's boot, at the start of each session and after each compaction, and each worker's brief carries a mission briefing from the territory map, not the whole map. 129	- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every edit of source code in the original tree starts from a failing test. The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The test and the fix may land in one commit. Why: the rule replaces one-off validation scripts, which no later build runs. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.
130	- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test's result is pass or fail, as the team designed the suites. A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. Why: when the suite's designers let a test pass without a further check, what it prints need not be checked.
131	- P-124 **The specification's examples are a step of the gate, and every one must pass.** `ant testSpecData` runs the examples extracted from `Specification/` under walk (F-114 says which 130 it runs), and the gate fails if any of them fails. When an example fails, the implementation is fixed: the example is not respelled to get around a gap in walk, and no list of examples allowed to fail is kept.
132	- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** `build.xml` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS` to 4 for the two suites, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`, so that every run of them uses four threads, whatever the calling shell sets. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.

- P-71 **An overflow guard tests for the type's most negative value, not for `a = -a`, so `|0|`, `-0` and `0 DIV -1` do not overflow.** On a signed fixed-width type, only the most negative value overflows when it is negated, taken in absolute value or divided by -1. The test `a = -a` is true for that value, and also for 0. Walk already gave 0 in the three cases. On the compiled path, the natives of negation, absolute value and division on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` test for the most negative value. The same faulty test sat in `ZZ64`'s multiplication, through which its `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD` and `LCM` compute, so `0 · 5`, `3 REM 5` and `12 GCD 18` raised; that multiplication now raises only when the exact product does not fit. Why: no reading of the specification makes the three cases overflow.
- P-72 **`narrow` keeps the low 32 bits of a value that the narrower type cannot hold, signed and unsigned, on both paths, and raises no `IntegerOverflow`.** The decision covers `narrow` from a `ZZ64` to a `ZZ32` and from an `NN64` to an `NN32`. A value that the narrower type holds is unchanged; any other becomes the value of the narrower type with the same low 32 bits. Why: the team's specification said nothing on `narrow`, and the team's boundary test `ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss` asserts the low 32 bits for `NN64` values. On the unsigned types, keeping the low bits is a bit operation, like a shift, and the signed `narrow` gets the same answer.
- P-73 **Under walk, fixed-width integer arithmetic raises `IntegerOverflow` when its result does not fit, on the unsigned `NN32` and `NN64` too.** The rule covers every operation whose result can leave its type, `^`, `CHOOSE` and `LCM` included (F-132 holds what is built and its tests). So a subtraction below 0 on `NN32` raises. Code that means to wrap uses the specification's wrapping operators ∔ (`DOTPLUS`), ∸ (`DOTMINUS`) and ⨰ (`DOTTIMES`), fully parenthesised, since the specification states their precedence only among the three. The specification's saturating operators, such as ⊞ (`BOXPLUS`), are not in the interpreter's library; they come in a later step of their own (row 797). Why: this is the specification's rule, and the compiled path already raised the error for addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, negation and absolute value on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`. The decision is walk's. On the compiled path the rule holds as the specification's (P-25, the standard), and the compiled path departs from it at `^` (rows 523 to 525).
- P-74 **Mixed integer widths convert by declared coercions: each wider integer type declares a `coerce` from each narrower integer type, as the compiler prelude does.** A conversion that is exact is implicit, and a conversion that can lose precision is written out. So `ZZ32` values and integer numerals coerce into `RR64` implicitly, and a `ZZ64` value into `RR64` is written out (P-66, Java's defaults corrected where they lose precision). A call of a generic function with arguments of mixed widths infers, on both paths, the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce. A range is over `ZZ32` only (P-77, the rule on ranges). The specification's `widens` declaration, which would make a narrow computation stored into a wide variable run wide, is deferred. The implicit coercion of `NN32` into `RR64`: P-75 holds it, with its conflict with the overloads of `RR64` and `ZZ64`.
- P-75 **`NN32` coerces into `RR64` implicitly, since every `NN32` value converts to `RR64` exactly.** Why: a conversion that fits is implicit, the rule of P-74 on mixed widths. With the coercion, an operator that both `RR64` and `ZZ64` declare is ambiguous on both paths for a `ZZ32` with an `NN32`, since neither `ZZ64` nor `RR64` coerces into the other. This is what the type system promises: a diagonal is a kind of matrix, with a faster product of its own. Row 299 records what the general product costs on a diagonal: 13 to 54 times as much as scaling the rows. Since the diagonal is read-only, a read-only matrix trait, `ReadableArray2`, which `Array2` would extend as `Array1` extends `ReadableArray1`, is also wanted (row 798): it is a library change, not a definition in the vocabulary.
- P-89 **`fill` takes a value, `tabulate` a function.** On the library's arrays, `fill(v)` fills an array with the value `v`, even when `v` is a function, and `tabulate(f)` fills it with `f` applied to each index. The function form, formerly an overload of `fill`, takes Scala's name `tabulate`. Why: in every peer language that has `fill`, `fill` takes the value.
- P-90 **`Maybe`'s empty case is the team's parametric `Nothing[\T\]`, in the one library and the specification.** The bare `Nothing` is future work: it needs a `where` clause that binds a type variable in an `extends` clause, which neither path implements, and it is not tried before then. Gating row 331 on static-argument inference instead is parked.
- P-91 **What an object with no `asString` prints: its bare Fortress type name, walk's spelling, on both paths.** An object with no `asString` of its own prints its Fortress type name as walk spells it, such as `Box`, or `Box[\ZZ32\]` for an instance of a generic object, with no marker and no hash code. A debug marker, such as the Java class name that the curator first leaned to, belongs in `asDebugString` if one is still wanted, not in the printed form; walk's `asDebugString` prints `a Box: Box`. Row 363: an `asDebugString` that prints as walk's does, where the compiled one prints `Box`. Row 321: printing an object that declares or inherits a zero-argument member named `toString`, which overflows the stack. Once the compiled path reads the one library, every object inherits such a member, the `getter toString` of that library's `trait Object`, so every object with no `asString` meets the overflow.

### The specification's revision

- P-95 **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** When the revival changes the language, it updates `Specification/` with the change, so that the text and the implementation do not disagree. The original text and the reasoning are kept, so that route C stays open. Route C is the design that P-43 set aside: a nested number tower, under the forest rule of the team's 2012 patent applications (F-46 gives what a return to it would need). Every such change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). The unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, is never touched. Why: an open disagreement between the text and the implementation would confuse a reader.
- P-96 **A change of the specification is shown in layers, as the team showed its own changes in the 1.0 release of 2008 and in the working draft of 2009.** This form is the revision form. A callout that prints in every build marks each changed passage; a `\note` will not do, since a release build hides it. Appendix I's revival section has an entry for each change: its reason, its original text, what a return to route C would mean for it, or that it would be the same under route C (P-95 says what route C is), and the decision that it follows. The front matter has one paragraph on the revision, and a document in the repository holds the full reasoning. Citations call the unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, the Working Draft of February 2011: the copy is that draft byte for byte, and only its `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the 1.0 release (F-163). The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` gives each part in full, including what else an Appendix I entry holds.
- P-97 **The specification's examples that break the exclusion rule take the library's shapes, and each original stays, marked "Not allowed".** The Working Draft offered such examples as legal. Each now shows the shape that the library uses for the same thing, with the original beside it under the specification's own mark, "Not allowed". The specification states the rule, which it calls instantiation exclusion, once, in the two parts of Luchangco's Types chapter of 2012 (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`; P-25): `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` says which instantiations exclude each other, and `basic/traits.tex` says that a declaration may not extend two that do. The covariance example, a trait that extends other instantiations of itself, is rewritten and marked in the same way. Its callout adds one sentence: the type group's later design, in the same Types chapter, declares variance with a `covariant` modifier, which neither walk nor the compiled path implements (row 404 records the gap). The calculi of Appendix A keep their rules as the team wrote them, under a callout that they predate the rule.
- P-98 **`TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, so that the library's `BIG MIN` and `BIG MAX` work over total comparisons.** It does so in the library's api and component, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss`. It keeps the five members that it restates by hand: `MIN`, `MAX`, `MINMAX`, `<=` and `>=`. Without the parent, walk finds no overload of `BIG MIN` or `BIG MAX` that takes total comparisons (row 461). Why: it is the library's own device, which its other ordered types use. The curator took it on the coordinator's recommendation. It stands and blocks no work.
- P-179 **The opening chapters of the revised specification keep the team's wording, and change only what is not true of the tree.** The preface and chapters 1 and 2 introduce the language to a new reader, who follows them with the implementation in the repository, so they must not describe what it does not do. A sentence that is true stays word for word. A sentence that is not true is cut, or changed only as far as makes it true. The revival adds no prose of its own there, and nothing on building the implementation, which the repository's `README.md` holds. Each change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). Why: text that describes what the implementation does not do misleads the reader, and a free rewrite puts the revival's text in the place of the team's.

### The suites and the gate

- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every edit of source code in the original tree starts from a failing test. The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The test and the fix may land in one commit. Why: the rule replaces one-off validation scripts, which no later build runs. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.
- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test's result is pass or fail, as the team designed the suites. A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. Why: when the suite's designers let a test pass without a further check, what it prints need not be checked.
- P-124 **The specification's examples are a step of the gate, and every one must pass.** `ant testSpecData` runs the examples extracted from `Specification/` under walk (F-114 says which 130 it runs), and the gate fails if any of them fails. When an example fails, the implementation is fixed: the example is not respelled to get around a gap in walk, and no list of examples allowed to fail is kept.
- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** `build.xml` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS` to 4 for the two suites, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`, so that every run of them uses four threads, whatever the calling shell sets. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.
- P-150 **No resident compiler is built.** A background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did, would save too little of the workers' time to be worth building (F-234), so the speed work goes to the checker itself (P-148). It is not tried again unless something significant changes.
- P-177 **QuickCheck is a testing tool that the project goes on relying on: it is to run on the compiled path after the switch-over, by its static choice of generators.** `QuickCheck` (`Library/QuickCheck.fss`) picks the generator for a property's static type, and imports no reflection. `ReflectiveQuickCheck` builds on it for generic properties: it picks random types for a property's static parameters through `Reflect`, whose 28 native bindings stay on walk's glue, for walk only (P-58, the exception for `Reflect`). So the reflective component runs under walk alone. Why: the curator calls QuickCheck an important testing tool. Detail: `reviews/quickcheck-widen.md`, sections 1 and 2.

1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37

# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

1	<!-- What is established about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as it stands now, grouped by area: each entry the fact, its source and its test. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `FACTS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. -->
2	
3	# Facts on record
4	
5	## Execution model
6	
7	- F-7 **Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases, and only the compiled path runs the static type checker.** Walk switches the checker off, and no switch turns it on. So walk checks no static types of expressions: an ill-typed expression shows only when it runs, as a failed dispatch or as another run-time error, such as F-239's refusal of an `if` on a value that is not a `Boolean`. At load, walk refuses some ill-formed declarations: the `fortress-repo` skill's `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists them, with their evidence in F-29 (`comprises` clauses), F-142 (the Meet Rule for Functional Methods) and F-145 (uncovered abstract methods and `override`). The phases and where the two paths part: the skill's "How a program runs". Detail: `explorations/repo-internals.md`, "The two worlds".
8	- F-9 **`fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's library, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, so it is no oracle for walk programs.** `Shell.java` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` for the command (row 69). P-12 has walk run the checker on its own programs after the switch-over, and walk cannot do so as it stands: it runs with type checking and the Scala checker off, the Java checker is gone (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:228-229`), and it has no case for the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, by reading (row 833).
9	- F-11 **The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main representational cost of microGPT-shaped array code.** So a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (the `fortress-repo` skill, "The compiled runtime"). In Java models of microGPT's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`. No such kernel compiles yet: the compiler prelude has no array type (row 305), and the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (P-37). In a hot compiled loop, escape analysis removes the temporary boxes, and one box per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration stays (F-301), as long as C2's inline depth reaches each box's constructor chain (F-302). Detail: `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4; `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` section 4.
10	- F-12 **On the compiled path, the scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` ran in 0.74 s in one session's measurement; the loop still pays for its generator, for boxing and for a transaction check at each use of its accumulator.** `bench1t` is `for i <- seq(1#20000000) do acc := acc 0.9999999 + 0.0000001 end` on a `var acc: RR64`, with both literals written in the loop. The time is the median of three loop-only runs at one thread (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Times taken in different sessions differ on this machine, so compare only times from one session. What the loop does, read in its bytecode (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 5): the `seq` loop becomes the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, which runs the iterations in order by a recursive split over boxed indices, with a closure call per element; each value is boxed (F-11); and the accumulator is a volatile cell whose read and write each first call `BaseTask.inATransaction`, as for every mutable local (F-40, what a size costs at run time, whose sized loop pays the same check). Within the boxing and the cell, the report counts four allocations per iteration, an interface call to the native wrapper and the casts, the part that unboxed doubles and `double[]` would attack. No share of the 0.74 s is measured.
11	- F-17 **The bytecode cache can come up empty after a library order that reports exit 0.** Running the same commands again, one at a time, made the jars. The cause is not known. Check the five jars before a compiled run (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`, "The library order"). Detail: `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 1.
12	- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled runtime" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becomes `LFRR64;` in `Box⟦FRR64⟧`, and `[D` is no class name, so stamping alone keeps every number boxed (F-11). The team left two separate traces for unboxing. The plan in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java` lists what to unbox: a primitive, a singleton object, unboxed fields, and a `comprises` clause whose types are unboxable; it says nothing of the loader or of instantiations. The loader has an empty "expando" stub (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`). A loader that stamps an `RR64` instance with a `double[]` field, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), does not exist and is unmeasured. Walk instantiates generics in its own evaluator, not by classes. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 1; `coordinator/array-design.md` section 2 (probe 1); `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 3, way A4.
13	- F-19 **By the specification, the iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments of a call or an operator may run in parallel, and a program must assume that they do.** A `for` loop is sequential only if every generator is, as `seq(g)` or `sequential(g)` makes it. An implementation may also run them one after another (`evaluation/parallelism.tex:88-90`), so a program cannot count on parallel runs either. For the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator, each path starts a task only where it judges it worth it: walk by `TupleTask.worthSpawning`, which also governs a call's arguments, and the code generator by `ParallelismAnalyzer`. Compiled, the arguments of a function call and of a dotted method call fork where the analyzer marked the argument tuple (`CodeGen.evalArg`; joins: F-350); it counts no call in the prelude's files (row 982) or of a function declared later in the file (row 987). A `for` loop over a range without `seq` runs by splitting the range into `do … also do … end` blocks. Under walk, every such block is a task, and walk's library splits a `ZZ32` range into chunks of at most 16 elements (F-350), and a range with a stride down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1498-1585`). Compiled, the first block runs in place, and each other block forks only where `BaseTask.forkIfProfitable` judges it worth it, as tuple elements do; the compiler prelude's `parloop` splits down to `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK` elements, 1 by default. `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the pool of worker threads (the `fortress-repo` skill, "Parallelism and mutable state"). By grep, no program under `explorations/`, the model programs and the probes, writes `spawn`, which starts an explicit thread, or an `also do` block, so their parallelism comes only from loops, tuples and arguments. The revival's tests under `ProjectFortress/` write both. Source: `Specification/basic/expressions/for.tex:28-32`, `tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:58-59`, `evaluation/parallelism.tex:50-80`.
14	- F-20 **Sizes, the `nat` and `int` static parameters, are values at run time; they check shapes, and no optimization uses them (F-40, what a size costs at run time).** The compiled checker checks them (F-67), and a sized program loads and runs compiled (F-129). Under walk, `Vector` and `Matrix` take their sizes from an array built at run time: `f[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\])` takes `s` from `array[\RR64\](3)`, and overloads on `Vector` and `Matrix` dispatch by rank (row 214). The array-type syntax `T[n]` with a `nat` parameter does not unify with such an array, "Cannot unify … with ArrayType", where `T[3]` with a literal size does (row 23). Walk matches sizes at dispatch. A mismatch, such as a `DOT`, the library's inner product, of a 2×3 matrix by a 2×3 matrix, whose inner sizes differ, is a `ProgramError`, "Failed to find any matching overload", that no `catch` takes (row 254). Source: `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:96`.
15	- F-21 **The February 2011 Working Draft's bare `Nothing`, one object for every `T`, is accepted on neither path: the grammar refuses its `excludes` clause, and without that clause `T` is undefined.** The declaration is `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:40`). Both paths stop at a syntax error at `excludes`, since an object has no `excludes` clause (measured: `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, E4). Without that clause, both report `T is undefined` at the `T` of the `extends` clause: a `where` clause on an object binds no type variable of its `extends` clause, as row 17 holds for a trait. Today's specification refuses the form in any case, by instantiation exclusion, and marks it "Not allowed" beside the parametric `Nothing[\T\]` that the interpreter's library writes (F-167). P-90 still calls the bare `Nothing` future work that waits for such `where` clauses, not tried before then. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-maybe/REPORT.md` section 5.
16	- F-22 **When a component's name differs from the api that it exports, neither path finds the component, for an exported function or variable alike.** The specification resolves an imported api to any component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex`). The tree looks only under the api's name, unless a user maps the api to its component by hand with `LinkShell`'s `alink` or `clink`. The linker's component repository looks this way (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`), so `fortress link` and walk print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" before any code is generated. The code generator names a reference to an exported declaration after the api, and the declaring class after the component. The link step rewrites such a reference to the component only when the repository names it, so files compiled one by one, without `fortress link`, die with `NoClassDefFoundError`. The missing step is the repository's: finding the component that exports the api. The report names two repairs, neither built: the repository could search the source path for that component, or the code generator could emit api-named forwarders, for which three comments in `CodeGen.java` leave a place. Walk and `fortress link` need the first. Workaround: name the api after its component. Gated by the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test` (row 320). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-export-var/REPORT.md`, "The measurement that separates them".
17	- F-23 **A comment placed after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span and of the unambiguous name the parser derives from it.** The parser's `createSpan` trims back over spaces only, and a declaration that ends in `end` is unaffected (row 359). So a comment-only library edit can change the syntax tree, and a before-and-after comparison of parse trees or diagnostics maps positions back first. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/REPORT.md` section 6, D1.
18	- F-24 **Under `walk`, a native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees.** It throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object, as `ZZ32.overflow()` does for `IntegerOverflow` (F-132; row 347, fixed). A native bound to a helper of `nativeHelpers/` raises the library's own exception where the helper raises a class of the compiled prelude, such as `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero`, so `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` (F-299, F-306, F-308, F-312). Any other Java exception of a native becomes a `ProgramError`, which no `catch` takes. Gated by the `overflows(...)` assertions of `tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`, and for a helper by `tests/NativeHelperRaiseWalk.fss` and, for each of the five types, `tests/<type>DivisionByZeroWalk.fss` and `tests/<type>RemainderByZeroWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md` section 4.1.
19	- F-25 **On the compiled path, the class loader loads each class under the JDK's class-loading lock, so the first load of an instantiation's class is safe on four threads at once.** `InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` holds `getClassLoadingLock(name)` for the whole load, as the JDK's own `ClassLoader.loadClass` does. Without the lock, two threads that first loaded such classes at the same time could race, and the run died with a `NullPointerException` (row 417, fixed). The test `compiler_tests/FirstLoadThreadsRungG` calls the generic overload `f[\T\](v: Vt[\T\])` at eight instantiations, `Vt[\A1\]` to `Vt[\A8\]`, from a parallel `for` loop of 800 iterations. Observed: at four threads it failed 5 runs of 5 before the lock, and passed 5 of 5 after. It is one of the gate's atomic runs, which run each program at four threads (`gate.md`). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1 (the runs) and 12 (why this lock).
20	- F-26 **Under walk, when one of two applicable declarations has static parameters of its own, the call chooses on their declared domains where exactly one lies inside the other, not by the order in which they are written.** It builds P-45, the choice among overloads by declared parameter types, under walk. A declaration has static parameters of its own if it is a generic function or constructor, or a functional method with static parameters in a trait or object without any. Its declared domain, walk's symbolic instance, is its parameter types with each type parameter standing for itself under its bounds. Where neither declared domain lies inside the other, where each lies inside the other, or where neither declaration has static parameters of its own, walk compares the domains of the instances that the call makes. So a functional method of a generic trait or object is compared on its instance, and a generic dotted method is chosen by F-253 (a generic method at a dotted call, also chosen on declared domains). If the chosen declaration is generic and its instance takes an argument only by a conversion, walk converts the argument and dispatches the converted arguments again, so the most specific declaration for the converted values runs. In two cases walk keeps the chosen instance, with no second dispatch: an overloaded dotted method, and a position whose conversion `Coercions.coercionFor` does not find, such as a tuple converted element by element. Two generic overloads whose static parameters agree in name, kind and bounds share one symbolic instance, even if their `where` clauses differ; no test or library declaration has such a pair (row 478). Gated by `tests/DispatchDeclaredDomain.fss` and `DispatchConvertedAgain.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.1, 5.2 (the second dispatch) and 5.5 (the symbolic instance).
21	- F-27 **Walk's load check reads again two kinds of overload pair that its parameter-by-parameter check refuses, and accepts those that pass: a generic declaration beside a plain one, read on their declared domains, and two plain top-level functions, not methods, whose overlap other declarations cover through `comprises` clauses.** To test a cover, the check cuts the overlap of the two domains, position by position, into parts by the `comprises` clauses. Each combination of parts must lie inside the domain of one declaration without static parameters that lies below both. So several such declarations may together cover the overlap. A search that does not settle refuses. A generic declaration beside a plain one passes where one declared domain lies strictly inside the other and the inner one's return type lies below the outer one's. Where neither lies inside the other, the pair needs the same cover, or declared domains that exclude each other read whole (F-258, exclusion over the whole parameter type). Equal declared domains are refused. It builds under walk P-46, by which a conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits, and P-60, by which several declarations below both may cover a meet. Two generic declarations are read on their declared domains too (F-252: the No Duplicates, Return Type and Meet Rules, each over its own instances). Walk still refuses the valid example of the POPL 2019 paper on symmetric multiple dispatch (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`, p. 11:13), a set of three generic declarations (row 539). Gated by `tests/ComprisesMeetWalk.fss` and `GenericBesidePlain*.fss`, among others. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.3 (generic beside plain) and 5.4 (the cover).
22	- F-28 **Walk instantiates a generic declaration declared to return `Any`.** `MakeInferenceSpecific` treats `Any` as it treats a trait type (row 157, fixed). Its visitor has no case for 11 of the syntax tree's 18 concrete type classes, and of those only the dimension forms can be written as a return type. Gated by `tests/GenericReturningAny.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` section 3.
23	- F-29 **Under walk, the load check refuses a trait or object that extends a closed trait of the program's main component where the trait's `comprises` clause does not allow it.** A closed trait is one with a `comprises` clause. The check reads every trait and object of every component of the program, the library's included, as a possible extender. An extender is allowed in three cases: it lies below a listed type; it is a trait whose own `comprises` clause lists only types that are allowed in turn; or it is a generic trait that some trait or object extends, and each of those extenders lies below a listed type (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`, "Trait Declarations"). The check does not yet read a clause declared outside the main component, the library's among them (row 551), or an object expression's `extends` clause (row 597). Nor does it check that each listed type extends the trait at every instantiation (row 598). A check that read the library's clauses would refuse at load every program that imports the library's `Reflect` (row 595), and three team tests and two demos whose objects extend `Exception` directly (row 596). Their repairs come before that check and are the curator's. Gated by `tests/ComprisesUnlistedExtender` and `ComprisesGenericChildUnlistedExtender`, refused at load, and by the `XXX` tests of rows 487 (a type of another component below a generic subtrait of a closed trait), 551, 597 and 598, which stay green while walk still loads their programs. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-load-check/REPORT.md` section 5.
24	- F-269 **Under walk, a program's declarations of a library operator name are checked against the library's only when the program declares two or more of that name, and only on a cold cache.** One such declaration is not checked. Two or more are checked with the library's declarations, and the check can refuse them beside the library's generic declarations, even where they are more specific than the library's. It refused C4's former pair of `MAX` between an `RR64` and an `Array[\RR64,I\]`, in both orders, which C4 dropped when F-119's scalar extension took its place (row 341). It refuses the `Matrix`-specialised elementwise `×` of `apl/mg/elemwise_nat_probe.fss` (F-155). Walk writes a component to its cache before it runs this check, and skips the check on a component that it reads back. So a refusal appears once, on a cold cache, and never again (row 342). The check runs only when walk analyses the library itself again: deleting the program's own cache entries does not bring it back (row 342). So a test that depends on this check must run from an empty cache. Detail: rows 341 and 342; `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/REPORT.md` section 4, a gated run that met a warm cache.
25	- F-291 **With the bound `Any`, the compiled path compiles, loads and runs generics at tuple and arrow static arguments as it does with `extends Any` written; `()` fails whatever the bound (row 339), and so does a generic operator whose one parameter has the type parameter's type, applied to a tuple (row 1056).** Measured once: generic functions, objects and traits, dispatch to a generic arm and `typecase`, at a pair or an arrow, with the static argument written or inferred. The class loader made the same classes by name, and the program jars read the same under `javap`, as the same programs with `extends Any` written under the compile command's bound `Object`. So the switch to the bound `Any` costs the run time no work for these shapes; its test cost is F-292. A generic dotted method with one tuple-typed parameter runs (row 832, fixed since). Not run: the one library's own instantiations at tuples, tuples of three or more and nested ones, generic functional methods at a tuple, a native that receives a tuple. With `extends Object` written, they are refused, or pass unchecked where the static argument is written (row 470); the compile command's bound is `Any` (`Shell.java:372`). No gated test. Detail: `perf-probes/bound-any-compiled/REPORT.md`, "The shapes by setting" and "What the class loader makes".
26	- F-301 **On the compiled path a native helper is called through a generated wrapper over the box classes, and once the loop is hot C2 inlines the whole path, so the call costs nothing of its own.** A binding `builtinPrimitive("pkg.Class.method")` and a written `import java` alias call compile to the same bytes: an `invokestatic` of `native.pkg.Class.method`, a class the compiled path writes into `nativewrapper_cache/`, which unboxes each argument with `getValue`, calls the helper and boxes its result with `make`, a new box each time (`compiler/nativeInterface/FortressMethodAdapter.java:303-327`; `compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32.java:32-34`). A functional method such as `ZZ32`'s `+` reaches the wrapper through the dispatcher, an interface call, the springboard and the trait's static body. C2 inlines all of these frames, the helper, `make` and the box's constructor chain; only C1's profiling code refuses the helper and the chain's deep frames. Escape analysis then removes every temporary box, a helper's result passed into another helper among them, and one box stays per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration: 16 bytes for a `ZZ32`, 24 for an `RR64`. The library's form and the prelude's allocate the same. Observed once on one small program, `perf-probes/helper-calls/HelperCalls.fss`, by `javap`, C2's inlining log and the bytes that JFR counted, with no timing, on a machine shared at a load of 20 to 25; no test checks it. Detail: `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` sections 2 to 5.
27	- F-302 **In those loops C2 inlines down to depth 12 from the loop, against the 16 at which it stops by default, and a temporary box whose constructor chain passes the limit is no longer removed.** At JDK 25's default `MaxInlineLevel=15` a frame at depth d inlines when d is at most 16. The prelude's `+` reaches `Object.<init>` under its result's box at depth 12, a top-level binding at 10. With the limit lowered to 8, a loop of two nested helper calls rose from 33 to 96 bytes per iteration, since its temporaries' chains no longer inlined. So an operator called from more than 4 further inlined frames keeps its temporary boxes. By reading, the one library's `ZZ32` springboard chain is two classes longer than the prelude's, `ZZ32`, `AnyIntegral`, `Number`, `AnyAdditiveGroup`, `Object`, `Any` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:846`, `:742`, `:381`, `:357`) against `ZZ32`, `Number`, `Object`, `Any` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:210`), since a springboard extends the springboard of its trait's first `extends` entry (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:5728-5735`). If `FZZ32` extends the one library's springboard after the switch-over, the margin is 2 frames; not measured, since nothing compiles against the one library yet. Observed once (F-301). Detail: `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` sections 3 and 4.
28	- F-348 **A compiled program initializes the class of every component that it uses before `run`, in a root task on a pool of one thread.** The classes are the program's component class, then that of each component whose declarations its classes name, at any depth; the class loader finds them by the class names in each component's jar. The program's arguments are set before the classes are initialized. So a numeral's place is filled inside a task with no transaction, the tasks that its coercion forks run in place one after another, and the coercion's side effects come before the program's first output. A top-level variable's initializer is not in the class's initializer: it runs at the variable's first use. A component that is imported and whose declarations no class names is not initialized so. This initialization adds about 40 ms to a compiled program's start: 249 to 313 ms with it, 214 to 263 ms before, five runs twice each, on rung N's code, which landed as `f36a651243`. Source: `runtimeSystem/MainWrapper.java:30-46`, `:92-95`, `runtimeSystem/FortressExecutable.java:113-141`, `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:185-248`. Tests: `compiler_tests/NumeralCoercionSpawnCompiled`, `NumeralCoercionSpawnImported`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-numeral-leftovers/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why" and "10. Points to report"; the start's cost: `reviews/batch-30-review.md`, "2. The three forks that landed at a default".
29	- F-350 **On the compiled path the arms of a parallel `do`, the elements of a tuple, the operands of an operator and the arguments of a call fork through one method, `CodeGen.genParallelExprs`, which joins every arm that it forked before an exception leaves the group; arguments fork where `ParallelismAnalyzer` marked the argument tuple.** The exception that leaves is that of the first arm, in the arms' order, that threw; when an exception leaves, an arm not yet forked is not run, and a `VirtualMachineError` leaves without the joins (`runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:113-131`, `joinIfForked`). The analyzer marks no call written in the prelude's files, so the prelude's reductions run in sequence until the switch-over (row 982); the one library's parallel `ZZ32` range splits only a range of more than `grainSize`, 16, elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:20`, `:1320`, `:1337`). What it means: compiled against the one library, a reduction over more than 16 elements will fork its halves, and an exception leaves no arm running. By reading, not run: microGPT's vectors are 16, 16, 4 and 4 wide (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss:17`), so a reduction over one of them forks nothing on either path. Tests: `compiler_tests/AlsoArmThrowsJoinsCompiled`, `CallArgumentsForkCompiled`, `tests/ParRangeGrainWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-forked-arguments/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "Points to report reached"; the model's widths against the grain: `reviews/batch-30-review.md`, "2. The three forks that landed at a default".
30	- F-351 **A compiled transaction validates itself and every ancestor, and an abort restarts the block whose transaction it names.** A compiled `atomic` block's transaction records no read of its own write; it records a read of an ancestor's write with that write, a read of the committed value with that value, and a read of an empty array element with a mark. Validation, at a read once the global lock has moved and at a commit that did not get the lock at its snapshot, covers the transaction and every ancestor. An abort names the transaction whose read failed; `abort()` names none. The block's handler takes every exception (`BaseTask.leaveTransaction`): it ends the block's transaction, starts the block again for an abort that names that transaction or names none (or any abort at the outermost block), and throws everything else on, after a nested transaction has handed its reads to its parent. A nested commit hands its parent its reads and its writes, also where it wrote nothing. The exception-table entry of a block or a `try` follows its body's code, so a nested one is taken first. Open: a nested block sees a plain write by another thread that runs its outer block (row 984). Source: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/Transaction.java:228-367`, `runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:293-314`,`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:2045-2077` (`forAtomicBlock`), `:2387-2391` (`forTry`). Tests: `compiler_tests/AtomicOwnWriteNestedCompiled`, `AtomicNestedSameBodyCompiled`, `NestedAtomicAbortCompiled`, `AtomicNestedViewCompiled`, `AtomicSharedReadsCompiled`, `AtomicThrowRevertsCompiled`, `AtomicNestedReadsKeptCompiled`, `NestedTryInnerCatch`; `ArrayStoreJUTest`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-compiled-transaction/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".
31	- F-355 **The pure-Java microGPT that P-7 names as the baseline is in `java-baseline/`: one training step at batch 1 takes about 0.10 ms after warm-up without the Adam update, and 0.113 ms with it.** It is the flat program line for line, in `double[]` and plain loops on one thread with the JDK alone, and it passes the flat program's 7 quick and 40 full checks against the same reference files at the same tolerances. Measured once, on a shared machine of 4 CPUs with OpenJDK 25: fork medians of 100.8 to 104.0 µs for one step in 10 fresh JVMs; as cold processes, 72 ms for the five-step run and 77 ms for the quick check. It is the careful scalar Java, not the fastest: HotSpot vectorises none of its matrix products, and the Vector API in the products alone gives 75 µs. In one session on that machine a step with Adam took 0.113 ms in this program, 0.20 ms in NumPy, 13 ms under dzaima/APL and 132 ms in pure Python, which computes 7.3 positions a step against 16. So a compiled Fortress step is measured against about 0.1 ms, and pure Python is about 1,200 times slower than this baseline. The program keeps the arithmetic of the Fortress source; only a sum of more than 16 terms is added in another order than the library's. No test checks the timings. Commands: `java-baseline/run.sh` and `run.sh bench`. Detail: `java-baseline/REPORT.md`, "4. Timings of the baseline" and "5. Vectorisation: what HotSpot did with the baseline's loops"; `java-baseline/python-comparison.md`, "1. The answer".
32	- F-356 **In the fork/join shape that the library and the compiled runtime give parallel work, a Java model of microGPT's step with unboxed arrays runs 19 to 80 times slower than plain loops at the library's grains, and 1.4 to 4.8 times slower with the matrix product stopped at blocks of 16.** The library's range stops its split at 16 elements (`grainSize`, `Library/RangeInternals.fss`; P-175), and its matrix product splits down to single elements (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3129-3187`). The model is the baseline of F-355 with its vocabulary on a `ForkJoinPool` and plain loops at the leaves, so its times are a floor for compiled Fortress with this structure. At the library's grains a step takes 19 to 32 times the plain step on one thread, 55 times on two and 80 on four. Threads gain only from a product of about 128 by 128 with blocks of 64, and a dot product only from about 260,000 elements with a grain of 1,024; the model's products are 16 by 16 to 64 by 16. So at microGPT's sizes the library's parallel shape costs time at any thread count, and the matrix product's missing grain is the largest part of the cost. Measured once on a shared machine of 4 CPUs; every configuration passes the checks. Commands: `java-baseline/run.sh steps`, `kernels` and `scale`. Detail: `java-baseline/REPORT.md`, "6. Fork/join: the baseline in the shape of the library and the compiled runtime".
33	- F-357 **`FlatData.parseFloat`, the flat program's reader of its weight files, is not correctly rounded: 699 of the 4,192 initial parameters differ from the double nearest to their decimal text, by up to 2 ulp.** It accumulates the mantissa digit by digit in a double and scales once. So a port of the model must port the parser to start from the same parameters, as the Java baseline does (F-355). No check depends on it: the loader check reads its reference through the same parser. Shown on the Java port of the parser, which keeps its arithmetic, by `java-baseline/run.sh parse`: '4192 numbers, 699 differ from Double.parseDouble, the worst by 2.0 ulp'; no Fortress was run for it. Detail: `java-baseline/REPORT.md`, "3. What could not be matched, and what was chosen".
34	- F-358 **In the scratch tree of F-352, a compiled loop over two `Array1` of 1,000 `RR64` against the one library ran about 45 times faster than under walk and of the order of 100 times slower than the same loop in Java; boxing explains 6 to 7 of that.** The loop is `s += a[i] b[i]`, 5 million iterations in the program's own `seq` loop: 1.4 s compiled as a process and 39.8 s under walk, about 0.8 s and 36 s without a one-line program's time. The Java loop over `double[]` takes 7.5 ms in a cold JVM and 4.4 ms warm. Each is one run; the Fortress and the Java ran in different sessions at different loads, the JIT's warm-up is inside the compiled 0.8 s, and the verifier was off. It is an order of magnitude and no more. Java models of the boxes put boxing at 6 to 7 times on a dot or matrix product (F-11). The rest has no measured share: the read through the store's wrapper with its checks and its `cast`, the range's closure for each iteration, and the transaction check and the box on the accumulator (F-12, row 641). It says nothing about microGPT's kernels: no matrix, no library reduction and no parallel loop ran. Detail: `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/switch-rehearsal.md`, "5. One timing"; `reviews/plan-review-2026-11-10.md`, "7.3 What the first compiled timing says, and what it cannot say"; `java-baseline/REPORT.md`, "7. The rehearsal's loop".
