<!-- What is established about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as it stands now, grouped by area: each entry the fact, its source and its test. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `FACTS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. -->

# Facts on record

## Execution model

- F-7 **Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases, and only the compiled path runs the static type checker.** Walk switches the checker off, and no switch turns it on. So walk checks no static types of expressions: an ill-typed expression shows only when it runs, as a failed dispatch or as another run-time error, such as F-239's refusal of an `if` on a value that is not a `Boolean`. At load, walk refuses some ill-formed declarations: the `fortress-repo` skill's `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists them, with their evidence in F-29 (`comprises` clauses), F-142 (the Meet Rule for Functional Methods) and F-145 (uncovered abstract methods and `override`). The phases and where the two paths part: the skill's "How a program runs". Detail: `explorations/repo-internals.md`, "The two worlds".
- F-9 **`fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's library, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, so it is no oracle for walk programs.** `Shell.java` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` for the command (row 69). P-12 has walk run the checker on its own programs after the switch-over, and walk cannot do so as it stands: it runs with type checking and the Scala checker off, the Java checker is gone (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:228-229`), and it has no case for the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, by reading (row 833).
- F-11 **The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main representational cost of microGPT-shaped array code.** So a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (the `fortress-repo` skill, "The compiled runtime"). In Java models of microGPT's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`. No such kernel compiles yet: the compiler prelude has no array type (row 305), and the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (P-37). In a hot compiled loop, escape analysis removes the temporary boxes, and one box per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration stays (F-301), as long as C2's inline depth reaches each box's constructor chain (F-302). Detail: `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4; `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` section 4.
- F-12 **On the compiled path, the scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` ran in 0.74 s in one session's measurement; the loop still pays for its generator, for boxing and for a transaction check at each use of its accumulator.** `bench1t` is `for i <- seq(1#20000000) do acc := acc 0.9999999 + 0.0000001 end` on a `var acc: RR64`, with both literals written in the loop. The time is the median of three loop-only runs at one thread (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Times taken in different sessions differ on this machine, so compare only times from one session. What the loop does, read in its bytecode (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 5): the `seq` loop becomes the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, which runs the iterations in order by a recursive split over boxed indices, with a closure call per element; each value is boxed (F-11); and the accumulator is a volatile cell whose read and write each first call `BaseTask.inATransaction`, as for every mutable local (F-40, what a size costs at run time, whose sized loop pays the same check). Within the boxing and the cell, the report counts four allocations per iteration, an interface call to the native wrapper and the casts, the part that unboxed doubles and `double[]` would attack. No share of the 0.74 s is measured.
- F-17 **The bytecode cache can come up empty after a library order that reports exit 0.** Running the same commands again, one at a time, made the jars. The cause is not known. Check the five jars before a compiled run (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`, "The library order"). Detail: `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled runtime" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becomes `LFRR64;` in `Box⟦FRR64⟧`, and `[D` is no class name, so stamping alone keeps every number boxed (F-11). The team left two separate traces for unboxing. The plan in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java` lists what to unbox: a primitive, a singleton object, unboxed fields, and a `comprises` clause whose types are unboxable; it says nothing of the loader or of instantiations. The loader has an empty "expando" stub (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`). A loader that stamps an `RR64` instance with a `double[]` field, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), does not exist and is unmeasured. Walk instantiates generics in its own evaluator, not by classes. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 1; `coordinator/array-design.md` section 2 (probe 1); `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 3, way A4.
- F-19 **By the specification, the iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments of a call or an operator may run in parallel, and a program must assume that they do.** A `for` loop is sequential only if every generator is, as `seq(g)` or `sequential(g)` makes it. An implementation may also run them one after another (`evaluation/parallelism.tex:88-90`), so a program cannot count on parallel runs either. For the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator, each path starts a task only where it judges it worth it: walk by `TupleTask.worthSpawning`, which also governs a call's arguments, and the code generator by `ParallelismAnalyzer`. Compiled, the arguments of a function call and of a dotted method call fork where the analyzer marked the argument tuple (`CodeGen.evalArg`; joins: F-350); it counts no call in the prelude's files (row 982) or of a function declared later in the file (row 987). A `for` loop over a range without `seq` runs by splitting the range into `do … also do … end` blocks. Under walk, every such block is a task, and walk's library splits a `ZZ32` range into chunks of at most 16 elements (F-350), and a range with a stride down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1498-1585`). Compiled, the first block runs in place, and each other block forks only where `BaseTask.forkIfProfitable` judges it worth it, as tuple elements do; the compiler prelude's `parloop` splits down to `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK` elements, 1 by default. `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the pool of worker threads (the `fortress-repo` skill, "Parallelism and mutable state"). By grep, no program under `explorations/`, the model programs and the probes, writes `spawn`, which starts an explicit thread, or an `also do` block, so their parallelism comes only from loops, tuples and arguments. The revival's tests under `ProjectFortress/` write both. Source: `Specification/basic/expressions/for.tex:28-32`, `tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:58-59`, `evaluation/parallelism.tex:50-80`.
- F-20 **Sizes, the `nat` and `int` static parameters, are values at run time; they check shapes, and no optimization uses them (F-40, what a size costs at run time).** The compiled checker checks them (F-67), and a sized program loads and runs compiled (F-129). Under walk, `Vector` and `Matrix` take their sizes from an array built at run time: `f[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\])` takes `s` from `array[\RR64\](3)`, and overloads on `Vector` and `Matrix` dispatch by rank (row 214). The array-type syntax `T[n]` with a `nat` parameter does not unify with such an array, "Cannot unify … with ArrayType", where `T[3]` with a literal size does (row 23). Walk matches sizes at dispatch. A mismatch, such as a `DOT`, the library's inner product, of a 2×3 matrix by a 2×3 matrix, whose inner sizes differ, is a `ProgramError`, "Failed to find any matching overload", that no `catch` takes (row 254). Source: `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:96`.
- F-21 **The February 2011 Working Draft's bare `Nothing`, one object for every `T`, is accepted on neither path: the grammar refuses its `excludes` clause, and without that clause `T` is undefined.** The declaration is `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:40`). Both paths stop at a syntax error at `excludes`, since an object has no `excludes` clause (measured: `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, E4). Without that clause, both report `T is undefined` at the `T` of the `extends` clause: a `where` clause on an object binds no type variable of its `extends` clause, as row 17 holds for a trait. Today's specification refuses the form in any case, by instantiation exclusion, and marks it "Not allowed" beside the parametric `Nothing[\T\]` that the interpreter's library writes (F-167). P-90 still calls the bare `Nothing` future work that waits for such `where` clauses, not tried before then. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-maybe/REPORT.md` section 5.
- F-22 **When a component's name differs from the api that it exports, neither path finds the component, for an exported function or variable alike.** The specification resolves an imported api to any component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex`). The tree looks only under the api's name, unless a user maps the api to its component by hand with `LinkShell`'s `alink` or `clink`. The linker's component repository looks this way (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`), so `fortress link` and walk print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" before any code is generated. The code generator names a reference to an exported declaration after the api, and the declaring class after the component. The link step rewrites such a reference to the component only when the repository names it, so files compiled one by one, without `fortress link`, die with `NoClassDefFoundError`. The missing step is the repository's: finding the component that exports the api. The report names two repairs, neither built: the repository could search the source path for that component, or the code generator could emit api-named forwarders, for which three comments in `CodeGen.java` leave a place. Walk and `fortress link` need the first. Workaround: name the api after its component. Gated by the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test` (row 320). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-export-var/REPORT.md`, "The measurement that separates them".
- F-23 **A comment placed after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span and of the unambiguous name the parser derives from it.** The parser's `createSpan` trims back over spaces only, and a declaration that ends in `end` is unaffected (row 359). So a comment-only library edit can change the syntax tree, and a before-and-after comparison of parse trees or diagnostics maps positions back first. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/REPORT.md` section 6, D1.
- F-24 **Under `walk`, a native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees.** It throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object, as `ZZ32.overflow()` does for `IntegerOverflow` (F-132; row 347, fixed). A native bound to a helper of `nativeHelpers/` raises the library's own exception where the helper raises a class of the compiled prelude, such as `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero`, so `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` (F-299, F-306, F-308, F-312). Any other Java exception of a native becomes a `ProgramError`, which no `catch` takes. Gated by the `overflows(...)` assertions of `tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`, and for a helper by `tests/NativeHelperRaiseWalk.fss` and, for each of the five types, `tests/<type>DivisionByZeroWalk.fss` and `tests/<type>RemainderByZeroWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md` section 4.1.
- F-25 **On the compiled path, the class loader loads each class under the JDK's class-loading lock, so the first load of an instantiation's class is safe on four threads at once.** `InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` holds `getClassLoadingLock(name)` for the whole load, as the JDK's own `ClassLoader.loadClass` does. Without the lock, two threads that first loaded such classes at the same time could race, and the run died with a `NullPointerException` (row 417, fixed). The test `compiler_tests/FirstLoadThreadsRungG` calls the generic overload `f[\T\](v: Vt[\T\])` at eight instantiations, `Vt[\A1\]` to `Vt[\A8\]`, from a parallel `for` loop of 800 iterations. Observed: at four threads it failed 5 runs of 5 before the lock, and passed 5 of 5 after. It is one of the gate's atomic runs, which run each program at four threads (`gate.md`). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1 (the runs) and 12 (why this lock).
- F-26 **Under walk, when one of two applicable declarations has static parameters of its own, the call chooses on their declared domains where exactly one lies inside the other, not by the order in which they are written.** It builds P-45, the choice among overloads by declared parameter types, under walk. A declaration has static parameters of its own if it is a generic function or constructor, or a functional method with static parameters in a trait or object without any. Its declared domain, walk's symbolic instance, is its parameter types with each type parameter standing for itself under its bounds. Where neither declared domain lies inside the other, where each lies inside the other, or where neither declaration has static parameters of its own, walk compares the domains of the instances that the call makes. So a functional method of a generic trait or object is compared on its instance, and a generic dotted method is chosen by F-253 (a generic method at a dotted call, also chosen on declared domains). If the chosen declaration is generic and its instance takes an argument only by a conversion, walk converts the argument and dispatches the converted arguments again, so the most specific declaration for the converted values runs. In two cases walk keeps the chosen instance, with no second dispatch: an overloaded dotted method, and a position whose conversion `Coercions.coercionFor` does not find, such as a tuple converted element by element. Two generic overloads whose static parameters agree in name, kind and bounds share one symbolic instance, even if their `where` clauses differ; no test or library declaration has such a pair (row 478). Gated by `tests/DispatchDeclaredDomain.fss` and `DispatchConvertedAgain.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.1, 5.2 (the second dispatch) and 5.5 (the symbolic instance).
- F-27 **Walk's load check reads again two kinds of overload pair that its parameter-by-parameter check refuses, and accepts those that pass: a generic declaration beside a plain one, read on their declared domains, and two plain top-level functions, not methods, whose overlap other declarations cover through `comprises` clauses.** To test a cover, the check cuts the overlap of the two domains, position by position, into parts by the `comprises` clauses. Each combination of parts must lie inside the domain of one declaration without static parameters that lies below both. So several such declarations may together cover the overlap. A search that does not settle refuses. A generic declaration beside a plain one passes where one declared domain lies strictly inside the other and the inner one's return type lies below the outer one's. Where neither lies inside the other, the pair needs the same cover, or declared domains that exclude each other read whole (F-258, exclusion over the whole parameter type). Equal declared domains are refused. It builds under walk P-46, by which a conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits, and P-60, by which several declarations below both may cover a meet. Two generic declarations are read on their declared domains too (F-252: the No Duplicates, Return Type and Meet Rules, each over its own instances). Walk still refuses the valid example of the POPL 2019 paper on symmetric multiple dispatch (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`, p. 11:13), a set of three generic declarations (row 539). Gated by `tests/ComprisesMeetWalk.fss` and `GenericBesidePlain*.fss`, among others. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.3 (generic beside plain) and 5.4 (the cover).
- F-28 **Walk instantiates a generic declaration declared to return `Any`.** `MakeInferenceSpecific` treats `Any` as it treats a trait type (row 157, fixed). Its visitor has no case for 11 of the syntax tree's 18 concrete type classes, and of those only the dimension forms can be written as a return type. Gated by `tests/GenericReturningAny.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` section 3.
- F-29 **Under walk, the load check refuses a trait or object that extends a closed trait of the program's main component where the trait's `comprises` clause does not allow it.** A closed trait is one with a `comprises` clause. The check reads every trait and object of every component of the program, the library's included, as a possible extender. An extender is allowed in three cases: it lies below a listed type; it is a trait whose own `comprises` clause lists only types that are allowed in turn; or it is a generic trait that some trait or object extends, and each of those extenders lies below a listed type (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`, "Trait Declarations"). The check does not yet read a clause declared outside the main component, the library's among them (row 551), or an object expression's `extends` clause (row 597). Nor does it check that each listed type extends the trait at every instantiation (row 598). A check that read the library's clauses would refuse at load every program that imports the library's `Reflect` (row 595), and three team tests and two demos whose objects extend `Exception` directly (row 596). Their repairs come before that check and are the curator's. Gated by `tests/ComprisesUnlistedExtender` and `ComprisesGenericChildUnlistedExtender`, refused at load, and by the `XXX` tests of rows 487 (a type of another component below a generic subtrait of a closed trait), 551, 597 and 598, which stay green while walk still loads their programs. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-load-check/REPORT.md` section 5.
- F-269 **Under walk, a program's declarations of a library operator name are checked against the library's only when the program declares two or more of that name, and only on a cold cache.** One such declaration is not checked. Two or more are checked with the library's declarations, and the check can refuse them beside the library's generic declarations, even where they are more specific than the library's. It refused C4's former pair of `MAX` between an `RR64` and an `Array[\RR64,I\]`, in both orders, which C4 dropped when F-119's scalar extension took its place (row 341). It refuses the `Matrix`-specialised elementwise `×` of `apl/mg/elemwise_nat_probe.fss` (F-155). Walk writes a component to its cache before it runs this check, and skips the check on a component that it reads back. So a refusal appears once, on a cold cache, and never again (row 342). The check runs only when walk analyses the library itself again: deleting the program's own cache entries does not bring it back (row 342). So a test that depends on this check must run from an empty cache. Detail: rows 341 and 342; `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/REPORT.md` section 4, a gated run that met a warm cache.
- F-291 **With the bound `Any`, the compiled path compiles, loads and runs generics at tuple and arrow static arguments as it does with `extends Any` written; `()` fails whatever the bound (row 339), and so does a generic operator whose one parameter has the type parameter's type, applied to a tuple (row 1056).** Measured once: generic functions, objects and traits, dispatch to a generic arm and `typecase`, at a pair or an arrow, with the static argument written or inferred. The class loader made the same classes by name, and the program jars read the same under `javap`, as the same programs with `extends Any` written under the compile command's bound `Object`. So the switch to the bound `Any` costs the run time no work for these shapes; its test cost is F-292. A generic dotted method with one tuple-typed parameter runs (row 832, fixed since). Not run: the one library's own instantiations at tuples, tuples of three or more and nested ones, generic functional methods at a tuple, a native that receives a tuple. - F-251 **A type `where`-clause variable of a `comprises` clause is opened at a call, as a size is, and `AnyList`'s clause, `comprises { List[\E\] } where [\E\]`, once a comment, is in the library.** To open a variable is to give it a fresh type of its own for the call, as the compiled checker already does for a listed type's `nat` and `int` sizes (F-146). So the checker gives an argument whose trait lists `Box[\E\] where [\E\]` a fresh type for the call, bounded by the bound of the clause's binding, `[\E extends B\]`, and by the clause's constraints on it (F-256). It refuses that type in a place whose declared type is another type, and it gives two values two types. It also refuses the shape of Amin and Tate's 2016 unsoundness example, where such a value would prove a subtype relation that does not hold. It does not open such a trait where it reaches it as a parent (row 752). Walk binds the variable as a symbolic type at load. On the rung's own tree the distance went from 49 to 45, row 636's four sites: `AnyList`'s `||` is now accepted through the opened type, and its `addLeft`, `addRight` and the list comprehension's unwrap were respelled. The count, and walk's element types, did not change. Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-anylist-comprises/REPORT.md`.
- F-254 **In the compiled checker, a function or method that leaves out its return type takes it from the one declaration of the exported api whose parameter types are the function's own.** `ApiTypeExtractor` compares the parameter types as the export check does (`ExportChecker.equalTypes`), and a parameter that the function leaves untyped matches any type. It takes the return type only if exactly one api declaration of the name matches. With none or several, it takes none, and the declaration is left as written. So the choice does not depend on the JVM's identity-hash order of the declarations, and no output of the count or distance stage is known to move with that order (F-232): the error at `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:131` (`BIG LEXICO`'s omitted return type), which came and went with that order, is gone from both stages. - F-255 **The compiled checker reads conditional extension in its subtype relation: a trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause that binds no variable and holds trait constraints only is a subtype of that type exactly where the constraints hold.** The `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member are checked with the constraints holding. The static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, its `excludes` and `comprises` clauses and its other `extends` entries are checked without them. The disambiguator drops every trait's and object's `throws` clause and contract, so these are not checked at all (row 781). A clause that binds a variable, or that holds a constraint that is not a trait constraint, is read as before: as a parent at every instance. Limits: a member checked under the condition stays callable where the condition fails (row 773), and walk and the compiled run time read the extension at every instance (row 774). Other readers of the `extends` clause in the checker ignore the condition. Those that go through the type's parents see a conditional parent at no instance: the ancestors (`TypeAnalyzer.ancestors`), which the overloading checker reads to let a concrete method implement an abstract one. Those that read the clause itself see it at every instance: the inherited `excludes` clauses (`TypeAnalyzer.excludesClause`). None of these readers moved a result on the library, and no ledger row holds them (report section 10). In the library, `List` extends `LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\]` only where `E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\]`; its `ZeroIndexed[\E\]` entry and its own element-wise `opr =` stand outside the condition, so every list keeps them (`Library/List.fss:106-107`, `:124-128`). On the rung's own tree, against climb batch 17's gate, this cleared the distance's site of `LexicographicOrder`'s `a CMP b` over an unbounded `E`, in `FortressLibrary.fss`, and added none. - F-256 **The compiled checker checks a `where` clause's trait constraints where they apply.** At a dotted call, a candidate whose `where` clause constrains its trait's or object's static parameter is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the constraint ('Method Holder[\String\].showIt is not applicable: its where clause requires String to extend Shows.'). If a function's or method's `where` clause has a trait constraint, the clause's `nat` and `int` variables become static parameters of its arrow, inferred at the call. - F-97 **The ladder-regression stage's baseline is `compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/`.** The gate compiles and runs the files of its `pass-list.txt`, and compiles only the eighteen components of the two microGPT programs, which its `microgpt-phase.md` holds at the phase disambiguate. The gate's step 7 runs the stage (`gateRole` in `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`; the `fortress-repo` skill's `gate.md`, "The ladder regression").
- F-98 **The harness's `run_out_WIcontains` key is whitespace-insensitive containment.** It collapses runs of whitespace in both the output and the expected string, where `_WImatches` collapses them in the output only. A key that `generalTestFailed` does not know sets no check, so a misspelt key checks nothing. A `run_out` with no check falls to the default: the output contains `pass` or `PASS`. Source: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/tests/unit_tests/FileTests.java:155-188`, `:276-282`.
- F-99 **The gate's thread count is pinned in the build file for the two suites, not in the calling shell.** `build.xml`'s `fastTrack` macro, which runs `testFast`, and its `systemShard` macro, which runs `testSystem`, set `FORTRESS_THREADS=4` (P-125). Without the pin, the suites would take the caller's count: half the CPUs if it is unset, or 1 under `env.sh` (F-203). `fastTrack` also pins `JAVA_FLAGS` to `-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, because a compiled test's run step takes its heap and stacks from it. With `JAVA_FLAGS` unset, a compiled test's run step (`bin/run`) gives its threads the JVM's default 1 MB stacks, and at four threads `library_tests/TimingRungT` overflowed in 8 of 12 runs (row 640). Detail: `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/build-efficiency.md` section 6.

After a deletion, `fortress run` dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32` until the library order refills the five library jars, in about two minutes (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`). A `fortress compile` after a rebuild of the compiler does not clear them. The linker writes a missing `global.map` again, empty. - F-114 **`ant testSpecData` runs 130 of the specification's 133 extracted examples under walk, as a gate step, and all 130 pass.** `SpecDataJUTest` runs `SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries` and `advanced`, not `library/`'s three, and `testFast` excludes it. It builds P-124. Five examples write no static argument on a generic big operator whose bound mentions its static parameter, and they pass only because walk leaves that parameter open (F-143; row 424, fixed). The count and the time: the last landed gate's `summary.txt`.
- F-203 **`explorations/experiment/env.sh` sets up a shell for the gate's runners, and sets `FORTRESS_HOME` from its own place in the tree.** It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` two folders above itself, replacing any value that the shell had (`env.sh:4`), so sourcing another tree's `env.sh` runs that tree's code. It also sets the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` and `JAVA_FLAGS`, and unsets `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`. It deletes a `/tmp/fortress*rats` parser folder only if nothing in it was written for an hour and every running `java` process started after its last write, so sourcing it does not break a live run. The compile ladder's drivers source it: `compile-ladder/run-ladder.sh` and its copy in `baseline-2026-09-19/`, and the two that the gate's ladder regression runs, `repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh` and `baseline-2026-09-19/microgpt-phase.sh`. Each of these sets its own `JAVA_FLAGS` after it. `experiment/setup.sh` sources it too. `microgpt-phase.sh` names the main tree's `env.sh` by its absolute path; the gate rewrites that path in its copy (the `fortress-repo` skill's `gate.md`, "The ladder regression"). The count stage's and the distance stage's `run.sh` do not source it: their headers tell the caller to source it first. A worker does not source it. It starts each Bash call with the `fortress-repo` skill's setup lines, which give the same settings (`build-and-caches.md`, "Setting up each call"). Evidence: read in the scripts; the deletion rule also in `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/build-efficiency.md` section 4.
- F-234 **A Fortress command that a worker types itself (`bin/fortress`, `harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh`, or `java` of a Fortress main class) starts a fresh JVM, and that start costs too little to pay for a resident compiler.** A resident compiler is a background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did. The suites start one JVM for each test class, and one for each of `testSystem`'s four shards, not one for each test: the harness runs each test file inside its JVM. Only a compiled test's run step and a `.sh` test, such as `tests/concurrentPrinting.sh`, start another process. In one measurement over 267 worker transcripts, the one-off commands took 17.5 % of the wall time of the workers' shell commands, and the suites, builds and stages 47.8 %. Over the workers' whole running time, the one-off commands took 6.4 % (11.6 % if every wait that the measurement could not tie to a run was theirs). Removing their JVM start-up would save at most 1.8 % (P-150: no resident compiler is built). What runs inside the suites and the stages was not measured. Detail: `coordinator/process-engineering/fresh-jvm-commands.md`, "Summary", "What a resident compiler could save, at most" and "Decisions not taken".
- F-283 **The 52 programs of the team's `DemoTests` reach their end under walk.** Run one at a time from `ProjectFortress/demos`, each exits 0 and prints no "fail", within a 600 s limit and on an empty input, with `wordcount2` run from the tree's root and `tennisRanking` given the three files of `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/tests/unit_tests/FileTests.java:809-818`. The demos run in no suite, so a batch that changes walk or its library runs them again (P-79). `Generator2Demo` draws its arrays by `random`, so a product of them can overflow in `PROD`, and one such `IntegerOverflow` stop in a run is not a regression (row 986). The compiled checker still refuses `trips.fss` (row 817). No gated test: the command is the driver in `compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md` section 13, and its output on the code that `4445d848b` committed is 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. Detail: the same report, section 3; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-27/REPAIR-review.md`, section 2.
- F-295 **The distance stage counts each api's own errors and crashes, so an error in an api that only a later target checks cannot hide.** `table.py` turns `#total` into `none:` for an api whose `@@TC API` line gives `errors=` above 0 and that printed no `@@SC` line of its own, naming it with its count, and turns an `@@TC API-CRASH` line into a `#crash` row of kind `api` (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/table.py:54`, `:61-67`, `:94-104`). It does not read the `@@TC COMPONENT-CRASH` lines that `tools/distance/shadow-patch.py:111-113` prints. Test: `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/test_classify.py`, `Readings`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-list-imports/REPORT.md`, sections 1 and 2.
- F-354 **Two compiles of one source by different builds of the compiler need not give the same bytes, so a comparison of jars cannot show that a change left the compiled code as it was.** The code generator writes a class's methods and a dispatch method's tests in an order that follows the JVM's identity hashes (row 996). Two cold compiles of the prelude by one build give equal classes, 590 of 590, because the default identity hash is the same sequence in each run. Under another hash mode 18 of `CompilerBuiltin`'s 312 classes differ: the same methods in another order. So the tests, not the bytes, show that a change of the compiler left the prelude undisturbed, and a result that depends on the order can come and go between builds. Measured once, on `832f7d0d91`'s code. Detail: `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/probe-y.md`, "6. A finding beside the question: the prelude's jars change with any change of the compiler".
## Landed semantics

- F-117 **A compiled mutable variable's cell holds the language's top type, so a mutable variable of arrow type compiles and runs.** The cell holds `fortress.AnyType.Any`, not `FValue`, because a compiled closure is not an `FValue`. The cell's gated tests, `compiler_tests/AtomicTopLevel*Var` and `MutableTopLevelVarInLoop`, run no variable of arrow type. Detail: `compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 4.
- F-118 **A numeral's value reaches the compiled code intact, and the compiled path prints a large `NN32` or `NN64` value unsigned.** A numeral that no place types becomes its default through that type's own coercion, which the checker inserts (`Functionals.scala`, `defaultNumeral`); only a numeral that the checker leaves without a coercion reaches the code generator's fallback, a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by exact bit length (`CodeGen.java`, `forIntLiteralExpr`), and which numerals do is not measured. Otherwise the clauses run once into the library's collector, `__elemsOf`, which keeps the elements in order, typed at the join of their run-time types, and the operator is instantiated at that join; the reduction then runs over the collected elements, so each body runs once. A declared type or a join that does not fit falls back to the instance that no hint gives: a plain-bounded parameter takes its bound, and an F-bounded one stays open (F-143). A big operator whose declared result is a trait of its own is read through the `BigReduction`, `Comprehension` or `BigOperator` that the trait extends (row 718, fixed). Still wrong, each a ledger row: an empty clause form that no declared type directs takes its bound or stays open (row 716); a comprehension that no declared type reaches is built at the join of its elements' run-time types, which a declared `List[\Shape\]` refuses where its elements are all `Circle`s (row 717); a clause form that is a call's argument gets no declared type (rows 510, 705). - F-252 **Under walk, where the parameter-by-parameter check refuses two declarations with static parameters of their own, or one beside a generic trait's functional method that declares none of its own, the load check reads the pair again on its declared domains, by the No Duplicates, Return Type and Meet Rules.** A declaration with static parameters of its own is a generic function, a generic object's constructor, or a functional method that declares static parameters in a trait or object that has none. Walk's load check first compares two overloads parameter by parameter, and a pair that it finds excluding loads, except a plain declaration inside an own generic's declared domain where the two lists differ only at object types, which it reads on the declared domains (F-375). Walk then reads such an exclusion again over the instances of each, and withdraws it where their instances do not exclude. Instances of one generic type exclude only where their static arguments cannot be equal. Any other exclusion stands where the two still exclude with their static parameters renamed apart. Or, read at the shared instantiation, it stands where every generic type that both extend forces their static arguments to be equal, since no type extends two instances of one generic trait: so `Array` and `ImmutableArray` exclude at every pair of instances through `ReadableArray`. A pair whose exclusion is withdrawn is read on its declared domains as a refused pair is. It reads a refused pair of two such declarations again, each over all its own instances, and loads the pair if it meets the three rules. An own generic beside such a functional method is read as two own generics, the trait's static parameters standing for the method's (F-318). A pair that the parameter check orders is read again only for the No Duplicates Rule (F-274). F-275 holds the Return Type Rule. The parameter check does not find two instances of one generic type at different ground static arguments excluding, such as `Tg[\3\]` and `Tg[\4\]`, so two plain declarations so typed are refused (row 416). Two declarations with static parameters of their own so typed load where the reading of the whole parameter type finds the instances apart, as `h[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\])` beside `h[\J\](a: Array[\ZZ32,J\])` loads and runs (F-155, F-258). For the Meet Rule, walk looks for a third declaration that covers the overlap only where, at each position, the two parameter types are equal, or one of them is a static parameter, or both are instances of one generic type whose static arguments match in the same way (row 539). This search reads a bound that names its own parameter from the declarations, so two such bounds meet, and unifies a symbolic size with a size parameter. A pair whose domains exclude when read whole also loads, where neither declaration has a `where` clause of its own (F-258; row 787). A pair with a varargs parameter is not read again and keeps the parameter check's refusal (F-257). At a call, walk compares a functional method of a generic trait or object on the instance that the call makes. F-253 gives the case of a generic dotted method, where one of the two declared domains can lie inside the other. Gated by `tests/DispatchRenamedGenericArmWalk`, `DispatchSwappedGenericArmWalk` and `GenericPairNestedBoundsWalk` (load and dispatch), and the expected failure `XXXOverloadExistentialMeetWalk` (row 539); for the withdrawal, as refusals at load, by `GenericBoundsNoMeetWalk`, `NoDuplicatesRuleWalk`, `NoDuplicatesRuleSizeWalk` and `GenericOverloadInstancesApartWalk`, and as programs that load, by `GenericBoundsMeetWalk`, `GenericFBoundsMeetWalk`, `GenericPairExcludingWalk`, `GenericSizePairNestedWalk`, `ShuffleTest` and `GenericPairExcludesTogetherWalk`. - F-257 **Under walk, a pair of declarations that the load check refuses after it reads the pair on its declared domains is refused in the name of the rule that the pair breaks.** The load check reads a pair on its declared domains where its parameter-by-parameter check refuses the pair and both declarations have static parameters of their own, or one has them and the other is a plain declaration or a generic trait's functional method that declares none of its own (F-252, F-27, F-318), and where that check finds a plain declaration inside an own generic's declared domain excluding at object types alone (F-375). Gated by `ProjectFortress/tests/GenericPairExcludesTogetherWalk`, `GenericPairForcedObjectApartWalk`, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/GenericPairExcludesTogether` and `GenericPairSharedSupertypeExclusion` (load, compile and dispatch), and `ProjectFortress/tests/GenericPairFreeArgumentWalk`, `GenericPairObjectSupertypeOverlapWalk` and `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXGenericPairFreeArgument` (refused). - F-259 **An object or trait whose `extends` clause names `Any` alone is an `Object` on both paths, but the library's `Index` (F-278), and such an object expression under walk, and `String`'s two top-level `||` over `Any` convert by the library's own way.** The pre-disambiguation desugaring that both paths run gives such a clause `{Object}`, as it gives an empty one, and leaves `Any`'s, `Object`'s and the library's `Index`'s own declarations as written; a clause that names only `Index` (and `Any`) gets `Object` beside it. `opr ||(a:Any, b:String)` is `("" || a) || b` and `opr ||(a:String, b:Any)` is `a || cast[\Object\](b).asString` (top-level since F-276); `FlatString`'s api states its component's header, with no `opr ||(a:FlatString, self)`. - F-262 **A numeral's sign does not reach its type on either path, so no overload on a numeral exponent's type can tell a positive exponent from a negative one, as in `x^16` and `x^(-16)`.** The numeral itself has no sign (`Specification/basic/lexical-structure.tex:1053-1080`). F-251 holds the same opening for a type variable. Gated by `compiler_tests/NatOpenChecker`, and under walk by `tests/NatOpenWalk` and `NatOpenUnlistedExtender`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-size-expressions/REPORT.md` section 1, "Fork 3, way 4a, under Q13.3", and section 12.

- F-372 **The code generator writes each inherited method once into a trait's or an object's class, runs the declaration of the lowest type that declares it, and forwards to a body that an imported api's trait holds.** For the class of a trait or an object the code generator leaves out each declaration whose method a type strictly below the declaring type declares again at the same parameter types, self apart. A dispatch method's gathering still compares declarations as schemas over each trait's own bounds, not at the instance. So the choice is a relation between two declarations, not the order of the gathered methods, and the library's shape of P-47, `MAX` in `StandardMinMax`, `StandardTotalOrder` and a type below, does not stop a class at load (row 990, fixed). A method that an imported api's trait declares without `abstract` counts as a body in that trait's class, so a trait that is not first in an extends clause gives its body, plain, generic and functional methods alike (row 732, fixed). A worker chose both readings, and the curator has not decided them; by the traits chapter's text, an object that reaches one method along two paths, one through a trait that declares it again, inherits both declarations, and the checker refuses that form where the traits are self-typed and generic (row 1037). A functional method with self not first is written once, not again beside the dispatch method of the same name (row 571, fixed), so such a class loads; but an object's dispatch method still tests the receiver in place of the argument, and where the receiver itself has the own declaration's parameter type, a call answers wrongly with no error: with `object Pq extends { K, P }` declaring `mark(x: K, self)` beside `P`'s `mark(x: Any, self)`, `mark(1, Pq)` gives 3 where walk gives 1 (rows 1038 and 573). Tests: `compiler_tests/TraitOwnMethodBesideInheritedCompiled`, `ApiTraitMethodNotFirstCompiled`, `TraitMethodDiamondRedeclaredCompiled`, `FunctionalMethodMeetNarrowedSelfNotFirst`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-method-forwarders/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".
- F-373 **The compiled path runs `label` and `exit`: an exit is a thrown `LabelExit` that names one evaluation of its label block, and reaches it from a loop's body and from another task.** `CodeGen.forLabel` makes a new target for each evaluation of the block and takes, in a handler, the exits that name it; `CodeGen.forExit` throws `LabelExit.of(value, target)` (`runtimeSystem/LabelExit.java`). A function expression or a task whose body exits captures the target as it captures any immutable variable. A group of forked arms joins the arms that it forked before the exit passes it: at four threads every forked iteration of a parallel `for` runs to its end or to its own exit, and the label's value is the exit of the first arm in the arms' order; at one thread the iterations after the exit do not run. No `catch` clause takes an exit. So the one library's `Indexed.indexOf` compiles in its own form (the test's `Holder.indexOf`), and row 81 is fixed. Three of the compiled answers were chosen as the path was built, and the curator has not decided them; walk answers each otherwise: which evaluation an exit leaves where the block is evaluated again inside itself, compiled the one in which the exit's function was made (row 1042); whether a `catch` of `Exception` takes an exit, compiled no (row 1040); and what an exit is after its label block has completed, compiled an uncaught `LabelExit` that ends the program (row 1041). Four limits stand, each with its test: an exit out of an `atomic` block loses the block's writes (row 1039); a `finally` clause on the exit's way does not run (row 890); a label block as a call's later argument fails verification (row 322); a label block whose value joins a numeral with a number stops the code generator (row 340), though by P-50 the numeral takes the label's expected type; a program binds the numeral to a typed variable first. Test: `compiler_tests/LabelExitCompiled`, which fails with 'Can't compile Label' without `forLabel` and `forExit`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-label-exit/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "Points to report reached".
- F-374 **A compiled object's `var` field lives in a cell that the object holds, and an atomic expression is its body in an atomic block.** On the compiled path a `var` value parameter or `var` field of an object is a `MutableFValue` cell in a `public final` JVM field, made by the constructor; each read and write checks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` and goes through the transaction or the cell, by the code of a top-level `var`, and a loop body or a function expression in the object's method captures the cell. A worker chose the cell, and the curator has not decided it. So an `atomic` block tracks a `var` field (row 319, fixed), and every access of one pays the transaction check, outside `atomic` too (row 641). A field without `var` holds its value and has no check. `atomic e` is compiled by `CodeGen.forAtomicBlock` on the block that holds `e` (row 875, fixed), with the block's limits (row 322); a numeral as its value at a place of declared type is refused or fails verification, since the checker carries no declared type into it (row 1043). So a change of the transaction's variable code reaches fields with no second edit, and a new kind of nested context must capture a var field's cell as it does a top-level `var`'s. A `value` object with a `var` field, which the specification forbids and nothing refuses (row 112), is not strictly equivalent to another built alike: `V(1) === V(1)` is `false`, since `SEQV` compares the cells by identity. The one library declares one, `Lazy` (`Library/Lazy.fss:18`). Tests: `compiler_tests/AtomicFieldCompiled`, `compiler_tests/VarFieldCapturedCompiled`, `compiler_tests/AtomicExprCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-atomic-expr-field/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "The bytecode".
- F-375 **Walk's load check reads a generic declaration beside a plain one over an object type by the Return Type Rule, and its check of value types passes a type parameter.** A plain declaration whose domain lies inside an own generic's declared domain is read on the declared domains even where the lists differ only at object types, which the team's shortcut takes to exclude: the pair loads where the plain result lies below the generic's by one of three readings that the report gives, and is refused, in the rule's name, where none of them holds (`OverloadedFunction.returnRuleAtObjectArguments`; row 998, fixed). A declaration that writes no return type is not judged there (row 1044), a `comprises` clause is not read (row 550's pair at `ZZ64`, fixed since `ZZ64` is an object, F-379), and two plain lists keep the team's shortcut (row 697). `FTraitOrObject.enforceValueness` refuses a declared type that is not a value type below a value type, and passes the symbolic type of a type parameter (row 997, fixed). The coordinator chose to read no `comprises` clause and to leave unjudged a declaration that writes no return type; a worker chose the three readings and the check of value types; the curator has decided none of them. With the merge of the number types with their objects (P-178, F-379) every generic-beside-plain pair over the five is read on its declared domains: walk's suite loads every pair it loaded before, and of its expected-failure tests none moves between a refusal at load and a failure at run time (`compile-ladder/rung-number-objects/REPORT.md`, "Every pair that walk refuses at load after the change and loaded before"). Where the reading and the team's shortcut differ, some pairs are refused and others load; the report runs each old against new. Tests: `ProjectFortress/tests/GenericBesidePlainObjectReturnRuleWalk.fss`, `GenericBesidePlainObjectValidWalk.fss`, `GenericBesidePlainEveryInstanceWalk.fss`, `TraitGenericMethodValueBoundWalk.fss`, `OverloadedGenericValueBoundWalk.fss`, `NonValueBelowValueTypeWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-value-bound/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "Programs run old against new".
- F-377 **The compiled code casts `self` where the checker reads it as a listed type or as the self-type parameter.** `CodeGen.castToTypeBelow` casts a value that has self's type (the checker's `TraitSelfType` with a non-empty list: a trait whose `comprises` clause lists types, or a trait with a self-type parameter) to a declared trait type or type variable strictly below its trait, at the argument of a call with one argument, of a function, a method or a constructor (`evalArg`; a call with several arguments casts each already), at a typed binding and an assignment (`forExprsSerial`) and at a method's returned value (`generateActualMethodCode`), also where the value is a typecase whose arms each have self's type. So `den(self)` for `den(r: R)` in `trait Q comprises { R }` and `twin(self): S = self` in a self-typed trait verify and run (rows 991 and 695, fixed), as the one library's `QQ comprises { Ratio }` needs. Only `self` gets the reading: the checker refuses a variable declared at the trait where a listed type is expected. A closure's returned value and a conditional's arms get no cast (rows 1050 and 1051), and a trait that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable gets none (row 307). An assignment from outside an object to its `var` field, of a value whose static type is a strict subtype of the field's type, fails at run time, `NoSuchMethodError`, also for `c.r := self` at a listed type (row 1053). No cast is added where the value's type is a subtype of the declared type by `extends`. One is added at a declared trait type strictly below self's trait, where the verifier, which checks no interface type, needs none; a worker chose it, and the curator has not decided it. Tests: `compiler_tests/ComprisesValueAtListedTypeCompiled`, `compiler_tests/SelfTypeReturnSelfRun`, `compiler_tests/SelfTypeReturnSelfAtTraitRun`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-comprises-cast/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".
- F-378 **A compiled method's JVM parameters follow its declaration, and two bridges join an instance's boxed tuple to a body's elements.** One parameter of a declared tuple type is the tuple's elements, one JVM parameter each; one parameter whose declared type names a type parameter is one boxed JVM parameter at every instance, a tuple among them. The code generator writes a method of the boxed signature that calls a body at the tuple type with the elements (`CodeGen.tupleElementsBridge`), and the class loader, in an instantiated class, a method of the elements beside one whose template's parameter the instance makes a tuple (`runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java:119-165`); a dotted call passes the tuple boxed where the receiver's type holds only such declarations (`CodeGen.callTakesTupleBoxed`). So the shape of the one library's arrays of rank 2 and 3, a generic trait's methods over its index parameter given bodies at a pair or a triple, compiles and runs against the prelude; the one library's own arrays run compiled only after the switch-over. Still failing: an object's method overloaded at a pair (row 1054), an object's one pair value parameter (row 1055), a generic operator applied to a pair (row 1056). Test: `compiler_tests/TupleIndexMethodCompiled.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-tuple-parameter/REPORT.md`, "The convention as built".
- F-380 **A numeral at the end of a block, or in a tuple, converts where it stands on the compiled path.** At a declared type (a return type, a typed binding, a parameter, an `if`'s other branch) the compiled checker converts a numeral that ends a block after a local declaration, and each numeral element of a tuple, by the type's own coercion of the numeral itself, so the code generator folds it into a constant (`scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala`, `numeralResult` and `joinInto`); such a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically, as at a block's end without a declaration (`NumeralConversion.outOfRangeAt` in `scala_src/typechecker/CoercionOracle.scala`). At a place that fixes no type, a block after a local declaration keeps its numeral's own type, and a later conversion of the variable dies (row 1060). Tests: `compiler_tests/NumeralEndsBlockAfterDeclarationCompiled`, `BlockEndsInTupleOfNumeralCompiled`, `TupleBindingIfBranchesCompiled`, `NumeralJoinBeyondRange.fss` with `XXXNumeralJoinBeyondRange.test`; `XXXNumeralEndsUntypedBlockCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-numeral-block-end/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why"; `compile-ladder/rung-numeral-block-end/SKEPTIC.md`, "Findings and fixes".
## The library's arrays and algebra

- F-151 **In the interpreter's library, `Vector`, `Matrix` and their factories and operators bound their element type by `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`.** `Number` declares no arithmetic, so the compiled checker accepts the bodies' arithmetic only through `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]`. `Number` stays in the bound, though it has no `comprises` clause now (F-324). The four juxtapositions of a vector or a matrix with a scalar `T`, in either order, stand beside the library's juxtapositions with a `String`, and the checker finds no error in them (F-53); no run measures what now keeps a scalar `T` apart from `String`. The vector norm is declared at each of the eight number types, by its own `asFloat` (F-324). The eight number types meet the bound. `Number` itself and the numeral types do not, since none is a ring at its own type. So `Vector[\Number,n\]` is not a well-formed type, and `array1` and `array2` have no branch for `Number`: called at `Number`, they give a plain array at run time, not a vector or a matrix (F-229). The checker accepts a call whose argument's type is built from the caller's own type parameter under the same bound, such as the norm's `squaredNorm(me)` (F-227). The scalar extension, the eight operators between an array and a scalar, has bounds of its own, also with `Number` (F-119). Gated under walk by `tests/ArrayElementAlgebra.fss`. The bound is the default that `reviews/array-fork2-judgement.md` recommended. Detail: that judgement, sections 2.5 (what `Number`'s `comprises` clause gives), 2.9, way 3 (the ring alone, measured) and 4 (the bound and its cost).
- F-152 **`Vector` and `Matrix` are the only array traits with an algebra, `AdditiveGroup`, and their element must be a `Number`.** They inherit `+`, `-`, unary `-` and `zero`, and nothing from another algebraic trait. `Array3` has no algebra (row 292). `×` reaches no array, by design: juxtaposition is the inner product (rows 109, 293). Walk accepts, unchecked, a carrier that extends both `Matrix` and `MultiplicativeRing`, and its `+` then fails (row 371). The specification's `T^n` denotes these traits (row 24), and neither path takes it. Detail: `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 2.
- F-154 **The library declares its matrix and vector products with shared `nat`s, so under walk a product of the wrong shapes stops the run at dispatch.** A shared `nat` is a size parameter that two parameter types name, as `m` in `DOT` and juxtaposition of `Matrix[\T,n,m\]` by `Matrix[\T,m,p\]`. The matrix-vector and vector-matrix products share theirs in the same way. Each product name is overloaded, so the stop reads "Failed to find any matching overload", with the argument types and their sizes. It is a `ProgramError` that no `catch` takes. A declaration that is not overloaded, such as the APL model's `pick`, fails instead with a unification error that names the size; no library product is such a declaration. Observed under walk for a mismatched `DOT` (row 254), and in a probe of the model's own sized declarations, where a `try` around a mismatched call caught nothing. Detail: `apl/mg/NOTES-swap.md`, "What the shared nats catch: the mismatch probe".
- F-155 **Under walk, two plain declarations of one name that differ only in the element type are refused at load, and two generic ones load; a rank-specialised declaration beside an index-generic one loads where it lies inside it.** The parameter check refuses the plain pair, as it refuses `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])`, "are unrelated" (row 416; F-252). `h[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\])` beside `h[\J\](a: Array[\ZZ32,J\])` loads and runs, since the reading of the whole parameter type finds the two instances of `Array` apart (F-252); `k[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\])` beside `k[\nat n\](v: Vector[\RR64,n\])` loads and dispatches. The rank-specialised `×` of `apl/mg/elemwise_nat_probe.fss` passes its own pair, then is refused beside the library's `MultiplicativeRing.×` (row 341). Walk checks as one family the overloads of one name that two imported apis declare, and an import alias does not separate them. So two such vocabularies cannot stand in one component. Detail: `apl/mg/NOTES-swap.md`, "Departures, each with its evidence", items 5 and 6; `compile-ladder/rung-walk-generic-pairs/REPORT.md` section 5.
- F-156 **The interpreter's library declares no reshape, plane, gather, outer product or ravel over its arrays.** A plane function takes one plane of a rank-3 array as a matrix. So Run C4's vocabulary (`explorations/run-c4/src/FlatArrays.fsi`) declares `view`, `heads`, `plane`, `gather`, `onehot` and `flat` itself, on the library as it stood. Such an operation belongs in the library (the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/library.md`). Read by a search of the library's apis (`Library/*.fsi`). Detail: `run-c4/probes/vocabulary/REPORT.md`, question 5 and section A.
- F-157 **An array is a trait with `get` and `put`, and a view is an object that implements it over other storage; this is the language's own idiom for a view of a runtime shape, as the library's own `TransposedMatrix` is.** Under walk, a subtype of `Matrix` that overrides `mul` gets its own product through the library's `Matrix` juxtaposition and `DOT`, which forward to `mul`. It needs no api line, since walk dispatches the method on the receiver's run-time type; the override was measured under walk only. In two measurements under walk at `b176a4b79`, views through the library cost more. On lifting a function over the rows of a 64 × 16 matrix, the row slice `m[i,:]` took five times as long as a six-line user view (row 298). The library's product with a diagonal that is a plain `Matrix` view, without the override, took 13 times as long as a row-scaling operator at n = 16, and 58 to 63 times at n = 64 (row 299, which says 54). Detail: `reviews/c4-flatarrays-review.md` section 1 (the idiom); `run-c4/probes/vocabulary/diag-override.md`, "Result" (the override) and "Timings against row 299" (the ratios).
- F-158 **`fill` takes a value and `tabulate` a function, both defined where the array diamond meets.** It builds P-89. `StandardMutableArrayType` and `ImmutableArray1`, the traits below both sides of the diamond, define them. `Vector` and `Matrix` also redeclare them at their own type, with the meet's bodies (F-264). A method declared only in each leaf leaves the meet refused by the checker's Meet Rule, so `copy` is declared on the meet too (row 467). Its factories are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`. Gated by `tests/TabulateRungA.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-tabulate/REPORT.md` section 2.
- F-159 **In probes of 2026-09-29, a generic factory with a written static argument selected a store written for `RR64` alone, through a witness `typecase` whose branch result was passed through `cast`, on both paths.** A store is the object that holds an array's elements. A witness is `__thrower[\X\]`, a function of type `() -> X` that is never called; a `typecase` on it chooses a branch by the type `X`. The probes declared their own one-method trait `Arr[\T\]` and two stores, `DStore` for `RR64` and a generic `BStore`; they used none of the library's array traits, and the compiled runs used the compiler's own prelude. A witness `typecase` whose `RR64` branch returns `DStore` ran under walk. The compiled checker refused the body, whose type is the union `OR(DStore,BStore[\T\])`, against the declared result `Arr[\T\]`. With that branch's result passed through `cast[\Arr[\T\]\]`, as the library's `additiveIdentity` does, it checked. Both paths then gave `DStore` for `mk[\RR64\](r)`, with `r: RR64`, and `BStore` for `mk[\ZZ32\](z)`. A plain factory for `RR64` beside the generic one, called from generic code, was accepted by the compiled checker and dispatched to the plain declaration. Walk refused that pair at load; its present load check (F-27), which reads a generic declaration beside a plain one on their declared domains, has not been run on it. The library's `array1` and `array2` take a witness of their result type, not of the element type, for the reason F-229 gives. - F-166 **On the topics of its Types chapter, such as the exclusion rule and covariance, the team's latest word is the unfinished restart, not `Specification/`.** The restart, `Documentation/Specification/`, was never adopted. Its Types chapter restates the exclusion rule as "instantiation exclusion" and adds `covariant`. On the rest of static parameters, and on traits beyond a stub, exceptions, components and the numeric library, `Specification/` is the only statement. Which text governs is the curator's: `Specification/` stays the standard, the Types chapter is cited beside it, and `covariant` is future work (P-25). The type group's POPL 2019 paper is later than both (F-271). Detail: `coordinator/spec-lineage.md` section 6 and its "Coordinator's check (2026-09-26)".
- F-167 **The specification states instantiation exclusion and keeps each example that the rule refuses, marked "Not allowed"; the calculi of Appendix A carry a callout that they predate the rule.** It builds P-97. It also bars a `where`-clause variable from an `extends` clause's static arguments. The covariance example, the empty list, the empty optional value and the root type `Object`'s algebraic supertraits each stand beside the library's shape, which runs on both paths except `Nothing[\String\]` on the compiled prelude (row 331). A subtrait of every instantiation stays as the counterexample that introduces the rule, and the internal appendix's refused examples get a callout each. The checker does not yet refuse two cases: an object that extends two instantiations that differ only in a `bool` argument (row 406), and one that extends two instantiations of one trait where one instantiation's argument is the object's own static parameter, such as `O[\nat n\] extends { Vec[\n\], Vec[\3\] }` (row 414). Detail and examples: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md` sections 2 and 3; its section 4.2 (the calculi's callout).
- F-168 **The specification's number chapters describe the flat library, and its advanced chapter on rational quantities stays word for word under a callout that marks it superseded.** The eight number types are siblings under `Number` (F-131). They convert by the library's coercions (P-74), and every other conversion is explicit, such as `asFloat(x)`. The sign-refined types, such as positive ℚ, are gone; a program tests a value's sign at run time (P-80). ℚ holds +∞, −∞ and 0/0, and claims neither a field nor a total order. `QQ` extends the four algebraic traits that the library declares on it, `StandardPartialOrder`, `StandardMinMax`, `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, and their laws hold for the finite rationals. F-172 gives the integer chapter's rules. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-numbers/decision-record.md` section 3; `Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex:245-250` (ℚ's traits); `Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex:14` (the callout).
- F-169 **The Working Draft never wrote static-argument inference, never named the type that a library gives an integer numeral, and never named a range's integer type; the specification's text on these is the revival's.** The Working Draft's inference chapter is a heading and notes. It described numeral types, such as `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]`, and said that libraries define coercions from numerals to integers and rationals. But a note of its own leaves the numeral types' hierarchy undescribed, and it names no type that a library declares for a numeral. Its ranges section names no integer type. The later restart adds nothing on the three. So a citation of the specification on them cites the revival, not the team. The revised text states F-173's inference rule and F-170's ranges, and gives an integer numeral the Working Draft's `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]`, its four numbers as static arguments (P-174). Detail: `reviews/numerics-plan-coordinator/evidence-B.md` sections 1 and 2; `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:87-96` and `:132-148` (the note and the coercions); `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:146-161` (the callout on the numeral types).
- F-170 **The specification's ranges are over ℤ32, and its own ranges over wider integer types are respelled.** An integer numeral, and a `nat` or `int` parameter, used as an operand of an explicit range, such as `a` or `n` in `a#n`, converts to ℤ32 (row 485, fixed). An operand of any other integer type is a static error. A loop whose counter must have a wider integer type runs over a range of ℤ32 values and widens each element. The two examples that built `ZZ64` ranges run over ℤ32, and `ant testSpecData`, a gate step, runs both (F-114). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-ranges/decision-record.md` sections 2 and 3; `Specification/basic/expressions/ranges.tex:42-60` and `:90-111`.
- F-171 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause as the restart's Types chapter does: every value of the trait is a value of a listed type.** So a trait or object that extends the closed trait must be below a listed type, with two exceptions. A trait with a `comprises` clause of its own may stay unlisted if each of its own listed types is below a listed type of the closed trait. A trait with static parameters may stay unlisted if at least one type extends it and every type that extends it is below a listed type. A listed type may be an instantiation at the trait's static parameters or `where`-clause variables. The text does not say whether a bare type variable may be listed; walk overflows its stack on one (row 407). The compiled checker departs in three ways: it checks only the closed trait's immediate subtypes (row 487), it reads the clause in the subtrait's own type-variable names (row 489), and it finds extenders by the simple text of a name (row 490). Whether the team's commented `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]` is valid is open (F-121). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-comprises/decision-record.md` section 2; `Specification/basic/traits.tex:246-269`.
- F-172 **The specification's integer chapter states the library's integer rules.** The getters `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` and `asZZ` keep the value or throw `IntegerOverflow`. `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the bits and throw nothing: `narrow` converts a `ZZ64` to `ZZ32`, and an `NN64` to `NN32`, by keeping the low 32 bits, so a value that does not fit wraps. `ZZ` has neither `narrow` nor `widen`. `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` work on the five integer types. On `ZZ` they are `shift`, which is exact at any count. On a fixed-size type, `LSHIFT` loses the bits shifted out and throws nothing. `GCD` and `LCM` are nonnegative, and one that a fixed-size type cannot hold throws `IntegerOverflow`. At a negative power, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 throws `DivisionByZero`, and any other base throws `IntegerOverflow`. The library follows the same power rule under walk; the compiled path's own library does not (F-263). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-integer-rules/decision-record.md` section 2; `Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:39-98` (the conversions and the shifts) and `:562-574` (the power); `Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:262-268` (`GCD` and `LCM`).
- F-173 **The specification's type-inference chapter states the rule that the compiled checker builds: the declaration is chosen first, then its static arguments are inferred.** It states P-46, P-48 and P-49. A type parameter that a parameter's declared type mentions inside another type, as `List[\T\]` mentions `T`, is fixed by the argument at that position. One that is the whole declared type of one or more parameters, as `T` is of `x: T`, and that nothing else fixes, takes the narrowest type, within its bounds, that every one of those arguments has or converts into: `ZZ64` for a `ZZ32` and an `NN32`. Where there is none, and no numeral settles the tie, it takes its bound, narrowed by what the call's expected type requires of the return type (P-48). So does a type parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes. Inference never gives a type parameter `BottomType`. The compiled path departs from the chapter in these ways, among others. Its prelude lacks the coercion of `NN32` into `ZZ64`, so a `ZZ32` and an `NN32` instantiate a type parameter at `ZZ`, not `ZZ64`; no callout names this (row 442, `compiler_tests/XXXInferPromoteNN32`). The callouts at `Specification/basic/inference.tex:285-347` and `:448-512` also give walk's departures, such as the return type `BottomType` that walk gives a function expression that declares none (row 587). Plain tests gate the rule for a type parameter that is a parameter's whole type, at its bound where no argument type is narrowest, on both paths: `compiler_tests/InferLone*` and `tests/InferLone*Walk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-instance-bound/REPORT.md` (the bound rule); `Specification/basic/inference.tex:45-125` (the chapter's rule).
- F-174 **The specification states the type group's 2011 overloading model: declarations of one name may differ in their static parameters, and a declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration over all its instances within its bounds.** It states P-45 and P-42. The section "Declarations with Static Parameters" states the OOPSLA 2011 paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Return Type and Meet. It gives one more restriction as the compiled path's, not the language's. Where one generic declaration is more specific than another with as many static parameters, the two must declare them of the same kinds, position by position. Also, the more specific one's return type must be a subtype of the other's when their static parameters are matched by position, so the checker refuses an override whose return type reorders its static parameters (row 398, fixed). The section "Principles of Overloading" forbids overloading a functional whose single parameter's type is a type parameter with the bound `Any` written, as `T extends Any`. A type parameter with no `extends` clause, whose bound is also `Any`, is exempt. Both paths refuse such an overload: the checker in `OverloadingChecker.checkBoundAny`, and walk since row 534's fix. Neither path runs every set that the rules allow. Appendix I's entry "Overloading with static parameters" names the sets that each path fails. In row 1048, the checker refuses a generic declaration beside a plain one over a tuple of object types, as `ident[\T\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: (Circle, Circle)): (Circle, Circle)`. In row 537, the code generator fails on two generic declarations whose bounds differ. In row 539, walk refuses at load the 2019 paper's valid set over an array list and a list. In rows 779 and 780, walk fails on two generic functional methods one of whose declared domains lies inside the other's: in a trait or object without static parameters it refuses them at load, and in a trait with static parameters it loads them, but a call to which both apply fails. Detail: `Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:134-150` and `:531-674`; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 3 and 4.
- F-175 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause at the level of values in every passage.** It builds P-60. Appendix I's entry "Traits with comprises clauses read at the level of values" records the change. A call whose argument's static type stands between two closed traits runs the declaration that covers its value. Where its declarations have no static parameters, its type is the intersection of its most specific declarations' return types. Appendix I names five places where the compiled path departs. The checker checks a `comprises` clause at the closed trait's immediate subtypes only (row 487). The code generator crashes on a method call on a result typed by that intersection (row 540). Where any declaration of the overload set has static parameters, the checker types such a call by one of its most specific declarations instead, a deliberate choice (row 543). The checker refuses the Meet Rule's example for closed traits when its declarations have static parameters (row 546). The checker's verdict on an overload set can depend on the components compiled before it in the same JVM (row 547). Detail: `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:3474-3670`, with the rows at `:1674-1677` and `:3740-3747`; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 8 and 9.
- F-176 **The specification allows arithmetic in a size, and two size arguments are identical when they are written alike once each operation whose operands are numerals is replaced by its value.** It states P-55. When walk infers a size parameter from a call's argument type, it matches a numeral and binds a name, and solves no size written as an operation: read in `IntNat.unifyStaticArg` (`interpreter/evaluator/types/IntNat.java:126-147`), and observed in row 767. #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Keep the revival page's "Where it stands" block current at a landing.

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/revival-page/update.py [--check] [--landing N] [--run-start T]

Reads every value from the record (PLAN.md's "Where we stand" and phase lines, the
batch's gate summary, FACTS' F-299), rewrites the block between <!-- stand:begin -->
and <!-- stand:end --> in revival-story.md and revival-story.html in its fixed form,
adds the landing's row to record-growth/landings.csv if it is missing, runs
record-growth/measure.py and chart.py, and sets the end of the date range in the
HTML's chart alt text to the data's last day; then it writes the GitHub Pages copy
(docs/revival-story/).  --pages writes only that copy.  With --check it reads the values and prints
the block it would write, and changes no file.  It never publishes: it prints the
commit and the republish that the coordinator then runs.

Where a source's form is not the one this script parses, it says so and stops.
The README beside this script names the source of each value.
"""
import argparse, csv, hashlib, html, os, re, shutil, subprocess, sys

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
ROOT = subprocess.run(['git', 'rev-parse', '--show-toplevel'], cwd=HERE, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()
EXP = os.path.join(ROOT, 'explorations')
PLAN = os.path.join(EXP, 'coordinator', 'PLAN.md')
FACTS_TOOL = os.path.join(EXP, 'coordinator', 'tools', 'facts-extract.sh')
PE = os.path.join(EXP, 'coordinator', 'process-engineering')
PAGE_MD = os.path.join(PE, 'revival-story.md')
PAGE_HTML = os.path.join(PE, 'revival-story.html')
RG = os.path.join(PE, 'record-growth')
LANDINGS = os.path.join(RG, 'landings.csv')
