For `fortress-repo`, the record-landing workflow runs this update itself after a landing. When the worker is done, tell the curator in one line, in your next message, with the commit, or the first and the last of several, and the page's link. Watch both pages for comments sent to Claude. If the curator asks to reverse a change, have the skill writer restore the old words when the curator asks, by a comment sent to Claude on the item or in chat, with no cold read. The reversal does not wait for the end of the curator's reading. A change that nobody reads can weaken how you and the curator work together, and nobody notices.
- A change that touches the curator's role and decisions (this section), the asks, the held list, the review list or the register in which you write to the curator (the bullets at the head of "Talking to the curator") waits for the curator's yes to its exact words. So does every rewrite of this skill's `SKILL.md` or of a whole part of this skill, since it can touch any rule. After its cold read and the skill writer's fixes, put it under "Proposed changes" on the page of skill drafts, so that the words that the curator approves are the words that land. If the skill writer revises it on the curator's comments, have the revision cold-read again before it goes back on the page, unless it only takes the curator's exact words. Such a change has no default: it stays out of the skill until the yes. If you are unsure whether a change touches these, it waits.
- Change the other skills by the method of `references/skill-rewrite.md`. No change of them waits for the curator's yes, a change of their `SKILL.md` or a new rule included. Each lands after its cold read and the skill writer's fixes. For `fortress-repo`, the bullet above on the page update and the one-line report gives the page of its landed changes, the report and the reversal. For `cloud-container`, tell the curator in chat when a change lands: what changed, why, what it fixes, and any risk to watch for. If the curator asks, reverse it as that bullet says. So that the curator notices a new rule, or a change of a rule's meaning, name it as such at the head of the chat line. For `fortress-repo`, have the page worker name it so at the head of the item's reason.

## The facts of this environment

- The curator reads on an iPhone, often while iOS Speak reads aloud at a fast rate, and writes by dictation.
- A repository path does not open on the phone. A page link does, and so does a pushed file's GitHub URL: `https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/<path>`.
- The curator's client can show stale state. Answer what is in flight from the tree.
- The curator's time zone is Central European. The container's clock is UTC.
- The context is compacted when it grows long. The container can be lost, and a VM restart can roll the disk back. Only what is pushed survives.
- The session runs in auto mode. Its permission check can refuse a step after the curator's go (`fortress-repo`, its session part).
- The prompt cache lives an hour for the main session and a headless session, and five minutes for a subagent.
- A process stop comes about every 13 hours. Check-ins, reminders armed with `send_later` 45 minutes apart, wake the session within the cache's life (`cloud-container`, its stops part).
- A message that the curator sends during a turn is queued. An interrupt kills every running agent.
- The git-check switch, `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, turns the platform's git-check hook off at every start of the process and at every turn's end (`cloud-container`, its hooks part). Its reminders are advisory. If a git-check reminder still comes, the switch missed that turn: answer it as "Quiet times" says.
- Cached reads are almost free on the curator's plan, so a cost counts tokens written only.
- A worker runs on Opus unless `references/delegating.md` names another tier. Sonnet writes nothing that the curator reads.
- The curator picks this session's model, for its register and for Fable's weekly limit. The boot note names it.

## Talking to the curator

- Write plain short sentences, with contractions, halfway to ASD-STE100: active voice, one word for one thing. Keep replies brief.
- Give advice as instructions, in literal words. Use no metaphor, no flourish, no closing line that sums up, and no coda after a semicolon.
- Use no internal shorthand, and no label that you coined, unless you defined it to the curator earlier in this conversation. A label that you coined in your reasoning is not yet in the conversation, so it is new to the curator. The curator knows the terms that the glossaries of the project skills define. Define any other term where you use it, even a common term of the work, such as reshape, outer product, Ring or matrix multiplication.
- Never quote an entry's bold title as the curator's words. It is the record's handle.
- Use lists, not tables. The iOS client shows a table as one line that scrolls sideways.
- Write numbers as K or M: 5K, 1.2M. Give few, each with its meaning.
- Read the clock before you write any time, in a call of its own. Take a past event's time from the record: the commit, the transcript or the log. Give a time in UTC and in the curator's time. Never place an event from feel, such as "yesterday".
- Give estimates in the project's units, such as rungs, never in days. Give costs in tokens written, never in dollars.
- Do not use the AskUserQuestion tool: its prompt times out after about 60 seconds in the iOS client. If that timeout ends, the rule lapses.
- Put every result in the turn's final text, never between tool calls. The client folds text between tool calls out of view.
- If you think the curator is wrong, say so and show why.
- If the curator remembers a thing differently from a report, an entry or your own summary, take neither side. Have the point rechecked at its source (`references/delegating.md`, "Which tier runs what"), and give the curator the source's words and what each side got right. This holds over the bullet above.
- Once after each boot, at the first explanation or ask, read `explorations/coordinator/curator-profile/PROFILE.md` (about 9K characters). It grades by topic what the curator knows: pitch each topic at its level. POSITIONS' "History he knows" holds the project history that you do not explain again. Where the two disagree, POSITIONS rules: fix the profile.

**An ask.** Put decisions one at a time, one ask in a message. If the curator asks to see a subject as a whole, give it in one message: what its cases share, then each fork with its options and your recommendation, with no separate ask for each fork. An ask goes in this order:

1. The question, in one line.
2. The context, in short bullets. Start with a short primer in plain words, with a Fortress example. Say why the design exists. Say what the team's earlier text and its later word say, and which way they point. Then give the library's own way, and how to judge the fork. Give what the peers do as context. If the fork rests on a rule that refuses something, say what the library does instead.
3. The options, numbered so that the curator can answer "3b": what each does, produces, touches in the tree and costs. A peer's way is an option only where the peers weigh ("The curator's role and decisions").
4. How the options weigh against each other: what each gains, and what it gives up, next to the others.
5. Your recommendation, in one line, last, never in place of the explanation.

Before you put a question, run every probe that it needs. Say whether the path to the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library, needs its answer. Give what the probe measured: the distance to the switch-over and the checker count, and for a fork on microGPT, also its lines and its speed. Put an item of the review list as a decision already taken, by a batch or by you, that waits for the curator's review. Never put it as a hold.

Give each decision a default, the option that stands unless the curator picks another. Never tell the curator to take it unread: each ask is how the curator learns what the decision changes in the tree. Put the argument in a pushed review under `explorations/reviews/`, and link it. Offer no option that does nothing.

**Quiet times.**

- While the curator is away, keep your messages to the minimum: gather evidence and do the work. The curator is away:
  - after the curator has said that they are away or asleep;
  - in a turn that a check-in or a hook started, not a message of the curator's.

  Send no running commentary, and no line that the curator cannot act on, such as a closing offer of queued questions. Hold the reports of skill changes until the curator is back, and send them then in one message.
- Tell the curator of each change to POSITIONS in your next message, with its old and its new words. Past three changes, give each in one line, with the entry's number and what changed, and link the commit on GitHub for the words. While the curator is away, hold this report with the reports of skill changes. Leave out a change that writes down a decision that the curator stated in this conversation. Tell the curator of no other edit to the record, apart from naming each decision that landed ("The curator's role and decisions"). When the curator asks you to record words, reply "noted".
- Say nothing about a running batch until it lands or fails, not even that it started. If the curator asks, answer from the tree. At a check-in (a `send_later` reminder) during a batch, check the run, resume it if it stopped, and reply "." alone.
- Answer the git-check hook's reminders silently. Never commit unready work to satisfy one.
- The curator deletes the branches on GitHub, when they get to them. Never ask the curator to delete a branch on GitHub, and never remind them of one, in chat, in a message for their return, in a push notification or on a page. Drop a branch's deletion from every ask, close and list that the record holds. A branch that waits for the curator is state: write it in the boot note, and put it on no held list, review list or docket. If the curator asks about branches, answer from the tree.
- Send a push notification (the PushNotification tool) only for a long run's end, a hold or the model check's alarm. In it, say what happened, and name the batch by its number or the run by what it does. Say which go or answer the work waits on, or that the work waits on nothing from the curator. It reaches the phone only outside the app.

**While the curator reads turn by turn,** hold the points. An answer to each point as it comes buries the curator in text.

- Write each point on the held list, one line in your words, with the UTC time of its message.
- Reply with that line and "holding", in three lines at most.
- Answer nothing until the curator says the reading is done. Being on the list answers nothing, so never cite a held line as the curator's yes, in the record or to the curator.
- If the curator marks a point "now", act on it at once.
- While the curator comments on a page, the page keeps the comments, so each comment's turn stays small: "." in chat, and the point kept in your context. When the reading is done, write the points to the held list in one edit, and then act on the list. A comment that needs work now gets it now, such as a worker that fetches context that the curator asks for. A comment that opens a discussion gets its answer on its thread.

**Pages.**

- Send a document for approval as a page with the Artifact tool. Put each ask, and any other question for the curator, in chat, never on a page.
- On the page, each rewritten entry or section is one item, so that the curator judges each change in its context. An item holds, in this order:
  - its new text whole, with the added words marked;
  - its current text, collapsed;
  - what the change alters, and why, inside the item's Select range.
- On the page of skill drafts and the page of `fortress-repo` changes, an item of a change that landed holds its new text whole, with the old words shown struck through and the new words marked, and its reason inside the item's Select range. The reason says in plain words what was wrong and what the text now says. It never cites a cold read's flag by its code or number, a judge's ruling by its number, or an item of a task by its number. The item has no collapsed current text. An item that the curator has not said they read always shows the skill's current text: if a later change touches its passage, fold that change into the item, with its own reason beside the earlier one, in place of a new item.
- On every page, every text names the coordinating session in the third person, as "the coordinator", never as "you", the "why" of a proposed item included. The curator reads "you" on a page as the curator.
- The curator listens to a page with iOS Speak at a fast rate. So every page has a Select button beside each larger section's heading, and beside each item of a section. A section's button selects the section for Speak, its items included. An item's button selects that item.
- Put a section's references at its bottom, numbered by item, never inside the items. The Select button leaves them out, so that Speak never reads citations.
- Give every page the house style: the CSS and the Select button's script of https://claude.ai/artifact/FoTnH7KzXt5MtGk3tTcZ8W, the plan's page.
- Write a page's glossary as a dictionary does: the term, then a noun phrase with no article.
- After a compaction, publish a page by its URL: a publish by source path alone makes a new page. Rebuild a lost source from the published page.

## The record: what goes where

Under `explorations/coordinator/`:

- `FACTS.md`: what is true of the project now.
- `POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions about the project.
- `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md`: each entry's provenance and earlier lines.
- `INDEX.md`: one line for each note.
- `PLAN.md`: the phases, the questions for the curator in order, the parked items, and the review lists. Its first section says where the work stands.
- `PLAN-history.md`: the items moved out of PLAN, word for word, under a heading for the landing or the consolidation that moved them.
- The boot note, the one home of state: what runs, with each run's ID and estimate; what to do when it ends; a question waiting on the curator; the session's model; the one next process stop; the armed check-ins, by name; and the URLs of live pages. During a batch, the run's ID and the check-ins' IDs are in the check-in file that the boot note names (`references/batch.md`, "While it runs").
- The held list. Its last section holds the smaller items that the curator owns.
- `review-queue.md`: the review queue.

Elsewhere: the reports and notes, which hold the detail; the gap ledger, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, one numbered row for each known gap between the team's design and the tree; and the skills. This skill holds how you work with the curator and the workers. `fortress-repo` holds the rules that bind workers. `cloud-container` holds the platform.

FACTS and POSITIONS hold the project only, since workers read them. They state the present, and the history files keep how an entry came about.

- Search the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`: `'F-87'` prints an entry, `'F-87+'` adds its linked entries, `'history:F-87'` its history, `'index:WORDS'` INDEX lines.
- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py` (`references/record.md`).
- Keep one home for each thing, and point to it from elsewhere.
- Put on the held list each rule that the curator states about your work, and each change to how you work that you and the curator agree in conversation. Have the skill writer (`references/skill-rewrite.md`) put it into its skill at the next opportunity, as "The curator's role and decisions" says. That opportunity is the next task that you give the writer that has its own cold read, not a task that only fixes a cold read's flags. Before you give that task, read the held list, and add to the task each point that names the skill writer. Leave out a point of a reading that the curator has not said is done, and a point for `fortress-repo` while the record-landing workflow runs. The curator's rule in conversation is not a yes to the skill's wording. Keep it on the held list until its skill holds it. If a compaction comes before that, quote the held rule into the boot note, so that the session after the boot works that way.
- Commit only the paths that you name. Commit a tracked file with `git commit -- <paths>`, which is the same as `git commit --only <paths>`. For a new file, first run `git add -- <paths>`, with the paths named, then commit it in the same way. Never use `git add -A`, `git add .` or `git commit -a`, and never commit without paths: each takes changes that are not yours. The main tree is the checkout at `/home/user/fortress`, not a worktree, and a batch's gather stages its files there. While a batch runs, change the main tree only as `references/batch.md`, "While it runs", allows.
- Push after every commit, in the order of `fortress-repo`'s committing part. From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (`cloud-container`, "Rules for every agent").

## The boot

At session start and after each compaction, take these steps in order. If the curator names another form of the boot, that word replaces these steps. After a compaction, before step 0, load `fortress-repo`, then this skill, with the Skill tool. A copy of a skill or a part from before the compaction can be cut or old, so it counts as not loaded: load it again before its work.

0. Check the serving model: run `explorations/coordinator/tools/model-now.sh`, which prints the model of this turn's reply. If it prints nothing, use the `get_session` tool with no session ID: its `session_context.model` and `external_metadata.last_served_model`. If the model is neither Opus nor Fable, act as on the model check's alarm (below). Then check the transcript backup (below).
1. Run `explorations/coordinator/tools/positions-facts.sh`. It prints the FACTS entries that POSITIONS cites in numbered slices: with no argument, slice 1 and the number of slices. Print each later slice with `--part N`, to the last. Then read `POSITIONS.md` whole, in pages: it exceeds one page of the Read tool. So you read the decisions with the facts that they rest on.
2. `PLAN.md`, its first section.
3. The boot note, then the held list.
4. `git log --oneline -15`, for a worker's commit newer than the boot note.
5. If the boot note says that a batch runs, load `references/batch.md` and read what its "While it runs" names. Say nothing about the batch before that.
6. Load `references/delegating.md`, `references/record.md` and `fortress-repo`'s `references/records.md`.
7. Run `explorations/coordinator/check-index.sh | head -30`: it prints first the notes that lack an INDEX line. Add a line for each, without reading INDEX whole.
8. After a compaction, if the curator is not away ("Quiet times"), give a calibration check in a few short lines: your picture of the project's history, the current goals, where the work stands, and the next moves. It grounds you again in the work, and it shows your picture to the curator, who corrects it where it differs. Leave out a running batch.

`FACTS.md`, apart from step 1's entries, and `INDEX.md` stay unread. Before you state a fact, or put anything to the curator, search them with `facts-extract.sh`. Never read INDEX whole. Read FACTS whole only at a batch landing:

1. At the first batch landing after the boot, unless the boot was full, read `FACTS.md` whole, in pages. Do it before step 1 of `references/batch.md`, "The landing". If the boot falls inside a batch landing, take the boot's steps, read FACTS whole, then go on with the landing. Ask the curator nothing about the boot.
2. When the record-landing workflow of step 4 of "The landing" ends, read what it changed in FACTS and POSITIONS.
3. At a later batch landing before the next compaction, read only what it changed in the two files.

**The full boot.** Only at the curator's word, read `FACTS.md` whole in place of step 1's script, and `INDEX.md` whole after step 1.

**The transcript backup.** Check it at every boot and after every VM restart, since the backup fails with no message:

- If the backup's worktree, `/home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded`, is missing or not on its branch `transcripts-blinded`, re-arm the backup before the rest of the boot (the `cloud-container` skill, `references/container-loss.md`, "Re-arming the backup").
- Otherwise, read the last line of its `.backup.log`. If the line says `push=failed`, or its time is older than the machine's last start (`uptime -s`), run `scripts/backup.sh --run` in the worktree by hand, and read the new last line. A sound line ends `push=ok`.
- Re-arm only a worktree that is missing or broken. A snapshot, the backup's commit of the transcripts, older than the last restart is normal at the first boot after it: the backup runs only at a turn's end.

- Read nothing that the boot does not name. List no directory, and bound every command's output.
- To learn whether a worker runs, read the harness's notice at the top of the turn. After an interrupt or a process stop, check each worker before you say what ran or was lost: an Agent-tool worker in that notice, a Workflow agent by its `result` line in the run's journal. An output file is complete if it holds the last part that its brief asks for. Relaunch a killed worker only as `references/delegating.md`, "Interrupts and process stops", says.
- Rewrite the boot note whole at every change. Never append to it.
- The model check runs at every turn's end, in every session that loads the repository's settings, headless sessions included. Its alarm makes the session take one more turn, with a message that starts `MODEL ALARM`. On the alarm:
  - make the alarm the first line of your reply, and send it as a push notification;
  - do no other work until step 0's check shows Opus or Fable again, or the curator says to go on.

  The alarm holds over the rules of "Quiet times", also over the "." reply at a check-in. A go on holds until the model changes again. After it, put each later alarm in the first line of your reply, and send no push notification for it. A message that starts `MODEL CHECK FAILED` means that the check could not read the model. Then check the model with `get_session`, and tell the curator in the first line of your reply. If the model is Opus or Fable, go on. If it is not, act as on the alarm.

## The parts

- `references/delegating.md`: before you brief, launch, watch or resume any worker.
- `references/batch.md`: for a batch, from its preparation to its review.
- `references/road.md`: for PLAN's order, a fork, or idle time.
- `references/record.md`: before you edit FACTS, POSITIONS, INDEX, `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`.
- `references/skill-rewrite.md`: when a skill is to change.
- `references/analysis.md`: to measure the work, or find out what happened.
- `references/sources.md`: each rule's source, for maintenance only.

1	<!-- The curator's decisions about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as they stand now. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- P-48 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `POSITIONS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. How the curator and the coordinator work is that skill's, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. -->
2	
3	# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground
4	
5	## The goal
6	
7	- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** The revival judges what the designers intended by the team's own sources: its Working Draft of February 2011, its texts on types and its code. `Specification/` holds the Working Draft as a living document: the revival revises it and states each change (P-95). The texts on types include the Types chapter of the specification's 2012 restart (P-25). In `Papers/`, they include the OOPSLA 2011 paper, Naden's 2012 write-up and the POPL 2019 paper with its technical report. P-26 says when code counts, and which source wins where two conflict. The revival does not redesign the language. A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.
8	- P-8 **Where the designers' own sources, the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations, give no answer, the curator decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and he stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** On the way to a compiled microGPT, he accepts the language's unfinished corners as they are, so that the work does not stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and he takes the designers to have known more than he does.
9	- P-9 **The revival searches for the most readable expression of the microGPT algorithm.** C4 is the flat microGPT program (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), whose data layout follows Aaron Hsu's flat style of APL (P-29: C4 is not edited for speed before microGPT runs compiled). In C4, the polishing happens in the vocabulary, the array operations that the model's lines call: `FlatArrays.fss` beside C4, and what of it has moved into the standard library (P-27: what a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library). P-87 holds the limit: the model's text is the notation, and a change to a model line is shown to the curator as a diff first. C4 is the target form of the APL microGPT program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`): the APL program is written so that each of its lines expands into the line that C4 writes by hand. C4 writes its hyperparameters as tuple bindings, such as `(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)`, the form to which the APL sub-language (P-10) expands a strand assignment, APL's binding of several names at once. The one-line form, declarations separated by semicolons such as `nEmbd = 16; blockSize = 16; ...`, is not used: the APL sub-language has no use for it.
10	- P-10 **The APL side quest is closed: its sub-language covers only what the APL microGPT program needs, and the parts of APL that it left unbuilt, tacit functions, characters and nested arrays, are not pursued.** The side quest built an APL sub-language in `explorations/apl/`: a DSL grammar that expands APL text into Fortress code over Fortress's native arrays, not an interpreter of APL. Its microGPT program, `explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`, stays in the microGPT check under walk (P-30: the check's limit of one minute; what the check runs: the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/interpreter.md`, "The model program").
11	- P-11 **The 2D notation is a gimmick: no work on it unless the curator asks.** The 2D notation is Fortify's rendering. Fortify (`Fortify/`, run by `bin/fortify` and `bin/fortick`) typesets Fortress source as mathematics in LaTeX, for the specification and the papers. Taken as programming syntax, such a rendering fixes one view of a computation, though the same mathematics can be written in many ways. APL, with one symbol for each transformation of the data, expresses a computation better. The rendering is presentation only, off the revival's path, and no argument in favour of Fortress. The verdict is on that typesetting only: the Unicode operators, such as `∑` and `×`, are the language's own syntax.
12	- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types; F-9 and F-290 say what walk and the library lack for that step. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).
13	
14	## History he knows (do not re-explain)
15	
16	- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.
17	- P-19 **The tree is not described as the third-party port's migration grafted onto the team's history.** The port is a third-party port of the tree to Java 9, which commit `8fe1daa8f` copied onto the team's last commit (the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/records.md`, "The repository's history"). By history, `main` descends from that commit. By content, most of the port's files are removed or redone, and only one piece of the port's code still runs: the `FTypeArrayList` fix for the JDK 8 `TreeSet` crash (F-165). Why: the tree is not built on the port, and the record must not lead anyone to think that it is. The files that still describe the tree so wait for the lineage cleanup; `coordinator/lineage.md`, "Files that still repeat it", lists them.
18	
19	## Decisions on record
20	
21	### The standard and the sources
22	
23	- P-25 **`Specification/` stays the standard, and the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart is cited beside it.** The restart is a new specification that the team began in 2012 and left unfinished (F-166). Where its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, a worker cites it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, such as the exclusion rule, the chapter is the designers' latest intent, which the goal is to finish, and `Specification/` is revised to follow it. Three of the chapter's passages bear on the specification; P-97 holds how the revision uses the first two. It names the exclusion rule "instantiation exclusion" and gives it in two parts: which instantiations of a generic exclude each other (`types.tick:355-360`), and, in its note, a rule on trait declarations (`:361-376`). The revised `Specification/` takes that form: the first part in its chapter on types, the second in its chapter on traits. It adds a `covariant` modifier for a trait's static parameters, which neither path implements and which is future work, off the path to microGPT (P-62). Third, it says that `Bottom` cannot be written in a program, as `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` already says of `BottomType`.
24	- P-26 **The team's later decision wins over its earlier one, in a text or in code, where the team made it the language's rule.** P-7 names the texts, from the Working Draft to the POPL 2019 paper. Code counts as a decision where the team built it alike for all its types, or stated its rule in a commit message, a comment or the checker. Code that its author called a stub, and code that works around a limit of the JVM or of the checker, serve only the implementation. The decision that they depart from stands. "Later" is the date of the team's work on the point at issue. The revival revises `Specification/` to follow a later decision. The one library follows it too, in place of the team's earlier code, such as the interpreter's library. Where two later decisions conflict, the goal decides (P-8). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. Why: the Working Draft's early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run. So they learned what is feasible. They sought performance, and specialization was a must. Their later decisions include the exclusion rule, specialization and the number types of the compiler's prelude, siblings from 2009 to 2012 (P-43). The revival knows less than they did, so it does not second-guess them.
25	- P-27 **What a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library, in the library's own way.** A program written on this library has a part that states its algorithm, and it can have a part that builds domain-independent machinery that the library lacks, as both microGPT programs do. A form of that second part goes into the standard library when, on reasonable judgment, it is not an extension of the program's own domain; a form that the library has for one number type, rank or sibling trait and lacks for another is the plainest case. Whoever writes it there first studies how the library does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern, such as its `excludes` clauses. This rule governs how the library is extended; it does not choose between two of the team's designs of the language (P-26).
26	- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Its next layer is algebra: traits such as `Ring` and `Field`, which the library does not declare yet, and what machine learning's matrices and tensors need, so that the library's algebraic traits, such as `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, reach them too. Why: the curator wants those matrices and tensors to have the mathematical rigour that the library's way of building its types promises. The work edits the standard library itself, in `Library/`, not a separate tree of the revival's own outside it (P-27, how the library is extended). It is parked off the path to microGPT compiled. Two matrix ideas of his wait beside it: square matrices of one size as a multiplicative ring, and diagonal matrices of one size as a ring whose product commutes.
27	- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is far slower than Python's interpreter (`explorations/microgpt-port.md`, "Step-0 results", a measurement of 2026-08-23). Fortress's performance is judged on the compiled path, once the compiler runs programs. So no performance decision rests on walk's timings. In particular, until microGPT runs compiled, C4, the flat microGPT program, is not edited for speed. The gate never runs microGPT's two programs, C4 and the APL-style program, because they run too long to be tests. Why: walk is the unoptimised path, as a debug build is in Swift, where performance is not judged either.
28	- P-30 **The check of microGPT under walk after a batch must take less than a minute.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. The minute is the curator's goal, for a check that runs only about two forward-and-backward passes of the model, not a full training, and compares the results with reference values. That is enough to show that the model's mathematics still works, and that the library's changes, such as those to the arrays, did not break it. A slower check is to him a waste of time. The commit stage of each batch, the step that lands its changes, runs the check as `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh`, the quick versions of microGPT's two programs at once, outside the gate.
29	- P-32 **The record's maps are kept current and used, so that nothing that the record holds is worked out again from scratch.** The maps are `FACTS.md`, `INDEX.md` and the territory map, `explorations/coordinator/map/`. The territory map surveys the repository down to where the team wrote the intent of each design. Part of that intent is written only in the papers under `Papers/`, not in the specification. So the map covers the papers too, and shows where to look up a design's intent. `INDEX.md` is read whole at the coordinator's boot, at the start of each session and after each compaction, and each worker's brief carries a mission briefing from the territory map, not the whole map. The territory map's surveys date from 2026-09-16 (its README), so a status or a line number in them can be stale.
30	- P-33 **The work toward microGPT compiled follows the phases, in the order that the curator approved, and the rest of the switch-over takes microGPT's slice first.** These phases are steps of the work, not the compiler's phases, and they are numbered 3 to 6, after two earlier ones. Phase 3 ends when the compiled checker reports no error on the apis and components of the interpreter's library that the distance to the switch-over counts (F-53 defines the distance, says what it counts and holds its value). The library's other components are not part of phase 3: each is cleared before the first program that needs it, and at the latest before walk runs the checker (P-12), so `System` by the switch-over, since the compiler's tests need it (F-293); F-290 counts their errors. Phase 4, the switch-over: first the natives, the library's `builtinPrimitive` bindings made to run on the compiled path, then the compiled path reads the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude is deleted; phase 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's open gaps; phase 6, microGPT runs fast. The rest of phase 4 takes microGPT's slice first: the compile command selects the one library beside the prelude, one build serving both by a second set of the run time's value classes (F-353), so that each wall that only a tree switched onto the one library shows is met as one rung with its own test on `main`, under the gate, beside the code generator's walls; the move of the compiled tests and the prelude's deletion come last. Why: those walls stand one behind another (F-352), and this way gates each one, where the whole switch-over first lands them in one piece that no gate checks in parts. Code-generator work goes on beside that order, under either library (P-37). Row 320, an api implemented by a component of another name does not link, is part of the switch-over's design.
31	- P-175 **On the compiled path a call's arguments run in parallel where `ParallelismAnalyzer` judges them worth a task, as a tuple's elements do, so a reduction's two halves run in parallel; the one library's parallel range stops its split at a grain size, not at single elements.** The one library's range joins a reduction's halves as the arguments of one call, `red.join(loop'(lo, mid-1), loop'(mid, hi))`, and split down to single elements when the curator decided (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1312-1350`); the code generator evaluated a call's arguments in order, under the team's comment "Why isn't this parallel???", so every `SUM`, `DOT` and `BIG MAX` of microGPT would have run its bodies one at a time once compiled programs ran the one library. The split stops at a chunk that runs efficiently in sequence: in his words, "you need the right forking constants", as Steele's parallel trees end in sequential leaves and Clojure's persistent vectors take their branching factor from B-trees. It needs a group of forked arms to join every arm before it completes abruptly, which the compiled path did not do (`CodeGen.genParallelExprs` joined on the normal path only; `reviews/parallelism-foundations-2026-11-08.md`, section 7.1); F-350 gives what it does now. The library binding the halves as a tuple, and reductions left in sequence, are declined. Why: the specification evaluates each argument of a call in an implicit thread of its own (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex:60-64`), walk forks a call's arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:342`), and the model's parallelism is its reductions (the review, section 6). Detail: the review, sections 1.8, 6, 7.1 and 8.
32	
33	### The one library and the compiled checker
34	
35	- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). There are two exceptions, each so that both paths do the same before the switch-over, and each copy goes with the prelude: the numerals, where the prelude carries the design of P-174 and P-176; and the built-in number types, where it takes the form of P-178. The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.
36	- P-38 **The compiler prelude's own text is not repaired: its defects go with it at the switch-over.** A helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is fixed for the one library, and the prelude's value moves with it (F-313). Its `Maybe` block and its `REM` guard `if other = -1 then 0` stay as landed until the prelude is deleted, and their tests stay. Then the compiled tests respell its reversed wrapping and saturating operators (row 348), `ZZ64`'s compiled shift closes (row 381), and the specification's `shift` reaches the compiled path (row 383). `XXXShiftDeclRungI` is then promoted, and the switch-over batch finds the compiler tests that bind `shift`, a reserved name from then on.
37	- P-39 **Every batch's gate measures the checker count, and its total never turns the gate red.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. Its gate runs the gate's steps on their merged tree, and then the checker count, as step 8 (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`); the gate of `fortress-repo`'s gate part has no such step. The checker count and the distance to the switch-over both count the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library. The count stops where the checker crashes or meets an error that it cannot get past; the distance counts every error, over all apis and components (F-53 defines both and holds their values). A rise of the count's total is reported and never fails a batch on its own. The count's stage can still turn the gate red on the faults that F-66 names. One is a checker crash that no rung of the batch listed in advance as expected, in the field `expectedCheckerCrash` of the batch's manifest, the part of the batch's script that declares each rung's task. Until the switch-over lands, every batch's gate also measures the distance, in a stage that only reports. Why: the count checks only the `FortressLibrary` component (F-53), so a native binding moved onto a helper in another component is checked by the distance alone, and P-58 has each moved binding checked from the step that moves it.
38	- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size that inference leaves unknown is an error only where it is used.** A size is a `nat` or `int` static parameter, such as the length of an array in its type. The compiled checker checks sizes, and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140, the bound on both paths). The bound is this implementation's, for the sizes of arrays, vectors and matrices, to match the JVM's `int` indices; a numeral type's four static parameters have none, and read as values are `ZZ` (P-174). Wherever the array design, the compiled path's design for arrays (P-85), creates a JVM array, it checks the length there, at run time, and refuses one over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. So a declaration may declare a size that none of its types uses, and pass. A call that cannot fix a size of the declaration that it would choose is refused, also inside an overload set, instead of passing over that declaration. In the rule that no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait, two instantiations differ when any static argument but an operator differs, so `Vec[\3\]` and `Vec[\4\]` are two; boolean arguments count too once the checker has boolean parameters. A size used as a number, as in the range `0#n`, converts to `ZZ32` where one is needed, as a numeral does. The 17 vector and matrix operators of the `FortressLibrary` api declare only the sizes that their types use, the change of `explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch`. It finishes the team's own fix of 2008, which removed those sizes from the component only. The JVM length check waits for the array design; under walk such an array stops at its store's factory with walk's own error, which no catch sees (row 527). The checker still passes over a declaration whose unfixed size occurs in its own parameter type (row 400). The checker compares no boolean arguments (row 406).
39	- P-41 **On the compiled path, a size static argument travels at run time as a descriptor object, as a type argument does.** A generic type's descriptor has a field for each of its static parameters that is not an operator. The team's code generator already emitted that field for a size, with nothing to put in it, and the size's descriptor fills it. Each size value, such as the 3 of `Vec[\3\]`, has one descriptor, which `RTTIsize.of` takes from a table; no Java class is written for it. This is the team's pattern for instantiating types, applied to numbers. An operator static argument, by contrast, stays a name known only at compile time (F-39, how both paths carry it). The curator sees no need for an operator argument to be carried at run time the way types and sizes are. F-129 holds what runs and its open rows.
40	- P-42 **A type parameter declared without a bound has the implicit bound `Any`, not `Object`.** `Any` holds tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not. The library instantiates its generic containers at tuple types: its arrays indexed by pairs, such as `(ZZ32,ZZ32)`, are among them. The specification states the bound `Any`, with a callout that records that the Working Draft of February 2011 said `Object`.
41	- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.
42	- P-44 **`AnyIntegral` stays closed by its `comprises` clause, and the compiled checker reads the clause as the team's 2012 texts do.** The library's `AnyIntegral`, whose `comprises` clause lists the five integer types `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64`, stays closed. Beside the clause stays a comment in the team's `NOT YET` form, by which the team's library records a clause that it cannot write yet: here `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]`. The `where` form is built (P-151), but neither path takes this clause yet: the front end of both paths refuses it on a trait that declares a coercion (row 831), and walk refuses the library at load with it (row 804). `Integral[\I\]` extends `AnyIntegral` and is not in the list. The checker accepts such a generic trait below a closed trait when every type that the checker knows below it is listed. The clause's text in the library, and walk, stay as they are. Why: the team's 2012 texts, Luchangco's Types chapter and Welterweight, are its later word (P-25), and by them the clause is right as written. The rule leaves a hole that every way of closing `AnyIntegral` shares, except the team's 2008 way, a `comprises` clause on `Integral[\I\]` itself: a program's own subtype of `Integral`, declared in another component, is accepted although no listed type is above it. Row 487 records the hole, and this decision does not close it.
43	- P-45 **Overloaded declarations may differ in their static parameters.** The specification drops its sentence that forbids this, and keeps it as superseded text. It states instead the overloading model of the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which the compiled checker already used. The checker keeps the paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type. It checks the Return Type Rule over every instance of a generic declaration that the argument types allow, not over one guessed instance. One rule of the old sentence survives: if one generic declaration is more specific than another, their static parameters must line up position by position, as Java's rule for overriding a generic method requires. The compiled checker tests it only where the two declarations have as many static parameters of their own (F-75). Walk chooses among overloads by the parameter types that each declaration declares, not by the order in which they are written. At load, walk judges each pair of two generic declarations by the checker's rules on their declared parameter types. It does not refuse a pair only because none of their parameter types exclude, as when one declaration is more specific than the other. Walk and the checker must accept the same pairs. The library repairs, by declarations of its own, the overload sets that the checker refused, and no line of microGPT's two programs changes. Where walk or the checker still judges a pair against these rules: walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on the instance that a call makes (F-26); both paths refuse the paper's own valid example (row 539); walk refuses two generic functional methods of a trait without static parameters whose declared domains lie one inside the other, and fails at a call on such a pair in a generic trait (rows 779 and 780); and walk and the checker disagree on three kinds of pair (rows 786 to 788).
44	- P-46 **A conversion only makes a call possible: it never changes which declaration runs when one already fits, except a numeral's own conversion.** The declaration that runs is chosen on the parameter types that each overload declares: first those that apply, then the most specific of them (P-45). A generic declaration applies if some type within its bounds takes the arguments. Only then is the chosen declaration instantiated by promotion: at the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce (P-74). So beside `op(a: Any, b: Any)`, `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` applies to a call with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`, at `T = Number`. It is the more specific, so it runs, at `ZZ64`. Why: the curator wants fast generic code that a JVM can specialise. The exception is a numeral at a call. A comparison of a number with a numeral answers by the number's value, and the programmer does not retype the numeral: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, and no way that answers `false` is accepted. Of the ways to `true` that the review of them offers, the curator took its way B, whose rule is in the review's words, not his: a numeral is applicable to a parameter that fixes no type, at its default, and to a parameter whose type declares a coercion from the numeral's type, by that coercion (P-173); among the applicable declarations the most specific runs, and where two are not ordered, the one that the default fits. So `NN32`'s own `=` runs, and not the library's `=` over `(Any, Any)`, which the numeral fits at its default `ZZ32` and which answers `false` by `SEQV` (P-168). A value typed `Any` or `Number` fixes no type for the numeral beside it, which keeps its default. His own broader rule, to apply any conversion that reaches a specific declaration and to fall back to a plain one only when none does, so holds for a numeral's own conversion; for a value's coercion it is not taken. Walk and the compiled checker both infer static arguments with coercion, by the same promotion. The compiled path inserts the conversions statically. P-49 gives the order in which the checker tries a call. Row 537: the compiled dispatch between two generic declarations of one name with different bounds. Detail: `reviews/numeral-equality-ways-2026-11-10.md`, "Way B. A numeral goes to the most specific declaration that takes it; the default is the last resort".
45	- P-47 **Each integer type declares its own `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX`, instead of relying on those that it inherits from the generic order traits.** The integer types are the five that `AnyIntegral` lists: `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64`. Through `Integral`, each inherits the three operators from `StandardTotalOrder` and the `StandardMin`, `StandardMax` and `StandardMinMax` that it extends. `a MINMAX b` is the pair `(a MIN b, a MAX b)`. The `MAX` that a `ZZ64` inherits types `self` as the order trait, so neither it nor `QQ`'s `MAX` is more specific. Under walk, `b MAX 1` for a `ZZ64` `b` would then stop the run with "Ambiguous coercion". With their own declarations, these operators answer at the type that their arguments promote to (P-74), as `b + 1` does. Why: it is the library's own device. `QQ`, `RR64` and the compiler's prelude declare all three, and the specification's `ZZ` declares its own `MIN` and `MAX`.

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

- P-48 **A type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`.** The arguments leave a parameter unfixed when it occurs only in the result type; when two arguments meet at it with no narrowest type into which both convert (a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` have one, `ZZ64`, by P-74); or when dispatch, at run time, picks a generic declaration and must choose the instance to run. Its instance is then the intersection of its upper bounds (`Any` if it has none). At checking, that is narrowed by what the call's expected type (P-49 defines it) requires of the declared return type; at run time, by the static type that the checker gave the call. It is never `Bottom`, never the union of the arguments' types, and never the value's type alone. The rule sets the instance, not which declaration runs (P-46). Why: the rule is the team's later word, from the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch, and the curator trusts the team's later work above his own understanding. The rule changes nothing in microGPT, whose types are concrete. The library keeps the team's declarations of `fail`, `builtinPrimitive` and `List`'s empty comprehension, whose type parameters have no written bound, without the `extends Object` that a batch had added. Under walk, which has no static types, dispatch takes the value's type. Row 538: a compiled dispatcher that carries the static type that the checker gave the call, so that a generic declaration reached only at run time gets this instance. Rows 587, 591 and 612: three cases in which walk still gives `Bottom`.
- P-49 **The compiled checker tries a call first by subtyping, without the expected type, and coerces its arguments only when that attempt is not kept.** The expected type is the type that the call's context requires. The checker's first attempt checks the call by subtyping alone, without the expected type. It keeps that attempt when its result converts to the expected type, by coercion if need be. If it does not keep that attempt, it tries coercion of the arguments, with the expected type. So a declaration that fits the arguments as they are is not passed over for one that coercion reaches. A call with a numeral argument is the exception: where the numeral's own coercion reaches a more specific declaration than the first attempt chose, that declaration runs, so `u = 0` for `u: NN32` is checked at `NN32`'s own `=`, with the numeral an `NN32` (P-46 gives the numeral's rule and its ground). Why: in the curator's words, coercion should be tried when there are no matches.
- P-50 **The body of a `label` expression, and each value that an `exit` gives it, take the expected type of the whole `label`.** A `label` is a named block that code inside it can leave early with `exit`, giving a value with `with`. The specification types a `label` as the union of its body's last expression and the values that its `exit` expressions give. So when a `label` has an expected type, the compiled checker passes it into the body and into each of those values, as it does into each clause of a `typecase`. The specification's inference chapter lists the body and those values as contexts that carry an expected type. P-51 decides the same question for a call written as another call's argument. F-87 lists the checker's contexts that carry an expected type.
- P-51 **The checker retries a call written as another call's argument against each declaration's parameter type.** Take an outer call `f(g(x))`, whose argument is an inner call `g(x)`. If none of the compiled checker's attempts at the call accepts `f(g(x))` (P-49 gives the order of those attempts), the checker checks `g(x)` again, once for each declaration of `f`, with that declaration's parameter type at `g(x)`'s position as its expected type. The retry covers every inner call with inferred static arguments, not only one whose type parameter occurs in its result type alone. Why: the curator wants the type inference rules unified across contexts, which covers cases that the team did not build. As built, a generic declaration of `f` is first instantiated from the other arguments. The declaration whose retry succeeds is kept, or the most specific of several; otherwise the call goes on as it would without the retry. The measurement behind the decision is in `explorations/reviews/argument-context-probe.md`.
- P-52 **`narrowToRange` on a range of rank 2 or 3 checks containment corner by corner.** `r.narrowToRange(other)` must raise `IndexOutOfBounds` when `other` reaches outside `r` on any axis. Its bounds check compares the two ranges' lower corners, and their upper corners, by `PCMP`, the ranges' own point order, which compares each axis on its own. It does not use the tuples' lexicographic order, which serves sorting. So `((0,0):(9,9)).narrowToRange((2,-1):(5,5))` raises `IndexOutOfBounds`, since -1 lies below 0 on the second axis.
- P-53 **`String`'s `left` and `right` answer `Just(c)`, as their declared result type `Maybe[\Char\]` promises.** For a non-empty string, `left` answers `Just` of its first character, and `right` `Just` of its last; for an empty string both answer `Nothing`. The `left` and `right` of the library's ranges and lists answer `Maybe` values in the same way. So walk prints `Just(a)` for `"abc".left`, not `a`.
- P-54 **`QQ`'s `ceiling` and `truncate` keep `ZZ`, their declared result type, and raise an error at +∞, −∞ and 0/0.** The specification's paragraph on these methods said that they return the argument itself at those three values (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex`, "Rational Numbers"). That paragraph is revised. `floor`, `round` and the brackets ⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉ are built on `ceiling` and `truncate`, so they raise too. Why: the declared integer result and other languages win over the paragraph: Python's `math.floor(inf)`, for one, raises. The library raises `DivisionByZero`, as the revised paragraph says. After the switch-over, `QQ` follows the float ruling (P-68, on rounding the float types): `floor` and `ceiling` return `QQ` and pass the infinities through, and the brackets, `round` and `truncate` give `ZZ` (row 795).

Otherwise it compares two sizes by their written form: `s0 s1` is not the same size as `s1 s0`, though their values are equal. On the compiled path, the class loader computes a size's value when it makes the class of an instantiation. Walk already computes such a size exactly when it makes an instance. A callout in the coercion chapter (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex`) states the limit. Two expected-failure tests record it: `XXXCoercionStaticRungC`, the chapter's own printed example, and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC`. Where the rule asks for a declaration at the meet of two overloads' parameter types, several declarations below both serve, if together they cover the meet. So a call whose argument's static type stands between closed traits and their listed types may have several most specific declarations. ### Numbers

- P-66 **The integer principle: Java's and the JVM's defaults stay where they make sense, and are corrected where they fail high performance or mathematical precision.** The team did so with rounding. A hardware behaviour that bytecode can express gets its own explicit spelling, as the specification's wrapping and saturating operators do. Where the JVM prevents a correct implementation, the project gives way for now. The peers to compare are Julia, X10, Swift and Rust.
- P-67 **`round` on an exact half goes to the even integer, on both paths.** Under walk and on the compiled path, `round(2.5)` gives 2: an `RR64` or `RR32` value rounds an exact half to the even integer, as a rational does. This is the specification's rule for rationals, the default rounding of IEEE 754, and the rule of the team's own `round` on rationals.
- P-68 **On the float types, `floor` and `ceiling` return the same float type, while the brackets ⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ`, the unbounded integer.** So `floor(2.5)` is the `RR64` value 2.0, and ⌊2.5⌋ is to be the `ZZ` value 2. Row 330: one library rung after the switch-over, which first counts the interpreter tests whose output changes, then makes the brackets, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ` in each of the library's declarations of them; today `truncate` is `ZZ64` on both paths, the brackets are `ZZ64` under walk and `RR64` compiled, and `round` is `ZZ64`.
- P-69 **`LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` are bit operators on the fixed-width integer types, and `ZZ`'s `shift` is exact.** On `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, a shift loses the bits that it shifts out, silently, as in every peer language. A count at or beyond the width gives 0, or -1 for `RSHIFT` of a negative value, and a negative count shifts the other way, as Swift's and Julia's shifts do. The count may have any integer type, and the shift works at the width of the value shifted. On `ZZ`, the unbounded integers ℤ, `shift(x, k)` is ⌊x·2^k⌋ at any count; there the specification defines `x LSHIFT k` as `shift(x, k)` and `x RSHIFT k` as `shift(x, -k)`. On the compiled path, a shift of a fixed-width value works on the JVM's `int` or `long`, never through `ZZ`. Why: a shift through `ZZ` costs speed wherever the JVM cannot remove it. Row 442: the compiled `NN32` and `NN64` shifts, refused today. Row 383: `ZZ`'s `shift`, which the compiler's prelude does not declare. Row 381: a count of another integer type, where the compiled path refuses a `ZZ`, `NN32` or `NN64` count and computes a `ZZ64` count on a `ZZ32` at 64 bits.

The rule applies on both paths. Why: the specification says that both results are nonnegative, and its general rule raises `IntegerOverflow` for an integer result that does not fit. The same general rule makes `GCD` raise it where the divisor does not fit, as in the specification's example `-2^31 GCD 0` on `ZZ32`. Row 442: `GCD` and `LCM` on the compiled path's `NN32` and `NN64`.

The test `a = -a` is true for that value, and also for 0. Walk already gave 0 in the three cases. The revival adds no prose of its own there, and nothing on building the implementation, which the repository's `README.md` holds. Each change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). Why: text that describes what the implementation does not do misleads the reader, and a free rewrite puts the revival's text in the place of the team's.

127	### The suites and the gate
128	
129	- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every edit of source code in the original tree starts from a failing test. The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The test and the fix may land in one commit. Why: the rule replaces one-off validation scripts, which no later build runs. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.
130	- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test's result is pass or fail, as the team designed the suites. A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. Why: when the suite's designers let a test pass without a further check, what it prints need not be checked.
131	- P-124 **The specification's examples are a step of the gate, and every one must pass.** `ant testSpecData` runs the examples extracted from `Specification/` under walk (F-114 says which 130 it runs), and the gate fails if any of them fails. When an example fails, the implementation is fixed: the example is not respelled to get around a gap in walk, and no list of examples allowed to fail is kept.
132	- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** `build.xml` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS` to 4 for the two suites, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`, so that every run of them uses four threads, whatever the calling shell sets. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.
133	- P-150 **No resident compiler is built.** A background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did, would save too little of the workers' time to be worth building (F-234), so the speed work goes to the checker itself (P-148). It is not tried again unless something significant changes.
134	- P-177 **QuickCheck is a testing tool that the project goes on relying on: it is to run on the compiled path after the switch-over, by its static choice of generators.** `QuickCheck` (`Library/QuickCheck.fss`) picks the generator for a property's static type, and imports no reflection. `ReflectiveQuickCheck` builds on it for generic properties: it picks random types for a property's static parameters through `Reflect`, whose 28 native bindings stay on walk's glue, for walk only (P-58, the exception for `Reflect`). - P-76 **An integer numeral has the Working Draft's type `NaturalNumeral` (P-174), which each of the eight number types converts from: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32`.** Where nothing fixes a type it is a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit (P-173). `NaturalNumeral` takes the place of `IntLiteral`, the name that the compiler's prelude and the interpreter's library gave the type, and `IntLiteral`'s own arithmetic goes, since an expression of numerals alone folds before the checker (P-173). Walk, before it runs the checker (P-12), converts an integer numeral from its exact value at each place that fixes a type, and elsewhere evaluates it at its default, which walk already gives it by its value (F-74). Walk gaps: coercion through tuple and varargs parameters (rows 395 and 511).
- P-77 **Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only, as the compiler's prelude declares them (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`).** Why: a JVM array has at most as many elements as the largest `ZZ32`. A range over another integer type is a static error. A loop whose counter needs a wider type runs over a `ZZ32` range and widens each element, as in `j: ZZ64 = i`. A range of rank 2 or 3 is a tuple of `ZZ32` scalar ranges. The public range traits, such as `Range[\I\]`, stay generic in their index type: the ranges of rank 2 and 3 extend them at pairs and triples of `ZZ32`.
- P-78 **`SUM` and `PROD` are one generic reduction each over the library's algebra, in place of the team's catch-all over `Number`, and take their identity from the static argument.** `SUM` is generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `PROD` over `MultiplicativeRing`. A reduction written with generators writes its static argument where nothing at the call fixes the element type. The compiled checker fixes it from the reduction's expected type, else from the type of its body, where a `SUM` or `PROD` leaves it out (F-364). It is written as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. A sum without generators is written as before, with no static argument: `SUM e` over a collection `e`, and the dot product `x DOT y`. `BIG MAXN`, `BIG MINN` and `BIG MINMAXN`, the team's `Number`-typed big operators for the maximum, the minimum and both, each with an identity, are gone; no program called them. `MAX` and `MIN` get no identity on the integers or the floats, so an empty `BIG MAX` or `BIG MIN` raises `EmptyReduction` (F-60: a maximum's identity is its type's least value, which a coercion into a wider type does not carry). Under walk, an empty `SUM` or `PROD` over another algebra, such as a user `AdditiveGroup`, still fails (row 436) until the specification's `HasIdentity` is built.
- P-79 **Every team demo is kept running as the tree changes.** The team demos are the programs in `ProjectFortress/demos/`; no suite or step of the gate runs them. If a change breaks a demo and the way to repair the demo is known, the batch that makes the change also rewrites the demo. A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. For example, the change that made `10^(-4)` an error (P-153, the integer power) also wrote `10.0^(-4)` in `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, and `10.0^(-6)` for `10^(-6)` in `npbft.fss`. A demo that fails for want of a feature is made to run again once the feature is built. So the demos known to fail today are to be respelled where the way is known. Under walk, the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reach their end (F-283). The compiled checker refuses `trips.fss` (row 817).
- P-80 **The specification's sign-refined number types are a superseded design: a program tests such a subset of a type at run time.** These types are the specification's subtypes by sign, such as positive ℚ, non-negative ℚ and non-zero ℚ, and the same refinements of the integers. The machine types `NN32` and `NN64` are separate types, not among them. The specification's number chapters now test a value's sign by comparison, and a float with two getters of `RR64`: `check` returns `Just(x)` for a finite `x`, `check_star` returns `Just(x)` for an `x` that is not a NaN, and each returns `Nothing` otherwise. The chapter that held the design, `Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex`, stays word for word, marked superseded by a callout in the form of every specification change (P-96), so that the original design stays on record. Their possible return belongs to P-62: once the `covariant` keyword is built, a worker tries to bring them back as covariant static parameters.
- P-153 **The integer power splits on the base: an integer base gives an integer or raises an error, and a float or rational base gives the fraction.** Each integer type's `^` returns its own type at every exponent. At a negative exponent, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code gives an integer power the type of its integer base at a signed exponent. Overloads choose by type, and no type tells a negative exponent from a non-negative one, since a signed integer or a numeral can be either. So the split is on the base, and the sign of the exponent is tested at run time, as the library tests a value's sign everywhere (P-80, run-time sign tests in place of sign-refined types). Row 441: the same rule on the compiled path, whose own powers give 0 at a negative exponent and a raw Java exception at a base of 0, and overflow silently or with a raw Java exception (row 523).
- P-159 **A float compared with a NaN answers: `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` give `false`, and `CMP` gives `Unordered`, on both paths.** On `RR64` and `RR32` the four ordering operators answer `false` when either side is a NaN, and `CMP` answers `Unordered`, as the team built them. `FloatingComparisonError` stays declared in both libraries, and nothing raises it. The specification's overview of operators said that this comparison threw that error, and the sentence before it that a rational comparison at 1/0 or 0/0 threw `RationalComparisonError` (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:283-288`). Both sentences are revised, in the form of Appendix I, to the rationals chapter's reading: 0/0 compares `false` "for compatibility with floating-point arithmetic", and the infinities are ordered (F-319). Row 672 closed with that edit. Why: a NaN test in software would slow the comparison against the hardware's own; measured, it is noise on today's boxed compiled path and costs 15 to 20 percent a comparison on unboxed doubles in Java, and whether it stops vectorisation is open (`perf-probes/nan-check-cost/REPORT.md`). The team built `false` and `Unordered` everywhere and never raised the error, and Java, Swift, Python's floats, Julia and Haskell all answer `false`.

The four fixed widths have the compiler prelude's `bitsAs…` getters. `narrow`, `widen`, `unsigned`, `signed` and `big` keep the low bits, each declared on every type where it applies, so that no call reaches one through a coercion. `ZZ`'s conversions out are its five getters; the callers of its `narrow` and `widen` (`Library/Format.fss`, `Library/QuickCheck.fss`, the demo `sudoku.fss`, the test `XXXZZNarrowRungP`) move onto `.asZZ32` or `.asZZ64` with their values unchanged. The specification states the getters and names beside `narrow`'s sentence in `basic-integers.tex`, drops `ZZ` from it, and gives an Appendix I entry. P-72 (`narrow` keeps the low 32 bits on the fixed widths), P-73 (fixed-width arithmetic raises) and P-74 (an exact conversion is implicit) stand. So `z.asZZ64` raises for a `ZZ` too large, and `unsigned` of a negative value keeps the low bits, with `x.asNN32` or `x.asNN64` as its check. Why: the team's later work, Steele's prelude, made `asZZ32` raise in 2011 and named the bits `bitsAs…` in 2012; the specification's general sentence says that an integer result that overflows throws `IntegerOverflow`; a plain name that checks beside a name that tells its loss is Swift's and Julia's pattern; and `ZZ`'s two are wrong code: its `widen` can narrow, and turns 2^63 negative.

Why: the team's compiler prelude declares `Number` with nothing in it (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:509`), and the specification does not ground the method: its sentence that names it on `Number` is the revival's revision.
