Why: the Working Draft keeps a numeral unconverted, since "converting it immediately to a floating-point number may lose precision", gives 3.125 "the rational value 3125/1000", has the library coerce a compound numeral to the rationals, and converts a static rational expression into a float with "at most one floating-point rounding error" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-173`); the curator reads it so: nothing is lost in `QQ`, and a float of fixed size takes one rounding.
- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174); `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` where it is a size (P-40), and a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's four numbers (P-174). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. `gg(5, w)`, with `gg` declared at `(ZZ32, T)` and at `(Any, Any)`, runs the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49). The parameter types of the declaration that a call runs are places that fix a type, and a numeral argument goes to the most specific declaration that takes it, by its own conversion if need be, with its default as the last resort: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, the numeral an `NN32` at `NN32`'s own `=` (P-46 gives the rule and its ground; row 1016 holds where walk departs, and row 1017 where both paths do). Why: the design completes the Working Draft's, whose numerals have types of their own so that a library decides by coercions how they meet other types (P-174 gives that ground). It bends P-26 in two places, the numeral types, whose names and static parameters are the Draft's (P-174), and the places that fix no type, where the compiler's prelude, the team's later word, keeps the numeral's own type; the curator takes the bend by his right to finish the specification. He declined exact defaults, `ZZ` and `QQ` (the 2012 restart gives `NN` and `QQ`, `literals.tick:25`), since microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would then be rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. The Draft's text that it contradicts, for Appendix I: numerals "not directly converted" and "polymorphic" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-141`) at places that fix no type, and a `nat` parameter usable wherever an `NN32` variable is (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:84-86`); P-174 names the binary chapter's, which it leaves out. What it keeps and changes in form: the judgement's section 3, but for the numeral types' form, which P-174 holds. Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1 to 6 and the 42 test programs of its appendix; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`.
- P-174 **A numeral's type exists only at compile time: the Working Draft's `NaturalNumeral` or, with a radix point, `RadixPointNumeral`, below `Numeral`, with its four numbers as static parameters; every number type, the library's too, takes a numeral through a coercion generic over the four numbers.** The four numbers are the digit count `n`, the digits after the radix point `m`, the radix `r` and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`), so `3.125` is a `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`; the four are naturals of any size, and read as values in a coercion's body they are exact integers, `ZZ`; this implementation's `NN32` bound (P-40) is for sizes. The coercion's body calls the type's constructor on values computed from the four numbers, as in `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = Interval(roundDown(v, r, m), roundUp(v, r, m))`, and the compiler instantiates it for the numeral and folds it (P-176). No numeral value exists when a program runs: a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type, and is written only as a coercion's or an operator's parameter type. A numeral has no sign: at a program's type `-3` is the type's own prefix `-` applied to the coercion's result for `3`, and a type without `-` refuses it; any other expression of numerals alone folds first (P-173) and reaches such a type only through its coercion from the folded value's type, such as `QQ` for `1/2`, since coercions do not chain. The design leaves out the binary chapter's numeral coercion and `opr ||` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1662`). Why: the Draft gives numerals types of their own so that "library designers [can] decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations", and has libraries define the coercions into integers and rationals (`literals.tex:132-148`); the curator finishes that design, in place of the implementations' `IntLiteral` (P-76) and `FloatLiteral` (P-172). Rows 960 and 981 hold where the tree departs: the digit count of `00.5`, and walk running a numeral type written in a `comprises` clause.

Walk fixes the coercion's static arguments from the numeral's four numbers and keeps the result for the place; it refuses a numeral only when the place runs, until it runs the checker (P-12). Before the switch-over the compiler's prelude carries this design (P-37), so that both paths give one value at one place. Why: a numeral is a constant of the program, and a JVM class file holds no object, so a field filled once at load is the nearest form of an object constant. Row 957 holds where the tree departs: a place whose type names a type parameter.
- P-178 **Each built-in number type is one `value object` under its own name, and walk's native number objects `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` go.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN64` and `RR64` are each declared `value object`, as `NN32` and `RR32` already are, in place of a trait with one native object below it, such as `trait ZZ32 comprises { Int }` with `value object Int extends ZZ32`. An object is a leaf, so no type of a program extends a built-in number type; a program's own number type extends `Number` (P-160). Compiled code can then hold a value of such a type as a bare JVM `int`, `long` or `double` (P-17), and both paths take this form before the switch-over: the one library by the merge, and the compiler's prelude by an exception to P-37, as for the numerals, which goes with the prelude. For the number types it replaces the pattern that P-164's reason names, a trait with walk's native object below it. Why: the two names are a duality between the two libraries, which the curator called a problem that the revival makes for itself by keeping it; the second names are walk's internals, which a program is not to see (P-167); and the compiler prelude's open trait lets a program's object extend `ZZ32`, which a bare `int` cannot hold (row 866, such a program compiles and dies when it runs). Detail: `reviews/carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md`, "Way D. One object per type: each number trait merged with its one object"; the merge as probed: `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/number-object-merge.md`, "What was built".

### Arrays and the model program

- P-84 **On the compiled path, the array of every number type is to be stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, and every array is to have the most efficient store that its element type allows; arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** `RR64` goes in a `double[]`, `ZZ32` in an `int[]`, and so on, for each number type that has a Java primitive type; `RR64`'s `double[]`, the model's, is the first case. Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, on extending the library in its own way). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The class loader, as it makes a generic instance's class, only renames the type parameter, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field; a loader that would, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), is unmeasured (F-18).
- P-85 **The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with the array decisions A, B and D.** The array design is the compiled path's design for arrays. The three questions: how the array factory chooses the store of each element type; whether the store also keeps the size as a field, beside the size in the type; and whether a factory for a size known only at run time returns the unsized `Array[\E,I\]`, whose type holds no size. These questions are apart from decisions A, B and D: decision A is how an array of a number type, made through the library's generic array traits, gets its unboxed store, `RR64`'s `double[]` first (P-84); B is where unboxed arithmetic happens; and D is the sizes in the model's own types (P-87). The whole preparation for the array work is to be done before the switch-over; only the work itself waits.
- P-87 **The model's text is the notation, and the vocabulary is repaired around it.** The model is microGPT's two programs; the vocabulary is the array operations that they are written in (`FlatArrays.fss` for C4, the flat program, and `FlatArrays2.fss` for the APL-style one). No operator in the model is replaced by a function call to pass an overload check, as a proposed repair once wrote `planeSum(mask, x)` for `mask + x`; the vocabulary changes instead. Any repair that changes a line of the model is shown to the curator as a diff before it is built. Decision D, still open and returning after the switch-over with the other array decisions (P-85), is such a diff: it gives C4's arrays sized types, in its vocabulary's signatures and in the model lines that these force (`explorations/reviews/decision-d-diff.md`; the patch itself is only in git, in the parent of `84aef6a4f`). Nothing of decision D is applied before microGPT compiles, after the switch-over.
- P-88 **The model's vocabulary leaves `+`, `-` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar to the library's scalar-extension block, and its diagonal keeps its own product.** The vocabulary, the array operations that microGPT is written in, declares none of these six operators, an array with a number on either side; the library's scalar-extension block, in `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, serves them. `Diag`, the vocabulary's diagonal matrix, extends `Matrix` and overrides `mul`, the method that the library's matrix product calls, so `diag(v) m` scales the rows of `m` without forming the matrix. This is what the type system promises: a diagonal is a kind of matrix, with a faster product of its own. Row 299 records what the general product costs on a diagonal: 13 to 54 times as much as scaling the rows. Since the diagonal is read-only, a read-only matrix trait, `ReadableArray2`, which `Array2` would extend as `Array1` extends `ReadableArray1`, is also wanted (row 798): it is a library change, not a definition in the vocabulary.
- P-89 **`fill` takes a value, `tabulate` a function.** On the library's arrays, `fill(v)` fills an array with the value `v`, even when `v` is a function, and `tabulate(f)` fills it with `f` applied to each index. The function form, formerly an overload of `fill`, takes Scala's name `tabulate`. Why: in every peer language that has `fill`, `fill` takes the value.
- P-90 **`Maybe`'s empty case is the team's parametric `Nothing[\T\]`, in the one library and the specification.** The bare `Nothing` is future work: it needs a `where` clause that binds a type variable in an `extends` clause, which neither path implements, and it is not tried before then. Gating row 331 on static-argument inference instead is parked.
- P-91 **What an object with no `asString` prints: its bare Fortress type name, walk's spelling, on both paths.** An object with no `asString` of its own prints its Fortress type name as walk spells it, such as `Box`, or `Box[\ZZ32\]` for an instance of a generic object, with no marker and no hash code. A debug marker, such as the Java class name that the curator first leaned to, belongs in `asDebugString` if one is still wanted, not in the printed form; walk's `asDebugString` prints `a Box: Box`. Row 363: an `asDebugString` that prints as walk's does, where the compiled one prints `Box`. Row 321: printing an object that declares or inherits a zero-argument member named `toString`, which overflows the stack. Once the compiled path reads the one library, every object inherits such a member, the `getter toString` of that library's `trait Object`, so every object with no `asString` meets the overflow.

### The specification's revision

- P-95 **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** When the revival changes the language, it updates `Specification/` with the change, so that the text and the implementation do not disagree. The original text and the reasoning are kept, so that route C stays open. Route C is the design that P-43 set aside: a nested number tower, under the forest rule of the team's 2012 patent applications (F-46 gives what a return to it would need). Every such change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). The unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, is never touched. Why: an open disagreement between the text and the implementation would confuse a reader.
- P-96 **A change of the specification is shown in layers, as the team showed its own changes in the 1.0 release of 2008 and in the working draft of 2009.** This form is the revision form. A callout that prints in every build marks each changed passage; a `\note` will not do, since a release build hides it. Appendix I's revival section has an entry for each change: its reason, its original text, what a return to route C would mean for it, or that it would be the same under route C (P-95 says what route C is), and the decision that it follows. The front matter has one paragraph on the revision, and a document in the repository holds the full reasoning. Citations call the unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, the Working Draft of February 2011: the copy is that draft byte for byte, and only its `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the 1.0 release (F-163). The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` gives each part in full, including what else an Appendix I entry holds.
- P-97 **The specification's examples that break the exclusion rule take the library's shapes, and each original stays, marked "Not allowed".** The Working Draft offered such examples as legal. Each now shows the shape that the library uses for the same thing, with the original beside it under the specification's own mark, "Not allowed". The specification states the rule, which it calls instantiation exclusion, once, in the two parts of Luchangco's Types chapter of 2012 (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`; P-25): `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` says which instantiations exclude each other, and `basic/traits.tex` says that a declaration may not extend two that do. The covariance example, a trait that extends other instantiations of itself, is rewritten and marked in the same way. Its callout adds one sentence: the type group's later design, in the same Types chapter, declares variance with a `covariant` modifier, which neither walk nor the compiled path implements (row 404 records the gap). The calculi of Appendix A keep their rules as the team wrote them, under a callout that they predate the rule.
- P-98 **`TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, so that the library's `BIG MIN` and `BIG MAX` work over total comparisons.** It does so in the library's api and component, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss`. Why: it is the library's own device, which its other ordered types use. The curator took it on the coordinator's recommendation. It stands and blocks no work.

A sentence that is true stays word for word. A sentence that is not true is cut, or changed only as far as makes it true. The revival adds no prose of its own there, and nothing on building the implementation, which the repository's `README.md` holds. Each change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). Why: text that describes what the implementation does not do misleads the reader, and a free rewrite puts the revival's text in the place of the team's.

### The suites and the gate

- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every edit of source code in the original tree starts from a failing test. The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The test and the fix may land in one commit. Why: the rule replaces one-off validation scripts, which no later build runs. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.
- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test's result is pass or fail, as the team designed the suites. A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. Why: when the suite's designers let a test pass without a further check, what it prints need not be checked.
- P-124 **The specification's examples are a step of the gate, and every one must pass.** `ant testSpecData` runs the examples extracted from `Specification/` under walk (F-114 says which 130 it runs), and the gate fails if any of them fails. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.

1	# Running and reviewing a batch
2	
3	The batch workflow is `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual, `climb-batch-workflow.md` beside it. Its stages run in this order: the scatter of the rungs, the rung workers, the skeptics, the judges and the repair round, the gather, the merged-diff review, the gate, and the commit stage. Read a stage's section of the manual when you reach it: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md#<heading>'`.
4	
5	**batch record**
6	: `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<N>.md`, written by the planner before the launch. Its rung sections are the workers' briefs; its other sections are for the curator.
7	
8	**base**
9	: Commit that the batch starts from.
10	
11	**gather**
12	: Stage that merges the rungs and folds their reports and record lines into the tree.
13	
14	**merged-diff review**
15	: Review of the gathered diff, beside the gate, of the records, the reserved points and the routing.
16	
17	**repair round**
18	: One round of fixes after the merged-diff review or the gate.
19	
20	**commit stage**
21	: Last stage, which commits the landed tree and runs the pass of `references/record.md`.
22	
23	**reserved point**
24	: Point that a batch record keeps for the curator, such as a model or APL line beyond the approved ones, or an interpreter output that a rung cannot explain.
25	
26	**revival page**
27	: Page that tells where the revival stands: `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/revival-story.md` and its rendered `revival-story.html`, published at the URL that `explorations/coordinator/tools/revival-page/update.py` names, with a GitHub Pages copy under `docs/revival-story/`.
28	
29	**checker count**
30	: Errors that the compiled checker reports on the interpreter's library, up to each component's first error.
31	
32	**distance**
33	: All the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library, which must reach zero before the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library. The gate's distance stage counts them (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh`), and FACTS holds the current value.
34	
35	## The go
36	
37	- The batches of PLAN's phase 3 run on a standing go, in PLAN's order. Launch each when the batch before it has landed and its own batch record has no open question.
38	- Put into a batch record every piece of work on PLAN's road that moves the project forward and is well defined: its decisions are taken. A new deliverable still waits for its go (`SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions"). A piece that is not well defined waits. A well-defined piece waits only if it would put the batch's merge at risk. Two rungs put it at risk if the gather cannot merge their edits of one file or one declaration cleanly. A pair that merges cleanly but changes one behaviour two ways, or where one needs the other's result, goes in one batch only if one lands only with the other (the manifest's `landsOnlyWith`).
39	- If a question that the batch record raises is consequential (`SKILL.md`), put it to the curator first. Otherwise decide it and put it on the review list. While the curator is away, overnight, take its recommended default and put it on the review list. If that default would reverse a decision of the curator, hold that batch, and launch the repair batch (`explorations/coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`) in its place.
40	- Have one Fable review read each coming batch record before the launch, with a go in advance. It is written for the curator in place of reading the record. Treat its questions as the batch record's.
41	
42	## The workflow
43	
44	- Between batches, improve the script and the manual where a batch showed a problem.
45	- Let every step spend the fewest workers that it needs.
46	- Build the base once, yourself, in a worktree where nobody compiles or runs (`args.baseBuild`). Every rung worktree is seeded from it (`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean.
47	- No stage runs a build, a suite or a measurement again on a code state that another stage ran, and no agent reads again a log that has not changed.
48	- Let the planner give each rung its mission briefing, from the territory map (`explorations/coordinator/map/`), in neutral words: "the decisions on record", not the curator's name. Require no answers from the worker about how it searched.
49	- At each landing, report the share of briefed agents that read the briefing at all. Aim for all of them. By the brief's order, none reads it in its first turn.
50	
51	## The roles
52	
53	- The skeptic checks a rung's result after its worker, and builds nothing to check. It reads from the worker's transcript whether the test came first and failed. It runs its own small programs on the rung's build, and on the base through `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh` with a private caches folder. Where the rung changes the compiled checker, the skeptic also runs the count stage itself, on the base build and on the worker's commits, as `fortress-repo`'s `compiler.md`, "The checker's time", gives a reviewer. That run is the one exception to this bullet and to the rule that no stage measures a code state again.
54	- It checks the result against the library's way, the ledger, sibling sites and the decisions on record, and fixes what it finds, test first.
55	- A judge rules only on a fix that the skeptic marks contested, on a rung that the skeptic refuses, or on a rung whose worker reported that it could not go on. The first ruling runs on Opus, a second on Fable (`judgeTier`). A settled fix lands with the review and the gate as its check. Reaching a reserved point, or a file outside what the rung's section of the batch record names, does not make a settled fix contested: it lands, and the point or the file goes on the review list. A point that cannot be undone holds the batch.
56	- No batch compares the printed outputs of the suites' test programs, and no baseline is run to compare against.
57	
58	## The checker count and the distance
59	
60	Until the switch-over lands, the gate of every batch reports the checker count and the distance. Neither turns the gate red.
61	
62	- If a rung's test is the checker count or the distance, it takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values.
63	- If every file that a rung changes lies outside what the two measures read, the rung runs neither and lists those files (`STAGE_BLIND`). Its skeptic checks the list against the branch's diff.
64	- The review after the batch ties every new or risen row of the count's table to a named rung edit.
65	- The gate's comparisons hide Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions. Put every difference that they hid on the review list. Put there too each line of the team's tests that a rung rewrote to keep its checked value, with its before and after.
66	
67	## Reserved points and repairs
68	
69	- A reversible reserved point does not hold the batch. The batch lands with the point's default, and the point goes on the review list.
70	- An output that the base already varies from run to run, with the test's verdict unchanged, is a ledger row.
71	- After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green. Its findings go on the review list, for the batch after. The review runs once in each batch.
72	- A repair after the gate runs the gate again only if it changes what the gate reads (its part in `fortress-repo`).
73	- If the gate over a merged batch is red, do not bisect. Find the cause as a whole, and rework that part in the merged batch. If the gate is still red after its repair, the batch does not land: put it to the curator at once, as a hold.
74	
75	## While it runs
76	
77	- At a boot, read the batch record's sections for the curator, the run's journal (`references/delegating.md`) at the run ID in the check-in file (below), and the times of its agents' transcripts in the session's `subagents/workflows/<run>/`.
78	- The rungs, their skeptics and their judges work in their own worktrees, and do not read the main tree. The gather and the stages after it work there, and the gather needs `git status --porcelain` to print nothing. So until the gather starts, commit in the main tree as usual, by named paths, and push at once. From the gather's start until the batch's push, change nothing there. Keep `origin/main` at or behind the main tree's head, or git refuses the commit stage's push. So push `main` from no other tree. From the main tree, push nothing that the batch committed: the commit stage pushes it.
79	- Before the launch, name the check-in file in the boot note: `<scratchpad>/batch<N>/checkins.txt`, where `<N>` is the batch's number. After the launch, write the run's ID and each armed check-in's ID in that file. If the scratchpad loses a check-in's ID, find the check-in again with `list_triggers`.
80	- Workers push to their own `wip/` branches as they go. A branch holds only what `main` is to hold (`fortress-repo`, its committing part).
81	- If a process stop or the usage limit ends the run, resume it (`references/delegating.md`). The limit drops no rung.
82	
83	## The landing
84	
85	The landing check is `ledger.py landing-check BASE`, run by the gather and by the merged-diff review on the batch's base. It reports a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test removed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status. A finding the base already had counts too. The gather clears each finding before its commit, through `rewrite`, `close` or `note`, or by a reworded entry. The merged-diff review clears any that is left in its corrections commit. So a batch lands only when the check prints nothing.
86	
87	The batch workflow holds the push when a point to report still acts against a decision on record after the repairs. Its result then gives `pushHeld` true, and `heldBy` lists the points. If the batch's push is held for the curator, take steps 1 to 3 at once on the local commits. Only these wait: the push, the parts of step 3's routing check that need the pushed hashes, and step 4, since the record-landing workflow pushes `main` itself. If `heldBy` names either of these, push only after the curator's go:
88	
89	- a step that cannot be undone;
90	- a change that still acts against the curator's word.
91	
92	For every other held push, this paragraph is the standing go. If the last line of step 3's review names no change, push the batch yourself, by `fortress-repo`'s committing part. If the line names a change, put it to the curator as a hold, and push only after the curator's go. The review's commit of step 3 goes with that push. Then run step 4.
93	
94	1. Sweep the batch agents' to-dos from the session's shared task list: `explorations/coordinator/tools/sweep-tasks.py --delete`. If another workflow still runs, add `--running`, which removes only the completed tasks. The agents write these to-dos themselves, and the harness shows the whole list to every agent.
95	2. Name each decision that landed in one line, and put the items for the curator on the review list.
96	3. Have one Opus reviewer, which only reads, check the landed changes against the decisions on record and the library's way; measure misses by kind, the briefing's use and cost, and re-measuring; and run the routing check (the manual, "After the landing: the coordinator's routing"). If the batch's push is held, have the reviewer end its review with one line. The line names each landed change that must not reach `main`, or says that there is none. Have the review's section on cost count the tokens written in three spans, each on its own. Give the reviewer each span as two times, read from the commits and the workflow journals:
97	
98	   - the landing work of the batch before: from its commit stage's last commit to the end of its record-landing workflow;
99	   - the preparation: from then to the launch of the batch under review;
100	   - the run: from that launch to its commit stage's last commit, which stands also while the push is held.
101	
102	   Have the reviewer count a span as `spend.py` from its start less `spend.py` from its end, over the same folders. A transcript then counts in the span where it last changed.
103	4. After the post-batch review is committed, run the record-landing workflow (`explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/README.md`). It brings FACTS, POSITIONS, INDEX, PLAN and the review queue in line with the landing. Its Land stage, the step that lands its commits on `main`, also pushes them. Then it runs the orientation workflow in update mode itself, on the entries that the landing added or changed. The orientation workflow writes new text for each section of `fortress-repo`'s `revival-changes.md` that these entries touch. Next, the workflow has the skill writer install the sections that the orientation judge accepts. The writer also brings in line the sentences of `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md` and other parts that the landing's changes to FACTS and POSITIONS made false, and no others. A new rule, or a change of a rule's meaning, is not made in the workflow: the writer lists it for you in its reports, `writer-1.md` and `writer-2.md` in `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/skills/`. After the workflow ends, judge each such rule on its merits: what it protects against what it costs, its ground, and whether the skill already covers it. Then take it or drop it. Give the rules that you take to your own skill writer. They land after their cold read and the writer's fixes (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method"). Name the rules that you dropped, with their reasons, in one line of the message that sends the curator the one line for the page of `fortress-repo` changes (below). The workflow runs a cold read of the writer's changes, and the writer fixes its flags. Then it has a worker update the page of `fortress-repo` changes (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method", step 7), and pushes the writer's commits, as its Land stage pushes the record's. Last, if every push went through, it updates the revival page with `update.py`, commits and pushes the files that the script names, and republishes the page. No step of yours comes between. Its result gives one line: the commits and the link of the page of `fortress-repo` changes (the README, "The skill update"), then the revival page's commit and version (the README, "The revival page"). If the landing made no sentence of the skill false and the orientation judge did not run, no writer starts, and the line names only the revival page. While the workflow runs, start no skill-writer task of your own on `fortress-repo`.
104	
105	   Then read the workflow's commits on `main`, as the README's "Landing its result" says. If the result's `stopped` is set, take the step that the README gives for it there, or, for the revival page, in "The revival page": a stopped push leaves the commits on the local `main`, for you to push or take off. If a page's agent could not publish, the line names that page's files and URL: publish them yourself by that URL. File the orientation update's held sections, in its `queue.md`, in the review queue. Ask whether you would have done anything differently. Tell the curator of its POSITIONS changes as `SKILL.md`, "Quiet times", says. Send the curator the one line for the page of `fortress-repo` changes (`SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions") when "Quiet times" allows: while the curator is away, hold it with the reports of skill changes. Once the reviews show the workflow sound, stop this review, and rely on what the workflow does.

298	## 2. For the curator
299	
300	### The words this record uses
301	
302	- **Walk** is the interpreter. The **compiled path** first checks a program's types with the **checker**, then writes JVM bytecode with the **code generator**.
303	- The **prelude** is the small library that the compiled path uses today. The **one library** is the interpreter's library. The **switch-over** is the move of the compiled path onto the one library, after which the prelude is deleted.
304	- Your decision P-33 says how the switch-over's work goes: first microGPT's **slice**, the parts of the one library that microGPT needs. The **selector** lets one compile command read the one library beside the prelude. Each problem that only the one library shows is then fixed as its own small change, with its own test, under the full check.
305	- A **wall** is a place where the compiler or the compiled library stops.
306	- A **rung** is one change. One worker builds it, and a second, the skeptic, checks it. A **run** is one launch of the batch workflow. The **gate** is the full check before a run lands.
307	- A **value object** is an object without identity: two with equal contents are the same value. No type can extend an object.
308	- A **payload class** is a small class written by hand in Java that holds a bare JVM `int`, `long` or `double`. Under the chosen form, the code generator writes the class of `ZZ32` itself, on top of the payload class `FZZ32`.
309	- The **ledger** is the list of known defects. A **row** is one defect. An **expected-failure test** is a test that is known to fail and is marked so.
310	- **microGPT** is the model program. No rung changes a line of it.
311	
312	### The go
313	
314	None yet. You asked on 13 November for this batch to be planned, and said that its start is not authorized. The coordinator launches nothing until you say so. Each fork below has a default. None needs your answer before the start: none bends a decision of yours, and none touches microGPT.
315	
316	### The two runs

318	- **Run 1, climb batch 33, six rungs:** S, D, V, Q, I and C.
319	- **Run 2, climb batch 33b, four rungs:** N, W, G and R, on run 1's landed tree.
320	- **Why two runs.** N, W, G and R need S on `main` first. N's table of names follows S's selector, and the tests of W, G and R compile programs under it. A rung cannot build on another rung of its own run.

## 2. For the curator

### The words this record uses

- **Walk** is the interpreter. The **compiled path** first checks a program's types with the **checker**, then writes JVM bytecode with the **code generator**.
- The **prelude** is the small library that the compiled path uses today. The **one library** is the interpreter's library. The **switch-over** is the move of the compiled path onto the one library, after which the prelude is deleted.
- Your decision P-33 says how the switch-over's work goes: first microGPT's **slice**, the parts of the one library that microGPT needs. The **selector** lets one compile command read the one library beside the prelude. Each problem that only the one library shows is then fixed as its own small change, with its own test, under the full check.
- A **wall** is a place where the compiler or the compiled library stops.
- A **rung** is one change. One worker builds it, and a second, the skeptic, checks it. A **run** is one launch of the batch workflow. The **gate** is the full check before a run lands.
- A **value object** is an object without identity: two with equal contents are the same value. No type can extend an object.
- A **payload class** is a small class written by hand in Java that holds a bare JVM `int`, `long` or `double`. Under the chosen form, the code generator writes the class of `ZZ32` itself, on top of the payload class `FZZ32`.
- The **ledger** is the list of known defects. A **row** is one defect. An **expected-failure test** is a test that is known to fail and is marked so.
- **microGPT** is the model program. No rung changes a line of it.

### The go

None yet. You asked on 13 November for this batch to be planned, and said that its start is not authorized. The coordinator launches nothing until you say so. Each fork below has a default. None needs your answer before the start: none bends a decision of yours, and none touches microGPT.

### The two runs

- **Run 1, climb batch 33, six rungs:** S, D, V, Q, I and C.
- **Run 2, climb batch 33b, four rungs:** N, W, G and R, on run 1's landed tree.
- **Why two runs.** N, W, G and R need S on `main` first. N's table of names follows S's selector, and the tests of W, G and R compile programs under it. A rung cannot build on another rung of its own run.
- **Why I is in run 1.** Rung N of run 2 edits the same method of the code generator. In run 1 no rung edits it.

### Run 1, rung by rung

Each program is shortened to the lines that matter.

**S. The selector.**

- What it changes: the commands. `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` makes the compile command read the one library, with a caches folder of its own. A new group of tests runs that way inside the full check.
- The program that fails today:

      q: QQ = 1/2
      println(q)

- Today: `fortress compile` stops: 'QQ is undefined.' The prelude has no `QQ`, and the compiled path reads only the prelude.
- After, with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`: it compiles. A program of one `println` compiles too. Running either still fails: the one library is not yet compiled to bytecode. That is a later batch's work (section 2, "What the batch leaves out").
- A program that names `Array1` still stops, at row 1061. Rung R of run 2 repairs it.

**D. A `typecase` arm at a name that means nothing.**

- What it changes: the phase that binds names, which both paths run.
- The program that runs wrongly today:

      v: Any = 2.5
      typecase v of Int => println("an Int") else => println("other") end

- Today: it prints `an Int`, on both paths, with no message. `Int` names no type since your merge (P-178).
- After: it is refused: 'Int is undefined.'

**V. Two generic forms that the code generator refuses.**

- What it changes: the code generator.
- The program that fails today:

      trait AnyC comprises { C[\E\] } where [\E\] cat(self, f: AnyC): AnyC end
      trait C[\E\] extends AnyC cat(self, f: AnyC): AnyC = self end
      object Ci[\E\](item: E) extends C[\E\] end

- Today: the compile stops: 'E is not in the kind env'. A second form stops the same way: a `typecase` inside a generic function, where an arm binds a value at a type that names the function's type parameters and then uses that value. Four declarations of the one library, among them `List`'s, stop at this wall.
- After: both compile and run as under walk.

**Q. `self` returned from an arm, a closure or a default body.**

- What it changes: the code generator, and the class loader for the third form.
- The program that fails today:

      trait Tord[\T extends Tord[\T\]\]
          lt(self, other: T): Boolean
          mx(self, other: T): T = if lt(other, self) then self else other end

- Today: it compiles. When an object of that trait runs it: 'VerifyError: Bad return type'. The one library's `MIN` and `MAX` have this form, so the first compiled program on the one library meets it. That is review-queue item 572. The coordinator took it into this batch without asking you. You can still undo that before the launch.
- After: it runs. A function expression that returns `self`, and a default body that calls a method on another value of the same type, also run.

**C. Four of the checker's small gaps.**

- What it changes: the checker.
- One program that fails today:

      x = do k: ZZ32 = 3
          4 end
      y: ZZ32 = x

- Today: it compiles, and the run dies: 'NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerBuiltin$v'. Three more gaps go with it: `x[5]^2` stops the compile; `tally: ZZ32 := 0` does not match the interface file's `var tally: ZZ32`; and in `(total: ZZ64, part) = pair()` the type of `total` goes unchecked.
- After: each compiles and runs as under walk.

**I. A method call on a value of two types at once.**

- What it changes: the code generator.
- The program that fails today, where `choose` has one declaration for each of two traits and the checker types `choose(m)` as both results at once:

      choose(s: S): LeftResult = LeftResult
      choose(t: T): RightResult = RightResult
      println(choose(m).left())

- Today: the compile crashes: 'ClassCastException: IntersectionType cannot be cast to NamedType' (row 540). The one library's `__filter` stops at this wall.
- After: it compiles and runs as under walk. The checker's typing does not change.

### Run 2, rung by rung

**N. The prelude's seven number types become value objects.**

- What it changes: the prelude, the code generator and seven run-time classes. `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32` and `RR64` become value objects in the prelude, as they already are in the one library. The code generator writes each type's class on top of a small hand-written class that holds the bare value. That is the form that the review of the carriers recommended, form 2, and the detail of your decision P-178.
- The program that fails today:

      object MyNum extends ZZ32 end
      println(MyNum + 1)

- Today: it compiles. When it runs: 'IncompatibleClassChangeError: ... FZZ32, because it is not an interface' (row 866).
- After: it is refused when it compiles: 'Invalid type in extends clause: ZZ32'. That is the answer of your decision.
- What else a program sees: `add(a: ZZ32, b: ZZ32)` beside `add(a: List, b: List)` over a program's own trait `List` is refused today, and compiles after (row 698).
- The probe: I built this form in a scratch tree. The seven types compiled. Programs with each type ran. Both compiled test tracks passed, 1,694 and 263 tests, except four tests whose answer the change itself gives. On the one library, the same form adds no refused declaration.
- One build serves both libraries for these seven types. So the numbers need no second set of run-time classes (review-queue item 521, below).
- The one library's seven take this form later, in the rung where the first program runs on the one library, so that their test can fail first. This rung's code generator already serves them.

**W. Two hidden functions, one class name.**

- What it changes: the code generator's names for function classes.
- The program that fails today, with the selector:

      same(xs: List[\ZZ32\], ys: List[\ZZ32\]): Boolean =
          (|xs| = |ys|) AND: (BIG AND [(a, b) <- xs.zip[\ZZ32\](ys)] a = b)

- Today: the compile stops: 'ZipException: duplicate entry: ...$\=fn@5\!23-66.class' (row 315). The compiler makes two hidden functions from that line, one for `AND:` and one for `BIG AND`, at the same place in the source, and names both after that place.
- After: it compiles. The one library's `=` on lists has this form, and the compiled `=` on two integers needs its class.
- Its run waits until the one library compiles whole.

**G. Functions with a variable number of arguments.**

- What it changes: the code generator.
- The program that fails today, with the selector:

      count(xs: ZZ32...): ZZ32 = |xs|
      println(count(4, 5, 6))

- Today: the compile stops: 'Can't compile VarArgs yet' (row 624).
- After: it compiles. The extra arguments become one array that cannot be changed, as under walk. The specification and its revision say so already, so there is nothing to decide.
- The one library's `assert`, `deny`, list constructor, `print` and `println` take arguments this way, and `println` stands on the path of every program.
- Its run waits until the one library compiles whole, so the rung is checked by the compile and by a reading of the bytecode.
- Against the prelude it stays refused, since the prelude has no array type (your P-37).

**R. A method found by its interface on the compiled path.**

- What it changes: the code that gathers a trait's methods.
- The program that fails today, with `B` a trait of another component that has `tag(self, s: String)`:

      object O extends B
          tag(self, n: ZZ32): String = "num"
      end

- Today: the compile stops: 'Not in the trait table: B'. With the selector, `a = array1[\ZZ32, 8\]()` stops the same way (row 1061).
- After: both compile. Under the selector, a program with an array compiles against the one library.

### Item 521, answered by the probe

Probe Y asked whether the second set of run-time value classes is a map of names over the first set, or files of its own.

- For the seven number types: neither, by the probe's reading. Their hand-written classes extend no class that the code generator writes, so one set can serve both. They still name the prelude's string type in one method, `asString`. The string's own rung must free that. No program has run to show it.
- For `Boolean`, `Char`, the flat string and the Java-backed types: files of their own. The two libraries give these types different shapes, an object in one and a trait in the other, so a map of names cannot serve.
- No decision of yours is needed. P-33 already names the second set as the mechanism. That work is for the batch after.

### The merge

- Rung S: one change of the commands, no code-generator file.
- Rungs V, Q and I edit the code generator's main file, `CodeGen.java`, in different methods. D, C and S share no file with them.
- In run 2, N, W and G edit the code generator's table of names, `NamingCzar.java`, and N, G and R edit `CodeGen.java`, each in methods of its own. None needs another rung of run 2.
- No two rungs of one run edit the same method. Rung I of run 1 and rung N of run 2 edit one method, the dotted call's code, and N is read again on I's landed code. The order and the files are in section 4, "The rule the rungs keep".

### The measures

- **Declarations of the one library that the code generator refuses** (F-34): 17, in 5 kinds, on today's code. The script prints 18: it counts one declaration twice.
  - Run 1: V should take the 4 that stop at its wall, and I the 1 of row 540, so 12, if nothing stands behind them. Behind `List`'s `ArrayList` stands a second crash, row 812's, which V also repairs. So 12 to 17.
  - Run 2: G should take the 10 of varargs. In the planner's probe, 8 of them then compiled, and 2 stopped at another wall, one of which may be varargs' own operator form. W should take the 2 of row 315. So 1 or 2 after run 2, if nothing stands behind the walls removed.

# Keeping the record

How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.

**history**
: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.

**pointer**
: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, with a few words on its subject: "It builds P-48, on a type parameter that a call does not fix."

**pass**
: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.

## What an entry is

An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.

- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
- A POSITIONS entry states the curator's meaning in the record's register, and every fact in it is correct. It is the smallest text from which a fresh worker or coordinator, with the skills loaded, decides right. Workers and you decide by it where the curator is not asked, so a wrong premise in it spreads to each of those decisions.
- Give as an entry's reason the ground of its own case, such as the specification's text, the library's code or a measurement. Never give a rule that holds for every decision, such as the team's later word (P-26).
- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it, and its review-queue item names that entry.
- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.

Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:

1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.

In a consolidation of FACTS, judge each entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail, or unresolved where evidence is still needed, and quote the passage that fails:

- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim, and the entry states the kind of its evidence and its uncertainty.
- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.

An entry that fails scope, evidence or consistency is not kept as it stands: reword it to what its support holds, or investigate where the support is unresolved. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:

- keep: every check passes;
- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording, and do not delete the fact meanwhile.

Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.

## Reading and writing

- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
- Commit the record file and its history together.
- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.

## The pass

Run the pass when a worker finishes, and before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. In a batch, the commit stage runs it, with this part quoted in its prompt. After a lone worker, you run it.

The pass owns each entry's final wording. A rung writes its findings as draft entries: the claim, its conditions, its evidence and what it means.

1. Write each new fact as an entry, or rewrite in place the entry that it changes. A rung writes its entries in a file `record.md` in its worktree, and the gather folds them in with `record.py apply`.
2. Give each change its provenance: the report section, the commit, and why.
3. Check each entry against its source, with bounded `grep`s:
   - The cited report section holds what the entry left out.
   - The entry keeps the source's scope: the path (walk or the compiled path), the call form (a dotted method call against a top-level call), the range of values and the conditions. Ask: does the entry let a reader conclude more than the evidence shows?
   - If a behaviour changed, grep FACTS for it, linked or not. Each entry that states it is updated, or says how it differs.
4. Cut any plan or status from each entry (above). If the cut text named a PLAN item or a review-queue item, check that the item names the entry.
5. Report each entry over 600 characters, with the question that keeps its extra sentence.

Run the same pass on POSITIONS at each landing, and when the curator replaces a decision.

## A consolidation

A consolidation runs the pass over whole sections. After a batch lands, the record-landing workflow consolidates its entries (`references/batch.md`, "The landing").

- In a consolidation, by hand or by the clarity or mining workflow, run a pilot of three or four entries first. Show their new texts to the curator as a page, each with its old text (`SKILL.md`, "Pages"). Run the rest on the curator's go. The pilot shows the curator the form: the length, the register, and what belongs in the history. The other checks, the pass's step 3, the tools' cold readers and the quiz, test only the meaning. The record-landing workflow takes no pilot, since it lands with no step of yours.
- Split each section into chunks of 20 to 32 entries.
- For each chunk, a Sonnet scout gathers each entry's report sections, its commits and the curator's dated words.
- An Opus writer reads this part, the chunk and the scout's file, and writes an apply file. It runs `apply` and `check --base` in its own worktree.
- You apply each file on `main`, run `check --base`, commit and push.
- Have Opus workers check each new entry by the pass's step 3. Run no Fable review of the entries.
- Have a fresh Opus worker answer a small quiz of decisions from the new entries, on the records at hand, without the curator. The decisions must stay as good, and the worker must follow the pointers when needed. If something critical is lost, find the middle ground entry by entry.

## The consolidation tools

Four Workflow scripts keep the record and the worker skill current and readable. Each one's README says how to run it and what to do with its output. Give a run only its arguments and the input files that its README names. Add no rules of your own over the tool's briefs, and change the briefs only where its README says to, such as their paths. If the briefs do not fit the job, propose their change to the curator. Put the open questions of the runs on the review queue.

Pick the tool by the job:

- To bring the record in line with a landing: the record-landing workflow (`references/batch.md`, "The landing"). Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/README.md`.
- To find whether a POSITIONS entry comes from the curator's words or from an agent's summary or default: the mining workflow. Its writer changes only a sentence that is false, stale or not the curator's. Run it on the entries that it has not traced, before the clarity workflow rewrites them. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/README.md`.
- To make entries read on their own, with their meaning kept: the clarity workflow. For FACTS, it first judges every entry by the six checks of "What an entry is", and rewrites only those marked reword or reorganize. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/README.md`.
- To correct the entries that a review's findings name: the clarity workflow, with `findings.md` in each chunk's folder, in the form that its README gives. An entry changes only where a finding names it, and grows only by what the correction needs.
- To keep `fortress-repo`'s revival part short enough to read whole: the orientation workflow. Its update mode runs after each landing. Run its consolidate mode when a cold read or the regression quiz shows that the part no longer reads whole, or when an update cannot keep it within the README's budget. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/README.md`.

## INDEX and the gap ledger

- Give each new note under `explorations/` one line in INDEX, from its header comment's first sentence.
- Put a run's working files in an `evidence/` folder beside its results file: its briefs, chunks and checks, and the worker reports that the results draw on. Move them there with `git mv` once the results are judged. Only the results file gets an INDEX line. `check-index.sh` skips evidence folders. Do not add a folder's name to its list to let the folder pass.
- The gap ledger keeps its rows in topic sections. A row keeps its number for good. `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` is the only way to write it. Other views, such as `explorations/apl/lessons.md`, are derived from it.
- Split a rewrite of the ledger among small workers, each with a slice of rows that it can hold. Run a duplicate search first, as its own step.
- Ask the curator before you regroup the ledger's rows or derive its views again.

1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
55	
56	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
57	
58	## Reading the record
59	
60	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
61	
62	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
63	
64	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
65	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
66	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
67	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
68	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
69	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
70	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
71	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
72	
73	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
74	
75	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
76	
77	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
78	
79	## Writing to the record
80	
81	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
82	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
83	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
84	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
85	  - what it means for the work;
86	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
87	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
88	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
89	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
90	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
91	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
92	
93	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
94	
95	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
96	
97	To add a row:
98	
99	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
100	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
101	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
102	
103	To change a row:
104	
105	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
106	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
107	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
108	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
109	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.
110	
111	## The repository's history
112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
114	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
115	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
116	- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
117	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
118	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
119	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.
120
